sens: A man living during the time of the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah
Father of the prophet Zechariah, witness of the prophet Isaiah
H3000.detail: Berekiah is a minor character in the Old Testament, mentioned only once in Scripture. He is the father of the prophet Zechariah, who was called to serve as a witness to the prophet Isaiah during the reign of King Ahaz of Judah. His name appears in Isaiah 8:2, where Isaiah says: "I took trustworthy witnesses, the priest Uriah, and Zechariah, son of Berekiah." These men were chosen to attest to the words and actions of Isaiah during this critical period in the history of the kingdom of Judah.
H3000.origine: The name Berekiah means "Jehovah blesses" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: "berek" which means "blessing" or "to bless," and "Yah" or "Jahu," a diminutive of the divine name Jehovah. This type of theophoric name was common in Israel and expressed trust in the blessings of the Lord. The Hebrew word is related to the root "barak," which means "to bless."
H3000.emploi: Berekiah appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 8:2, where he is identified as the father of Zechariah. This man lived during the time of the Divided Monarchy, probably in the 8th century B.C., during the reign of King Ahaz of Judah and during the ministry of the prophet Isaiah. His role was to serve, alongside Uriah the priest, as an official witness to the prophetic acts and words of Isaiah. Although he is not well known, his appearance in this passage shows that he was a person of trust and established reputation in the religious and civil life of Judah.

sens: To lose all moisture, to become dry
To cease to flow, to run dry (for water)
To wither, to lose vigor (for a plant)
To be rendered powerless, to wither (in a figurative sense)
H3001.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: something loses all its moisture and becomes dry. This is what happens to the waters of the flood when they recede from the earth (Genesis 8:7), or to a stream that dries up for lack of rain (1 Kings 17:7).

2. For water or a watercourse: to stop flowing, to disappear completely. Job says that water flows and dries up (Job 14:11), and the prophet announces the drying up of the rivers of Egypt (Isaiah 19:5).

3. For a plant or grass: to lose its freshness and strength, to wither and then die. The grass flourishes in the morning but dries up in the evening (Psalms 90:6), the branches dry up and are broken (Isaiah 27:11).

4. In a figurative sense, speaking of a people or a person: to lose all vigor, all ability to bear fruit. Ephraim is struck, its root has become dry and it will bear no more fruit (Hosea 9:16). This is the image of divine punishment that renders one barren.
H3001.origine: The Hebrew verb yavesh describes the natural and observable process of drying up: something loses its water, its vital moisture. The root evokes the idea of absence of water, deprivation of what sustains and nourishes life and growth. In Hebrew, what is dry (yavesh) is opposed to what is alive, fresh, and capable of bearing fruit. The word appears in the Bible to describe both natural phenomena (the drying up of a watercourse, the withering of a plant) and situations that symbolize judgment, infertility, or spiritual death.
H3001.emploi: This verb appears 52 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical books, the Psalms, the Prophets, and the wisdom literature. It first describes concrete facts: the waters that recede (Genesis 8:7), the streams that dry up (1 Kings 17:7), the plants that wither (Psalms 90:6). But it gains deeper meanings: in the Psalms and among the Prophets, drying up becomes an image of misfortune, curse, and powerlessness. Isaiah uses it to describe the fleeting nature of all flesh in the face of God's word (Isaiah 40:7-8), while Jeremiah paints a land dried up by sin (Jeremiah 23:10). Hosea uses it as an image of spiritual sterility: Ephraim whose dry root will bear no more fruit (Hosea 9:16). The word can also refer to the divine action that dries up waters or withers plants to fulfill His judgment.
H3001.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that spiritual life needs a source of living water, just as a plant needs rain. Drying up symbolizes distance from God, a break with what nourishes the soul. Conversely, remaining attached to God's word and His love means staying fresh and fruitful. This image helps to understand why sin and unfaithfulness lead to inner sterility, while obedience maintains a fertile and abundant life.

sens: Lacking moisture, water
Having lost its natural moisture
Lifeless, without vigor
Exhausted, drained of strength
H3002.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: something that lacks water or moisture. The dried grapes of Numbers 6:3 are grapes from which the water has evaporated, preserving them. It is a stable state, a transformation of the fresh product.
2. An object that has lost its natural moisture becomes fragile and lifeless: a dried leaf (Job 13:25) breaks easily, a dry tree (Ezekiel 17:24) can no longer produce life. The image is one of decay.
3. In a figurative sense, dryness describes exhaustion or lack of resources. In Numbers 11:6, the dry soul of the people means they are at their wits' end, drained, without hope — they see only the monotonous manna and their hearts are empty.
4. The dried skin of Lamentations 4:8, clinging to the bones, shows extreme physical degradation: it is the visible sign of suffering and the approaching death.
H3002.origine: The Hebrew verb yavesh comes from a root that describes the drying up, the gradual desiccation. The basic image is that of water flowing or evaporating, leaving the matter lifeless. It is a process: something living and moist gradually becomes dry. The same root appears in several forms, some describing the active drying (to make dry) and others the state of dryness.
H3002.emploi: This word appears about ten times in the Old Testament, mainly in the poetic and prophetic books. It first denotes the objective state of things: the dried grapes one eats, the dead leaves. But it quickly takes on an emotional and spiritual significance: the soul dried up by lack, the heart empty of hope. Ezekiel uses it to speak of divine restoration (the dry tree revives), showing that dryness is not permanent. In Lamentations, it depicts the physical distress of the besieged. It is a word that moves from the concrete to the metaphorical without rupture: the dryness of the body reflects that of the soul.
H3002.portee: For the believer, dryness can evoke times when faith, strength, or joy seem exhausted. But as Ezekiel shows, God can transform the dry tree into a green tree: dryness is never the final word. This word invites us to view our moments of inner emptiness not as permanent states, but as calls to renew our expectation of God.

sens: city of Gilead, in Transjordan
site of a miraculous deliverance by Saul
city with heroic inhabitants
H3003G.detail:
1. Jabès is a city located in Gilead, beyond the Jordan, in the territory of the tribes of Israel. Its name literally means "dry" in Hebrew, probably referring to the arid geography of the region.
2. Jabès becomes famous when the Ammonite Nahash besieges it and threatens its inhabitants with servitude. Saul, inspired by the Spirit of God, gathers an army and delivers the city in a single night (1 Samuel 11:1-11), marking the beginning of his reign and his recognition as a military leader of Israel.
3. The inhabitants of Jabès demonstrate remarkable loyalty: after Saul and his sons are killed in the battle of Gilboa, the men of Jabès risk their lives to retrieve the bodies of the king and his son Jonathan from the walls of Beth-Shan, and honor them with a worthy burial (1 Samuel 31:11-13).
H3003G.origine: The name Jabès comes from the Hebrew yāveš, which means "dry." This name reflects the geographical character of the Gilead region, a semi-arid area beyond the Jordan. According to historical geography, Jabès would correspond to the present-day Wadi Yabès.
H3003G.emploi: Jabès appears ten times in the Old Testament, primarily in 1 Samuel 11 and the following chapters, as well as in Judges 21 and 1 Chronicles 10. The city comes into historical view during the siege by Nahash, an event that propels Saul to power. It reappears at the end of Saul's reign when its inhabitants undertake the courageous act of giving a burial to the remains of the king. These accounts make Jabès a symbol of loyalty to divine institutions and to Israel.
H3003G.portee: The story of Jabès teaches the power of deliverance by God acting through a consecrated leader: Saul becomes king not through personal conquest, but by rescuing a distressed people. It also illustrates the recognition of those who have protected us, even after their death: the inhabitants of Jabès honor Saul because he saved them. These acts of loyalty and gratitude remain a model for the people of God.

sens: Father of Shallum, king of the Northern Kingdom
Man from the kingdom of Israel during the divided monarchy
H3003H.detail:
1. Jabesch is the father of Shallum, who became the 15th king of the Northern Kingdom (Israel). Shallum reigned only one month before being overthrown and killed by Menahem (2 Kings 15:13-14).
2. Jabesch himself was a man from the kingdom of Israel living during the time of the divided monarchy, during the reign of King Uzziah of Judah (2 Kings 15:10).
H3003H.origine: The name Jabesch means "dry" or "dried up" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking an arid region or a physical characteristic. It shares its root with the Hebrew word that denotes dryness or aridity.
H3003H.emploi: Jabesch appears three times in the account of 2 Kings 15, solely to be identified as the father of Shallum. These three mentions occur during the short and turbulent period when Shallum ascended to the throne of the North: his coup against King Zechariah, his own one-month reign, and his assassination by Menahem. Jabesch is never described by his own actions; he is known only through his son.

sens: City of Gilead, east of the Jordan
H3003I.detail: Jabès is a city located in Gilead, a mountainous region east of the Jordan. Its name means "dry" or "arid" in Hebrew, likely evoking the desert-like character of this border region. The city appears at crucial moments in Israel's history: during the judgment of the tribes in Judges 21, when the assembly of Israel sends twelve thousand soldiers against its inhabitants; during the siege by Nahash the Ammonite in 1 Samuel 11, where Saul comes to its aid; and when its inhabitants, grateful to King Saul who saved them, go to meet his body after his death to pay their last respects (1 Samuel 31:11 and 2 Samuel 21:12).
H3003I.origine: The name Jabès comes from the Hebrew yavesh (יָבֵשׁ), which literally means "dry." It is a geographical description: the city is situated in an arid and mountainous region of Gilead. The same Hebrew word is used in the Bible to denote drought and aridity (for example, when speaking of dry land or a desert).
H3003I.emploi: Jabès is mentioned ten times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the books of Samuel and Judges. It first appears in Judges 21:8-10, where it is the target of a punitive attack because its inhabitants did not participate in the assembly of Israel at Mizpah. It later becomes famous for the siege it suffers from Nahash the Ammonite (1 Samuel 11:1-9), a siege that Saul lifts by achieving a great victory. This deliverance creates a bond of gratitude between Jabès and Saul: years later, after the king's death in the battle of Gilboa, the inhabitants of Jabès risk their lives to retrieve his body from the hands of the Philistines and give it an honorable burial (1 Samuel 31:11 and 2 Samuel 21:12).
H3003I.portee: Jabès illustrates how a small city and its inhabitants can play a pivotal role in the history of God's people. It also shows loyalty and gratitude: the people of Jabès do not forget that Saul saved them, and they honor him despite his defeat. It is an invitation to honor those who have helped us, even in adversity.

sens: emerged land, not covered by water
dried, arid land
H3004.detail:
1. Dry land refers to emerged lands, the continent as opposed to water. It is the solid ground on which one can walk. In the creation account, God separates the waters so that "the dry appears" (Genesis 1:9): thus He creates a habitable space. During the crossing of the Red Sea, the children of Israel "went into the midst of the sea on dry ground" (Exodus 14:22), walking on ground cleared of all water — an image of divine deliverance.
2. Dry land can also refer to arid, parched land lacking water and life. In Isaiah 44:3, God promises to pour out water "on the dry land" to symbolize the renewal of the people by His Spirit. The context shows that this lack of living and moist land contrasts with the blessing of water and the Spirit that God will grant.
H3004.origine: The Hebrew word yabasha comes from a root meaning "to dry up," "to become dry." It describes the state of the soil when water is absent. The same root produces the adjective "dry" (yabesh) and the verb "to dry." This word refers to the fundamental biblical image: life arises from the separation of water and soil, from the earth emerging from aquatic chaos.
H3004.emploi: This word appears 14 times, mainly in the creation and exodus narratives. It first appears in Genesis 1 during creation, where God brings forth the land from the water to create a habitable space. It powerfully returns in chapters 14 and 15 of Exodus for the crossing of the Red Sea: the children of Israel walk on dry ground in the midst of the waves, making this miraculous dry land a sign of God's power and deliverance. It is also found in Isaiah 44:3 applied to dry land awaiting rain, an image of the people waiting for renewal. Jonah 1:9 and 2:11 use it for the dry land that the prophet sees or asks to see again.
H3004.portee: This word reminds us that God creates a habitable world for man, and that He masters the waters. Walking on dry land in the midst of the Red Sea becomes for the believer a sign that God removes obstacles and creates an improbable path. It is an image of supernatural deliverance and trust in the One who commands nature.

sens: Man of the tribe of Issachar, son of Tola
H3005.detail: Jibsam is a man of the tribe of Issachar, living during the time of the wilderness after the exodus from Egypt. He is one of the sons of Tola, who is himself a son of Issachar (1 Chronicles 7:2). Along with his brothers Uzzi, Rephaja, Jeriel, Jachmaï, and Samuel, he is mentioned as a chief of the household and a valiant man of his generation.
H3005.origine: The name Jibsam means "pleasant" or "agreeable" in Hebrew, formed from a root expressing sweetness or delight. It is a typical name among the families of Israel in ancient genealogies.
H3005.emploi: Jibsam appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:2. He is listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Issachar, enumerated among the sons of Tola who were heads of paternal households and valiant warriors during the time of King David. Although little known, his inclusion in this genealogical list shows the importance that Scripture places on each lineage of Israel.

sens: the dry land, as opposed to water or the sea
the soil, the habitable surface of the world
H3006.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to dry land, that is, the terrestrial surface in contrast to water. This is why in Exodus 4:9, it is contrasted with the water of the Nile: Moses must pour this water "on the land" to turn it into blood. The idea of "dry" and "solid" is at the heart of the word.
2. More broadly, it refers to the soil, the habitable surface of the world that God created. In Psalm 95:5, the sea belongs to God "and the land also, His hands have formed it" — this is the visible creation, the realm of the living, formed by God Himself.
H3006.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew-Aramaic root meaning "to be dry" or "to dry up." This root evokes the idea of what is firm and stable, as opposed to moisture or blur. Yabbeshet ("land") is closely related to the biblical concept of "dry" as that which emerges from the primordial waters — seen in the Genesis account where God says, "Let the dry land appear" after separating the water from the sky from that which covers the ground.
H3006.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. The first time in Exodus 4:9, in the context of the signs that Moses must perform before Pharaoh: he transforms the water of the Nile into blood "on the land," showing that God's power extends beyond the sacred waters of Egypt to the very ground itself. The second occurrence is found in Psalm 95:5, a hymn of praise where the psalmist affirms that the land and the sea belong to the Lord, both created by Him. In both cases, the word emphasizes the physical, tangible reality of the created world.
H3006.portee: This word reminds the believer that everything visible and created — water and land, the moist and the dry — belongs to God and remains under His sovereign control. No earthly power, not even that of Pharaoh, escapes His authority. The dry land we tread on every day is the work of His hands.

sens: the solid matter of the earth, the soil
the habitable surface of the world, all the continents
humanity living on earth
H3007.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the very substance of the soil, dry land as opposed to water — the tangible matter that forms the continents and on which we walk.
2. In a broader sense, it refers to all the inhabited lands, the known world considered as a geographical whole. This sense is found in Daniel 2:10, where the king says that there is no one on the "earth" who can interpret his dream: he speaks of the entire inhabited earth, of the whole civilized world of the time.
3. By extension, the word also refers to the inhabitants of the earth, humanity itself — that which lives and breathes on this earth.
H3007.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of dryness and solidity. The basic image is that of dry land, the stable and solid ground in contrast to the waters. This is why the Bible sometimes uses this word to oppose land to sea: the "earth" is what is dried up, habitable, firm. This same idea is found in other Hebrew words of the same family that express aridity or cultivated land.
H3007.emploi: This word appears once in the provided texts, in Daniel 2:10. In this context of the book of Daniel — where the king of Babylon asks his wise men to interpret a dream he has forgotten — "earth" means the entirety of the known civilized world. The Chaldeans assert that no man on all the earth has the power to do what the king demands. The word expresses here the idea of universal authority, without geographical limits: it refers to an entire world.
H3007.portee: This word reminds us that we live on a concrete, solid earth created by God. It brings us back to tangible reality: we are not disembodied spirits, but beings who inhabit a place, who walk on the ground, who are rooted somewhere. In the context of Daniel, the word also speaks to us about the extent and limit of human power: even the greatest sages of the earth can do nothing without God.

sens: One of the twelve explorers sent by Moses into Canaan
Representative of the tribe of Issachar among the spies
H3008G.detail:
1. Jigual is one of the twelve men that Moses chose to explore the land of Canaan before Israel's entry. Each tribe sends a representative, and Jigual represents the tribe of Issachar. His name literally means "He redeems," which evokes the power and deliverance of God (Numbers 13:7).
2. Like all the explorers, Jigual's role is to scout the terrain, the cities, the fertility of the land, and the strength of its inhabitants before the people advance. Although the Bible does not recount any of his specific actions during the mission, his name appears in the list of these twelve trustworthy men chosen for this crucial task.
H3008G.origine: The name Jigual comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to redeem" or "to loose," expressing the idea of divine deliverance. This name belongs to a family of Hebrew words related to redemption and liberation, central themes in Israel's history. The name reflects trust in God's saving power, which was particularly significant for a man chosen to explore the promised land.
H3008G.emploi: Jigual appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 13:7, in the list of the twelve spies sent by Moses. He is identified as the son of Joseph and representative of the tribe of Issachar. Although his name is preserved in Scripture, the Bible does not report anything about his personal reaction to the discouraged report of the other explorers or his role in the events that followed. He remains a secondary figure in this historical mission.
H3008G.portee: Jigual reminds us that every believer, even if their role seems discreet or poorly documented, is chosen by God for a particular mission. His presence in this list of spies shows that God takes account of each one and that every tribe has its part in the advancement of the people toward their destiny. It is an invitation to faithfully accept the task entrusted to us, even if it never receives prominent recognition.

sens: One of David's warriors, son of Nathan of Zobah
H3008H.detail: Jigueal is a warrior who was among the valiant men serving King David. He was the son of Nathan, from Zobah (a region of Aram in Syria). His name appears in the list of David's thirty-seven elite warriors, recorded in 2 Samuel 23:36.
H3008H.origine: The name "Jigueal" comes from Hebrew and literally means "He redeems" or "He redemption." It bears the mark of a confession of faith: the father who gives this name to his son recognizes in God the one who redeems and delivers. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the affirmation of faith in God's saving action.
H3008H.emploi: Jigueal is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:36, in the role of a warrior of King David. No other information is given about his life or particular exploits. The Bible simply records him as part of those valiant men who surrounded David and served him, and that is enough to honor him.

sens: Man of the time of the divided monarchy, descendant of the tribe of Judah
H3008I.detail: Jigueal is a man of the people of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Schemaeja, who is himself the son of King Zedekiah. He has brothers Hattush, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat (1 Chronicles 3:22). His name means "He redeems," expressing confidence in divine redemption.
H3008I.origine: The name Jigueal comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to redeem" or "to deliver." It evokes the action of God who frees His people from servitude and purchases them for Himself. This name reflects hope in God's intervention to save His people.
H3008I.emploi: Jigueal appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:22, in the genealogy of the royal house of Judah. He is listed among the sons of Schemaeja, a genealogy that traces back to Zerubbabel and the return from exile. His inclusion in this list shows that he survived or lived after the exile, as a descendant of the kings of Judah.

sens: to work the land, to plow it to grow crops
to be a farmer, a tiller of the soil
H3009.detail:
1. The verb describes the concrete action of working the land, preparing and maintaining it to produce crops. It is the work of the farmer who plows his field. In 2 Kings 25:12 and Jeremiah 52:16, during the fall of Jerusalem, Nebuzaradan leaves "some of the poorest of the land" as "tillers": these men were to remain behind to cultivate the lands abandoned by the exiles and maintain the vineyards.
2. By extension, the word designates one who performs this work: a tiller, a farmer, a peasant attached to the land. It is a social condition, that of the man who lives by the work of the fields, humble and indispensable.
H3009.origine: The verb יָגַב (yagav) belongs to the family of Hebrew words related to the work of the land and agriculture. Its root evokes the idea of cultivating, of putting the land to use. The biblical context shows that this work was considered fundamental to the life and survival of the people, especially after national catastrophes like the Babylonian exile.
H3009.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in two parallel and identical passages: 2 Kings 25:12 and Jeremiah 52:16. These two verses describe the same historical event, the capture of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. by Nebuchadnezzar. After the destruction of the temple and the deportation of the elites, the chief of the Babylonian guards decides to leave behind some of the poorest to cultivate the lands and vineyards. These tillers represent those who will remain to maintain the agricultural resources of the occupied land.
H3009.portee: This word reminds us that the work of the land is a fundamental element of human life and the economy of God's people. Even in judgment and exile, God provides for material survival through work; the "poor" left to cultivate are not abandoned to death but remain rooted in the land and its resources. It is a lesson of providence and continuity, even in the darkest hours.

sens: cultivated land, land prepared for sowing
a piece of land belonging to a person or family
real estate, agricultural inheritance
H3010.detail:
1. The word designates cultivated land, prepared by plowing to receive sowing. It is a field that has been worked, as opposed to wild or fallow land. In Jeremiah 39:10, after the destruction of Jerusalem, Nebuzaradan leaves the poorest some vineyards and fields—productive lands that will allow them to live.

2. The field is also a property, a piece of real estate that belongs to a family and can be passed down as an inheritance. In Israel, land was the basis of wealth and social stability: giving fields to the poor is offering them a means of subsistence and dignity.
H3010.origine: The Hebrew word yagev comes from a root that evokes the idea of plowing and working the land. It specifically designates a field that has been plowed or cultivated, as opposed to raw or unproductive land. It is a concrete word from the agricultural vocabulary of ancient Israel, where agriculture was the dominant activity and the source of all wealth.
H3010.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 39:10. It is a word from the Babylonian Nebuzaradan, who applies a policy of selective deportation after the fall of Jerusalem: he deports the notables and leaves behind the poorest with vineyards and fields to cultivate the land. This usage shows that the field was considered a basic asset, an integral part of the agricultural heritage.
H3010.portee: This passage reminds us that, in the Bible, the land is a gift from God meant to nourish His people. Even in the midst of judgment, God does not leave His children without resources: the poor receive fields to live. This invites Christians to recognize that the work of the land and material resources are forms of God's care for His creatures.

sens: Fortified city of Transjordan, built and controlled by the tribe of Gad
H3011.detail: Jogbeha is a city located east of the Jordan, in the territory assigned to the tribe of Gad during the division of the Promised Land. Its name means "lofty," which likely reflects its geographical position at a height. The city was fortified, meaning protected by walls and defenses, as indicated in Numbers 32:35 where it is listed among the cities that Gad built and strengthened. It held strategic importance: during the pursuit of the Midianite army by Gideon and his three hundred men, Jogbeha and its surroundings served as geographical landmarks to locate the unsuspecting enemy camped (Judges 8:11).
H3011.origine: The Hebrew name יׇגְבְּהָה (yog.be.hah) derives from the root meaning "height" or "elevation," evoking a place situated on a height or overlooking a plateau. This type of descriptive and topographical geographical name was common in Canaan: it designated cities by their physical position in the landscape.
H3011.emploi: Jogbeha appears twice in the Bible. First in Numbers 32:35, it is mentioned as one of the cities that the tribe of Gad built and fortified during its settlement in Transjordan, alongside other strongholds like Atroth-Shophan and Jaazer. It reappears in Judges 8:11 during the account of Gideon's victory over the Midianites: the city serves as a geographical landmark to locate the enemy army's camp, which believed itself to be safe. These two mentions show that Jogbeha was a well-known fortress and an important strategic position in the Gadite region.

sens: man of God during the time of Josiah
H3012.detail: Jigdalia is a man of God mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time of King Josiah. He is the father of Hanan, and his house in Jerusalem contained a room that the prophet Jeremiah used to teach the Rechabites (Jeremiah 35:4). His name means "the Lord is great," reflecting the piety of his family.
H3012.origine: The name Jigdalia literally means "Jehovah (the Lord) is great." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "gādal" (to be great, to grow) and "Yah" (short form of the divine name). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common among pious Hebrews.
H3012.emploi: Jigdalia appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 35:4. He is presented as a man of God and the father of Hanan. The context shows that his house was respected in Jerusalem and that it had a reserved room, suggesting that he was an important spiritual figure. Jeremiah brought the Rechabites there to test them by offering them wine, to demonstrate their faithfulness to the command that their ancestor Jonadab had given them.

sens: Causing suffering or pain to someone
Making someone sad, overwhelmed with grief
Humiliating, reducing someone to helplessness
Experiencing pain or grief oneself
H3013.detail:
1. To afflict primarily means to cause physical or moral suffering to someone: to overwhelm them with blows, harsh words, or misfortunes. Job says to his friends: "How long will you afflict my soul and crush me with your words?" (Job 19:2) — he accuses them of harming him with their reproaches.

2. The word also designates the state of one who is consumed by grief, who suffers internally. The virgins of Zion are "afflicted" in mourning for their people (Lamentations 1:4): they are plunged into sadness and despair.

3. To afflict can also mean to humiliate, that is, to reduce someone to helplessness and dominate them. The Lord has "humiliated" Jerusalem by delivering her to her oppressors (Lamentations 1:5): she has lost her power and honor.

4. More rarely, the word expresses the suffering that one endures oneself. This is the sense of the participle "afflicted" — one who suffers under the weight of misfortunes: "Look and see if there is any pain like my pain, which has been inflicted on me!" (Lamentations 1:12).
H3013.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of pressure, of weight that crushes. It is related to the image of the burden imposed on someone to dominate or punish them. The word appears mainly in the books of lamentation and in biblical poetry to describe inflicted or endured suffering.
H3013.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Lamentations (where destroyed Jerusalem speaks of her affliction) and in other passages of suffering or judgment. In Job 19:2, it is the friends who afflict; in Isaiah 51:23 and Lamentations 1:5, it is the oppressors. The Lord also "afflicts" (Lamentations 1:12 and 3:32), but His motivation is justice, and He tempers His affliction with mercy: "When He afflicts, He has compassion according to His great mercy" (Lamentations 3:32). The word always carries a nuance of moral or physical violence.
H3013.portee: This word reminds us that suffering is not abstract — it is inflicted or endured concretely. It helps the reader see that God does not afflict out of cruelty, but sometimes out of justice and correction (Lamentations 3:32-33). For the one who suffers, the word provides a language to express their true pain and call upon God for compassion.

sens: Removing something from the way
Making an obstacle disappear
Pushing away, rejecting
H3014.detail:
1. The word describes the action of removing or taking something away — here, literally, the body of Amasa is removed from the road so that the soldiers can pursue their enemy (2 Samuel 20:13). It is a practical and physical act: removing from the road what blocks it.
2. By extension, to remove means to make disappear or take away what hinders, what obstructs. The meaning remains concrete: it is about taking away, setting aside what hinders.
3. The verb can also express the idea of pushing away or rejecting, a more figurative sense: pushing someone or something away from oneself.
H3014.origine: The verb יָגָה (yagah) is formed from a simple root meaning "to push" or "to remove." It is a particular form of the verb (Hiphil in Hebrew), which intensifies the action: not only does one push, but one forcefully pushes away, resolutely removing. The root evokes the physical gesture of moving something by pressing it.
H3014.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in the episode of Sheba's uprising against David (2 Samuel 20). Joab kills Amasa and has his body removed from the road so that his soldiers can advance without obstruction. The usage is concrete and dramatic: it is at the heart of a scene of violence and politics. The context shows that the word applies to the action of moving a corpse to allow free passage.
H3014.portee: For the Bible reader, this word emphasizes the harshness of the political and military stakes of David's time. To remove such an obstacle — even if it is a dead man — expresses the ruthless determination to achieve one's goal. It is a reminder that biblical stories do not hide the violent realities of human life.

sens: Physical or emotional suffering
Deep grief in the face of loss or misfortune
Anguish, overwhelming distress
Affliction that consumes the soul and body
H3015.detail:
1. Pain is primarily a suffering that one feels intimately — whether it is physical, like the pain that wears down the body, or emotional, like the grief that weighs on the heart. Jacob fears that Benjamin's death on the journey will burden his last days with pain (Genesis 42:38).

2. It also designates the deep grief caused by an irreparable loss or misfortune. This pain invades the soul: the psalmist cries that his life is consumed in pain and his years in sighs (Psalms 31:11), as if grief were eating away at him from the inside.

3. Pain takes the form of an anguish that grips — the cords of death and the pangs of the grave seize the one who suffers (Psalms 116:3), creating a choking sensation from which one cannot escape.

4. It is an affliction that can consume the entire body, wear down strength, and exhaust bones. Jeremiah asks why he was born to see suffering and pain (Jeremiah 20:18), suggesting a pain that permeates all existence. But the Lord promises that pain and groaning will flee far from His redeemed, replaced by eternal joy (Isaiah 51:11).
H3015.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of grieving, groaning, or lamenting. It describes an affliction that affects the person deeply, uniting emotional heart and body in a single experience of suffering. The word belongs to the Hebrew vocabulary of lamentation and mourning, frequent in the Psalms and among the prophets who express the groans of the oppressed or exiled people.
H3015.emploi: This word appears 14 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms (5 occurrences) and in Jeremiah (4 occurrences). It is also found in the patriarchal narrative (Genesis), in a historical text (Esther), and in prophetic oracles (Isaiah, Ezekiel). The pain described is sometimes personal (the psalmist who suffers), sometimes collective (the people in distress or exile). Esther 9:22 is remarkable: it recounts the miraculous reversal where the pain and desolation of the Jews become a day of celebration and joy. The prophetic texts (Isaiah, Jeremiah) promise that this pain, while real and overwhelming, will ultimately be removed by God's salvation.
H3015.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals that the Bible never idealizes suffering: it is true pain, affliction that can consume body and soul. But it does not have the final word. The texts promise that God sees the pain of His people (Psalms) and that one day it will disappear into eternal joy (Isaiah 51:11). This encourages not to deny one's grief, but to entrust it to God who can transform it.

sens: to experience fear in front of someone or something
to dread someone or their power
to have anxious apprehension
H3016.detail:
1. To fear is to experience fear in the face of a real threat. In Jeremiah 22:25, the prophet tells the king, "those before whom you tremble": this is fear in the face of powerful enemies who threaten life. It is a physical and concrete emotion.
2. The word also denotes the apprehension inspired by an authority, a power capable of doing harm. In Jeremiah 39:17, the Lord promises the servant that he will not be "delivered into the hands of the men you fear": this is the fear of a person who has the power to harm, here the enemies of the Babylonian Ebed-Melech.
H3016.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the shudder, the trembling of the body in the face of danger or fear. It is related to other Hebrew words expressing fright and anxiety. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this verb expresses a visceral fear, the kind felt when facing a tangible threat or someone more powerful.
H3016.emploi: This verb appears twice in the book of Jeremiah, in serious political contexts. In both cases, it describes human fear in the face of enemy powers. In Jeremiah 22:25, the king of Judah fears the king of Babylon and those who serve him. In Jeremiah 39:17, it is the opposite: a man fears being delivered to enemies, but God promises to deliver him. The word always denotes a personal and conscious fear, an apprehension in the face of danger or authority.
H3016.portee: This word reminds the reader of a deep reality: the fear of men and the powers of this world is real and normal, but it should not be our final word. In Jeremiah 39:17, God promises deliverance to the one who fears Him more than men. It is an invitation to place one's trust in God rather than remain paralyzed by the fear of human powers.

sens: City in the south of Judah, near the border of Edom
H3017.detail: Jagur is a city of Judah located in the Negev, the arid region of the south. It is among the southernmost cities of the territory of Judah, close to the border with Edom, the neighboring kingdom to the southeast (Joshua 15:21).
H3017.origine: The name Jagur comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to sojourn" or "to dwell temporarily." This name evokes the idea of a place of habitation, although the city itself is established permanently in the territory of Judah.
H3017.emploi: Jagur appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:21, in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the territory among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. It is mentioned among the southern cities, located in the most remote and inhospitable lands of the kingdom of Judah.

sens: Effort, physical or intellectual labor
Productive activity that requires energy and time
Product, harvest, goods acquired through labor
Fruit of work, what one obtains from one's efforts
H3018.detail: 1. Work is primarily the effort itself, the laborious activity: this is what Jacob reproaches Laban by saying "the work of my hands" (Genesis 31:42), it is the tiring work that locusts ravage in Psalms 78:46. 2. It is also what results from labor, the product or goods one acquires: Nehemiah speaks of the "goods" that must be preserved (Nehemiah 5:13), and the psalmist sings the joy of enjoying "the work of your hands" (Psalms 128:2). 3. Sometimes the word designates the toil itself, the fatigue: Job asks if God takes care of human works (Job 39:14). 4. In Isaiah 55:2, God criticizes those who "work" for the useless, that is, who exhaust their energy pursuing what does not nourish the soul.
H3018.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to make effort, to work." The family of words includes the idea of weariness, fatigue, exhaustion — the image is that of the body wearing out from effort. It is a concrete word, rooted in the daily experience of agricultural and artisanal labor in Israel.
H3018.emploi: This word appears sixteen times in the Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Psalms) and the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah). It designates either the effort itself (Genesis 31:42, Job 39:14) or what one derives from it (Psalms 128:2, Nehemiah 5:13). The Segond translates it as "work" in most cases, but also as "product," "goods," "work," or even "to worry" (Isaiah 55:2, where the verb literally means "to work"). The context changes the nuance: in a context of blessing, it is the fruit of labor that brings joy; in a context of judgment, it is the harvest that is destroyed (Psalms 78:46, Deuteronomy 28:33).
H3018.portee: This word reminds us that work, in the biblical vision, is neither a curse nor an end in itself: it is the activity through which man collaborates with the created order and provides for his needs. Enjoying the fruit of one's work is a blessing (Psalms 128:2). But the Bible also warns against work that strives to accumulate the useless: it is a call to direct one's efforts toward what truly nourishes the soul.

sens: Who has lost strength, who is exhausted by effort or suffering
H3019.detail: 1. This word describes one who has exhausted their strength, who has no energy left: work, suffering, or struggle has drained them. In Job 3:17, the "weary" are those who finally find rest after pains; it is the eternal rest that awaits them beyond this life, far from the turmoil of the wicked. The word emphasizes less a simple lack of sleep than a deep exhaustion of body and soul.
H3019.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of fatigue and accumulated weariness. In Hebrew, this family of words always refers to the weariness of one who has worked hard or suffered long, without the possibility of easily recovering.
H3019.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament. Job uses it in his discourse of despair (Job 3), where he enumerates those who finally find peace in death: the "weary" are listed alongside those "without strength." The context reveals that these are not simply people tired from a day, but men worn out by years of suffering, for whom death becomes a deliverance.
H3019.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible acknowledges real fatigue, physical suffering, and the weight of trials. It does not deny them, but situates them within a greater hope: that of eternal rest and divine comfort for those who endure.

sens: Character from the time of the exodus and the desert
Father of Bukki, prince of the tribe of Dan
H3020.detail: Jogli is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Moses designates the leaders who will direct the conquest and division of the land of Canaan. He is the father of Bukki, who is chosen as prince (leader) of the tribe of Dan for this important mission (Numbers 34:22).
H3020.origine: His Hebrew name יׇגְלִי (Jogli) means "he is exiled" or "one who is in exile," perhaps reflecting a family or personal situation at the time of the desert. It is a typical patronymic name from the patriarchal period and the desert.
H3020.emploi: Jogli appears only once in the Old Testament, in Numbers 34:22. He is identified as a Danite, meaning belonging to the tribe of Dan, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. His importance lies solely in his relationship with his son Bukki, whom God chooses among the princes of Israel to oversee the allocation of lands to his tribe during the conquest of Canaan.

sens: To perform difficult and prolonged work that exhausts one's strength
To become exhausted, to lose strength due to fatigue or effort
To cause fatigue to someone, to subject them to hardship
To waste one's energy, to expend strength in vain
H3021.detail:
1. The word first paints the image of the worker who toils: the one who plows a field, who accomplishes a long and hard task (Joshua 24:13 mentions the vineyards and olive trees that the people did not cultivate). It is the prolonged effort that demands a lot of energy.
2. This accumulated fatigue eventually exhausts the one who endures it: the psalmist says, "I am weary with my groaning" (Psalms 6:7), showing how continuous effort weakens both body and soul. Tears and weeping illustrate this decline.
3. The verb can also mean to impose fatigue on others: to inflict hardship, to compel to arduous work. God says to Israel, "I have not wearied you with incense" (Isaiah 43:23), showing that sometimes exhausting work is neither just nor brings anything.
4. Finally, the word reveals the bitterness of exhausting oneself for a vain result: God's servant says, "I have labored in vain" (Isaiah 49:4), expressing disappointment when effort seems to have served no purpose. A striking contrast: God "does not grow weary, he does not faint" (Isaiah 40:28).
H3021.origine: The Hebrew root יגע evokes the idea of fatigue and hard work. It is related to physical effort and the wear of strength. The word appears in three verbal forms in Hebrew: the simple form describes the work and exhaustion themselves, the intensive form emphasizes the idea of causing fatigue, and the causative form highlights the action of imposing hardship. These nuances express a complete arc: from work to fatigue, then to the action of wearying others.
H3021.emploi: The word appears 25 times in the Old Testament, especially among the prophets (notably Isaiah) and in the Psalms. It describes the ordinary work of the people (cultivating fields in Joshua 24:13, the warrior's battle in 2 Samuel 23:10), but also spiritual fatigue: that of the believer who prays and suffers (Psalms 6:7), that of the prophet discouraged by his seemingly barren ministry (Isaiah 49:4). An important usage: God who never grows weary (Isaiah 40:28-31), contrasting with man who exhausts himself. The word can carry a moral shade: exhausting oneself for what is worthless (Isaiah 57:10, Habakkuk 2:13), or conversely, working in full confidence in God.
H3021.portee: This word reminds the believer that fatigue is real and serious: it is not a sin, but a human condition. It also invites trust: only God does not grow weary, and he promises rest to those who exhaust themselves in seeking him (Isaiah 40:31). Finally, it warns against vain labor — effort that does not rest on God. It is a word of hope for the discouraged.

sens: The product of work, what one earns by working
The profit derived from labor and effort
What enriches the one who works
H3022.detail: 1. Gain refers to the concrete fruit of work — what one obtains in exchange for their labor, what one earns by the sweat of their brow. In Job 20:18, the wicked must return what he has "gained": this refers to the goods accumulated through work, but also through cunning and injustice. 2. This word evokes the idea of profit and enrichment: what fills the purse of the one who strives and toils. It is the sense of the reward due to effort. 3. By extension, gain can also refer to all that one possesses thanks to work, the amassed wealth — but always with the underlying idea that they are the fruit of activity, of toil.
H3022.origine: The Hebrew word יָגָע (yagua) comes from the root יגע, which means "to work with effort," "to toil," "to become weary." The noun naturally designates what one obtains through this labor: gain, the fruit of work. This root evokes the image of the body that expends itself, that wears out in labor — hence the idea that gain is the compensation, the price of this exhausting effort.
H3022.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 20:18. It refers to the gain accumulated by the wicked who oppresses others and violates justice. Zophar, Job's friend, describes divine punishment: the wicked will lose what he has "gained" unjustly, he will have to return everything. The context emphasizes the contrast between labor (often unjust) and loss: ill-gotten gain never remains in the hands of the one who has seized it.
H3022.portee: This word reminds every believer that honest work and loyal effort produce gain that is worth keeping, while riches acquired through injustice or oppression will be taken back. It is a word of consolation for those who work righteously and a word of warning for those who steal or exploit.

sens: Physically tired, without strength, worn out
Weakened, unable to resist
Exceeding the measure, excessive
H3023.detail:
1. The word describes the state of one who has lost their strength from walking, working, or suffering. In Deuteronomy 25:18, Israel in the desert was "exhausted" after long days of travel — a deep fatigue that renders one vulnerable. It is the image of a body emptied, that can no longer go on.
2. This fatigue also weakens the ability to fight or resist. In 2 Samuel 17:2, a king "weary" and with "weakened hands" cannot defend himself: exhaustion leaves him at the mercy of the enemy. It is a fatigue that paralyzes.
3. In Ecclesiastes 1:8, the word takes on a different hue: things are "beyond" what can be said, that is, excessive, exceeding all measure. The eye and the ear are never satisfied — what is extraordinary, what tires from being endless.
H3023.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that fundamentally means "to be overwhelmed, to be submerged." It evokes the image of one who will bend under the weight or who will collapse at the end of a long effort. The word designates both the physical state of exhaustion and, by extension, what exceeds ordinary strength.
H3023.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always to speak of fatigue or limitation. In Deuteronomy 25:18, it describes the vulnerable state of the people of Israel on the march. In 2 Samuel 17:2, it shows how exhaustion weakens a fighter. In Ecclesiastes 1:8, it takes on a broader sense: what is "beyond," excessive, inexhaustible. The context shifts the meaning from the physical to the moral, from exhaustion to excess.
H3023.portee: This word reminds us that the human body has limits, and that God knows them. It also speaks to us of compassion: recognizing those who are exhausted, as God sees those who drag themselves along. It finally invites moderation in the face of what seems inexhaustible — a lesson in wisdom before the endless desires of the heart.

sens: State of physical and mental exhaustion caused by prolonged effort or work
Weariness of the body due to excessive activities
Difficulty, tiring nature of a repeated action
H3024.detail:
1. Fatigue is the state of exhaustion that sets in after prolonged or intense effort, whether physical or mental. It is the gradual wear of the body and mind in the face of labor. The Preacher in Ecclesiastes 12:14 illustrates this by speaking of the fatigue caused by much study: the intense work of the researcher who accumulates books and knowledge ultimately exhausts the body.
2. Beyond the simple rest that one demands, fatigue expresses the idea of a burden that weighs down. It describes less a fleeting moment of weariness than a lasting weakening due to the accumulation of efforts.
H3024.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be tired, to be worn out." It belongs to the family of terms that express physical and spiritual exhaustion. In biblical Hebrew, this same root is used to describe both the fatigue of the body and that of the soul, reflecting an integrated view of the person.
H3024.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ecclesiastes 12:14. The Preacher uses it in his concluding discourse on the limits of human wisdom: accumulating books and study also means accumulating the fatigue of the body. This context reveals that the sacred author considers fatigue not as a virtue or an inevitable evil, but as a concrete reality that human pursuit of knowledge must confront and weigh.
H3024.portee: This verse invites the believer to a balanced wisdom: knowledge, however precious, has a real cost for the body and soul. Ecclesiastes reminds us that we are finite creatures, and recognizing the limits of our strength is also recognizing our dependence on God. Working endlessly, accumulating without measure, is to forget that rest and moderation are part of divine wisdom.

sens: To be afraid of something, to dread an evil
To tremble before a threat, to be in fear
To feel aversion for something unpleasant
H3025.detail:
1. To fear is to be afraid of a danger or misfortune that might happen. Moses says to God: "I was terrified at the sight of the anger of the Lord" (Deuteronomy 9:19), he feels fear in the face of God's terrible power in anger. It is an anxious anticipation of evil.
2. This verb also designates the state of one who trembles under the effect of fear. The Hebrews feared "all the diseases of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 28:60), meaning they had a visceral fear of them. Fear manifests in the body, through fear and apprehension.
3. To fear can also mean to dread or to have an aversion to something, to loathe it. Job says: "What I fear comes upon me" (Job 3:25), expressing his horror at the misfortunes he anticipates or endures.
H3025.origine: The verb יָגֹר (yagar) comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of trembling, shivering before what is frightening. It is a verb of intense emotion, painting a physical as well as psychological feeling. The family of the word includes other terms expressing fear, but this particular verb emphasizes the aspect of trembling and dread before a feared evil.
H3025.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the wisdom and historical books. Moses uses it to express his fear before divine anger (Deuteronomy 9:19), the image of the plagues of Egypt also illustrates this (Deuteronomy 28:60). Job uses it twice to express his existential anguish: he dreads suffering and trembles under the weight of pain (Job 3:25 and 9:28). The psalmist uses it to plead with God to remove what he fears (Psalms 119:39). In all cases, it is a concrete fear, attached to a specific evil, never a mere vague anxiety.
H3025.portee: This word shows us that fear is a natural human feeling, even among great saints like Moses. It invites us to acknowledge before God the fears that inhabit us. But it also teaches us that our anticipated fears, so often vain, can be placed in the hands of the One who controls all events. The Bible does not deny fear; it calls us to transform it into trust in God.

sens: Aramaic name given to a heap of stones erected as a witness between Jacob and Laban
H3026A.detail: Jegar-Sahadutha literally means "heap of witness" in Aramaic. It is the name that Laban gave to the pile of stones that Jacob and he together gathered in memory of their covenant. Jacob called this same place Galeed in Hebrew, which also means "heap of witness," but in the language of the Hebrews. This heap was a visible monument, marking the place where the two men parted in peace, after an agreement not to harm one another (Genesis 31:47-52). The two names, although in two different languages, have exactly the same meaning and remind us that God was the true witness of their pact.
H3026A.origine: The word יְגַר (yegar) is Aramaic and means "heap" or "pile." It is related to the Hebrew root גַּר (gar), which evokes an accumulated mass. The word "Sahadutha" (סְהַדוּתָא in Aramaic) comes from the root "sahad" which means "to witness" or "to be a witness." Together, "Jegar-Sahadutha" paints the image of a heap of stones that cries out: "We are witnesses!" — a silent yet eloquent structure of a solemn meeting.
H3026A.emploi: Jegar-Sahadutha appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 31:47. It is the moment when Jacob and Laban, after years of living together and conflicts, decide to part and seal a covenant. Each names this heap of stones in their own language: Laban in Aramaic (Jegar-Sahadutha) and Jacob in Hebrew (Galeed). This linguistic detail emphasizes that, although speaking different languages, the two men agreed on one God as the witness of their mutual peace.
H3026A.portee: This dual name reminds us that God hears and understands all peoples in their own languages, and that He is the ultimate witness of our covenants and commitments. The fact that silent stones serve as witnesses invites faithfulness: our words and promises remain engraved, and He who sees all things calls us to sincerity.

sens: the heap of witness stones erected between Jacob and Laban
H3026B.detail: Jégar-Sahadutha is the Aramaic name given by Laban to a heap of stones he erected as a witness and boundary between himself and Jacob. The word literally means "the heap (jégar) of witness (sahadutha)": the stones serve as a silent witness to the covenant made between the two men and the separation they accept. Jacob, for his part, calls this same place Galed, which in Hebrew means "heap of witness," expressing the same idea in his own language.
H3026B.origine: The Aramaic word sahadutha comes from the root meaning "witness." Laban speaks Aramaic, the language of his ancestors in Mesopotamia, while Jacob speaks Hebrew. This moment reveals the existence of two distinct languages in the ancient world: the double name of the same place shows that Laban and Jacob were from different linguistic traditions, yet they together concluded a covenant.
H3026B.emploi: This name appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 31:47. The context is that of Jacob's flight from Laban's house in Upper Mesopotamia. After a pursuit, the two men reconcile and erect this heap of stones as a visible sign of their agreement and the boundary that Laban commits not to cross. The verse immediately mentions the equivalent Hebrew name given by Jacob, showing that although strangers in language, they together accomplish a solemn act of peace.
H3026B.portee: This account teaches that God recognizes the covenants made between men, even when they unite peoples or families in tension. The material testimony of the stones reminds us that commitments must be visible, memorable, and known to all. It is also an example of God's wisdom that allows Jacob and Laban, despite their differences, to part in peace under the gaze of God who "watches over the covenant."

sens: Member of the body located at the end of the arm, equipped with fingers for grasping and acting
Strength, power, ability to act
Dominion, authority, control over someone or something
Side, region, direction of a territory
Part, portion, share of a property
H3027G.detail:
1. The hand is the member of the body used to grasp, touch, and act: it is the instrument of concrete action. In Genesis 3:22, man stretches out his hand to take the fruit; in 1 Samuel 14:13, Jonathan uses his hands and feet to climb.
2. The hand represents strength and power in action: it is through it that one accomplishes, creates, and fights. Jeremiah 21:5 speaks of God's "outstretched hand and strong arm" to fight — an image of His fearsome power.
3. The hand symbolizes authority and control: to have a hand over someone is to dominate them. Leviticus 4:24 describes the ritual gesture of the priest placing his hand on the head of the goat — an act of authority and transfer.
4. The hand also designates a direction, a side, a region of a territory, or a share of inheritance — a less visible meaning but present in narratives of sharing and boundaries.
5. The hand can mean a part, a portion, or a share of a property, a fraction intended for someone.
H3027G.origine: The Hebrew word יָד (yad) primarily refers to the member of the body. It has given rise to many compounds and idiomatic expressions in biblical Hebrew. It is a basic, very ancient word that refers to one of humanity's most characteristic tools. By figurative extension, it symbolizes action, power, and authority — for the hand is what one uses to exercise their will.
H3027G.emploi: The word "hand" is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible (over 660 occurrences). It appears mainly in Genesis and the historical books: narratives of action, sacrifice, blessing, and dominion. Genesis 3:22 and Exodus 3:20 to 14:27 show the hand as an organ of human and divine action. The passages in Nehemiah 6:9 and Psalms 149:6 reveal its figurative use: losing courage means the hand weakens; praise requires an armed hand. The meaning varies according to the context: physical in ritual gestures, metaphorical in expressions of power or authority.
H3027G.portee: Understanding the biblical word "hand" enriches prayer and reading: the Bible does not oppose physical action and spiritual power. The "hand of God" is not a poetic fancy, but the affirmation that God truly acts in history. Recognizing that our hands are instruments of obedience or rebellion reminds us that every gesture matters before Him.

sens: Member of the body used to grasp and act
Power, strength, or authority
Control, dominion, or power over someone
Protection or support from God
Side, direction, or region
Part, portion, or share
H3027H.detail:
1. The hand is the member of the body that grasps and acts: it is the instrument par excellence of human action. When Moses receives the tablets of the Law, he carries them in his hands (Exodus 32:15); when someone is "delivered into the hands" of a king, they are placed under his control (1 Kings 22:12).

2. The hand symbolizes power and strength, especially that of God acting with might: the miracles of Moses are accomplished "with a mighty hand" (Deuteronomy 34:12; Jeremiah 32:21), an expression that describes God's miraculous intervention as an act of irresistible power.

3. To have someone "in hand" or "in the hands" means to dominate, control, or hold them in one's power: this is why we ask God to deliver us "from the hand of the Philistines" (1 Samuel 7:3), meaning from their dominion.

4. The "hand" of God signifies His benevolent protection and active support: Nehemiah recounts that "the good hand of my God was upon me" (Nehemiah 2:18), meaning that God guided and supported him in his project.

5. The hand can also designate a side, a direction, or a region: thus, "the right hand" or "the left hand" of a territory indicates its bank or boundary (Genesis 48:22; Deuteronomy 23:31).

6. Finally, the hand represents a part or a portion: when something is distributed "from hand to hand," it signifies a sharing or allocation (Genesis 30:35; Leviticus 25:28).
H3027H.origine: The Hebrew word yad primarily refers to the physical hand, this visible and tangible member of the body. The image of the hand naturally extends to everything it expresses: strength (for it is with the hand that one acts), mastery (for one holds what they grasp), direction (for it is the hand that points). The hand thus becomes a rich symbol of action and power. In the Greek Bible (the Septuagint), this word is regularly translated by the Greek "chéir," and this same symbolic richness is found in the New Testament.
H3027H.emploi: The word "hand" (yad) appears 512 times in the Old Testament, making it a fundamental word. It is used very concretely: holding an object, grasping someone, making a gesture (Exodus 4:21: Pharaoh "hardened his heart"). But it quickly takes on a figurative and theological meaning: "to be delivered from the hand of someone" means to be saved from their oppression (1 Samuel 7:3), and especially "the hand of God" describes divine intervention, sometimes terrible (the plagues of Egypt, Exodus 3:19), sometimes protective and benevolent (Nehemiah 2:18). The expression "with a mighty hand" becomes a formula for powerful and decisive divine action (Deuteronomy 34:12; Jeremiah 32:21). The word also nuances in legal and administrative terms: "to hand over" means to transfer responsibility or possession.
H3027H.portee: For the believer, the "hand of God" is not a distant or abstract image: it is the assurance that God acts concretely in history and in their life. Discovering that the "good hand" of God is upon oneself (Nehemiah 2:18) means recognizing that God does not let things happen: He supports, guides, and protects. Conversely, fearing to fall "into the hands" of an enemy shows that the Christian knows where true power lies: not with the powerful of the world, but with the One whose hand can accomplish all things.

sens: Part of the arm that grasps and acts
Strength, power, capacity for action
Side, region, location next to something
Share, portion, what belongs to someone
Chosen offering, voluntary gift
H3027I.detail:
1. The hand is the part of the body that performs gestures: grasping, holding, giving, building. It acts concretely as the organ of grasping and work. In Genesis 35:4, Jacob asks his family to give him the idols "in their hands" to bury them — the image is that of a material gesture.

2. The hand also signifies power, the capacity for action, especially in combat or authority. When one escapes from the "hand" of an enemy (2 Chronicles 16:7), one escapes from their domination and strength. It is the idea that the one who holds in hand possesses and controls.

3. Placed "next to" something (or "at hand"), the hand expresses proximity, adjacency. In Nehemiah 3:5, the Tekoites work "next to" (literally "at hand") those who precede them in building the wall — it is the spatial order.

4. The hand can also mean a share, a portion, or what is due to someone. The idea is that everyone receives their "hand," their share, their measure.

5. The hand symbolizes voluntary choice, particularly in offerings. In Deuteronomy 12:11, the "firstfruits" (literally "what raises the hand") are the offerings that the heart freely offers to God — the gesture of extending the hand expresses the gift of oneself.
H3027I.origine: The word יָד (yad) is a very ancient root in Hebrew, probably related to the idea of grasping and directing. It appears in other Semitic languages with the same meaning of hand and power. The hand, in the Old Testament, is the quintessential instrument: it is by it that man acts, dominates, offers, or submits. God Himself possesses a "hand" — that of His power and action in history.
H3027I.emploi: The word יָד appears 67 times in the Old Testament (Segond 1910). It primarily denotes literally the hand of the body (Genesis 35:4, Exodus 32:4). Early on, it takes on a sense of power and authority: one escapes from the hand of an enemy, one falls into their hand. In the context of worship, it denotes offerings and firstfruits — what the hand of the heart freely offers. Due to its position, the hand also comes to signify the side, the region, the place located near something, particularly in the architectural descriptions of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah). Each meaning remains concrete and rooted in the experience of the gesture.
H3027I.portee: The hand reminds us that the believer acts in history: it is through their hands that they build, give, and serve. But they also discover that there is a power above their own — the hand of God — which controls events and directs history according to His plan. Understanding that so many things escape us, that we do not hold them in hand, invites us to place our lives in the hands of the Lord.

sens: The body part used to grasp, hold, and act.
Strength, power, capacity to act.
The side, region, direction of a place.
The intermediary through which something is communicated or transmitted.
The moment, time, occasion when something occurs.
The instrument, means by which an order or word is executed.
H3027J.detail:
1. The hand is primarily the part of the human body intended to grasp and hold: it is the organ of action and work. When speaking of someone's hand, it often refers to their active presence, their concrete ability to do or build.
2. Figuratively, the hand represents strength and power: to possess something "in hand" means to control it, to have power over it. This is why saying that God acts "by His hand" or "through His hand" means that He acts by His sovereign power.
3. The hand can also designate a side, a region, or a direction: "on the right hand" or "on the left hand" indicates a spatial location or position. It is thus a way of speaking about geography, territory, the place one occupies.
4. The hand becomes the instrument of transmission: when a law or word is given "by the hand" of a person, it means it passes through them as an intermediary (Exodus 9:35: "by the hand of Moses" = through Moses as messenger).
5. The hand can also express the moment or occasion: the Hebrew context allows this word to designate the time, the "time" when something occurs, particularly in the repetitive formulas of biblical narratives.
6. By extension, the hand is the authority that gives an order or executes a word: when God "addresses" something (Zechariah 7:12: "addressed by His Spirit"), He does it through a hand, that is, through a will, an active power.
H3027J.origine: The Hebrew word יָד (yad) primarily denotes the visible and tangible body part. It is very ancient and very common in Hebrew. From the concrete (the limb), the word has extended to the figurative to signify strength, authority, action: for the hand is the natural expression of what one can do or possess. In biblical Greek, several terms translate this word depending on the context, notably χείρ (cheir) for the physical hand and for action, and δύναμις (dynamis) for strength. This richness reflects Hebrew thought: one does not separate the physical organ from what it represents spiritually.
H3027J.emploi: The word יָד appears about 72 times in the provided passages, especially in the historical and prophetic books. It is used first in the literal sense: the physical hand of a man or woman (1 Samuel 4:13: "sitting by the way"). But very often it is used figuratively to express mediation or transmission: a law given "by the hand" of someone is given through their intermediary (Exodus 9:35: the word of the Lord "by the hand of Moses"). The meaning also extends to the expression of time and repetition: "a first time," "a second time" (recurring formula in the books of Numbers and Kings). In narratives, the hand can also indicate the region or side (1 Samuel 4:13: "near the way"). In each occurrence, the meaning adjusts to the context, but the central idea remains that of action, power, or the means by which something occurs.
H3027J.portee: Understanding that the "hand" in biblical Hebrew denotes not only a limb but also power and authority enriches the reading of Scripture. When speaking of the hand of God, one is not merely using a poetic image: one asserts that God truly acts, that He exercises His sovereignty, that He protects us. Similarly, when the Bible says that a word came "by the hand" of a prophet, it emphasizes that this prophet is the living instrument of God, responsible and active. This understanding helps us grasp how divine action in biblical history is never abstract: it passes through people, concrete events, visible gestures.

sens: Member of the human body that grasps and acts
Power, strength, authority
Side, direction, region
Portion, part, share
Monument, sign
Support, technical device
H3027K.detail:
1. The hand is the member of the body that allows one to grasp, hold, and act: it is the instrument of human action. In Genesis 9:5, God says, "I will require the soul of man from man," literally "from the hand of man," for it is by his hand that man acts and becomes responsible.

2. The hand represents the power and authority of a person or an army: to have something "in hand" or "under one's hand" means to have it under one's control or protection. In 2 Chronicles 34:10, the money is handed "into the hands of those who were appointed" for the work, meaning under their responsibility and authority.

3. In geographical descriptions, "hand" refers to a side, direction, or region. In Numbers 34:3, the boundary of the desert begins "near Edom" (literally "at the hand of Edom"), indicating the side or direction toward Edom.

4. The hand can signify a portion or a part in the sharing of goods or power, like a fraction of a whole.

5. In the context of the tabernacle and the temple, the hand can refer to a monument or a sign, a memorial object.

6. Technically, the word can also describe supports or devices, like the tenons of the tabernacle or the axles of chariots.
H3027K.origine: The Hebrew word יָד (yad) comes from a very ancient root designating the most active and visible member of the body. It is the only ordinary Hebrew word for "hand." The word has naturally extended from the concrete meaning (the member) to the figurative meaning (the power that acts through the hand) and to the spatial meaning (the side, the direction, as directions are designated by right and left). In the Greek Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it is rendered by χείρ (cheir), "hand."
H3027K.emploi: The word yad appears 65 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Pentateuch and historical books. It primarily denotes the human hand, the organ of the body (Exodus 2:5, where Pharaoh takes a child from the water). Very often, it signifies power and authority: "the hand of God" evokes His all-powerful action (1 Samuel 5:11, "the hand of the Lord was heavy"). In geographical contexts, especially in boundary descriptions, yad designates a side or direction: "toward the south" (Numbers 34:3). The word can also express possession or control: to have something "in hand" or "under the hand" means to have it in one's power. Finally, in the technical vocabulary of the temple and the tabernacle, it describes structural elements.
H3027K.portee: Understanding that "hand" often means "acting power" or "authority" enriches the reading of the Bible: when it speaks of "the hand of God," it affirms that God acts concretely in history and in the lives of His people. When a passage says that something was done "by the hand" of someone, it shows that this person bears the responsibility. This is why Genesis 9:5 links moral responsibility to the power to act: God holds accountable the one who has the power to act, for the hand is the sign of power and guilt.

sens: Repetition of an action or state
Multiple or proportion of a quantity
Part, portion of a whole
Side or direction
H3027L.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a repetition or occurrence: when one says "ten times," one counts the number of repetitions. In 2 Samuel 19:43, the men of Israel declare that the king belongs to them "ten times as much" — meaning much more, repeating the idea of possession.

2. It can express a ratio or a multiple: Benjamin receives "five times more" than his brothers in Genesis 43:34, which means a quantity multiplied by five. This is also the idea in Daniel 1:20, where the young men found wise are "ten times better" than the magicians: ten times their worth.

3. It designates a part or a portion of a whole. In Genesis 47:24, the Egyptians will give "one-fifth" to Pharaoh and keep "the other four parts" for themselves — the word "hand" or "part" literally enumerates the fractions of the goods.

4. It can mean a side or direction, a section of a group. In Nehemiah 11:1 and 2 Kings 11:7, "the others" refer to the remaining portions of the people or divisions: those who are not part of the group just mentioned.
H3027L.origine: The Hebrew word yad primarily means the hand, the grasping member — the instrument of taking and action of man. The hand is the source of multiple images: strength (one grasps with the hand), possession (one holds what one possesses), direction (one points with a finger or palm), part or portion (one distributes by hand). From this last image gradually arises the meaning of "times" or "part" — one enumerates portions by counting them, as one counts on one's fingers. This evolution moves from the concrete (body member) to the metaphorical and numerical (multiplicity, fraction).
H3027L.emploi: The word appears six times in the provided usages, almost always in a context of counting or distribution. In Genesis 43:34 and Daniel 1:20, it expresses a multiple: five or ten times more. In Genesis 47:24, 2 Kings 11:7, and Nehemiah 11:1, it designates a part or portion of the whole — the four-fifths remaining, other divisions, the other inhabitants. The common idea is one of enumeration and subdivision: one counts by hands, that is, by discrete units. This numerical sense is merely a specialization of the primitive meaning of the word, which always rests on the image of the hand that separates, shares, and counts.
H3027L.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible counts everything in hands — the portions, the goods, the lives. The hand, instrument of work and sharing, becomes the unit of divine calculation. This speaks to us of the control that God exercises over the distribution of goods and lives: nothing escapes His count, and He distributes according to His justice. For the reader, it is an invitation to recognize that every portion received comes from the hand of the Lord.

sens: Member of the human body's hand
Power, strength, domination
Side, region, part of a territory
Place, station, established position
Mark, sign, monument
H3027M.detail:
1. The hand is the member of the body that grasps and acts: it is the instrument of work and action par excellence (1 Samuel 14:34: each one brings his ox "by hand" to slaughter it).
2. Figuratively, the hand signifies the power, decisive action, or authority of someone: to have something "in hand" means to control or accomplish it.
3. The hand also designates a region, a side, a part of a space: just as the hand delineates and divides what it touches, the word describes a portion of territory or a locality.
4. The word can mean a place or an established station or refuge: in Deuteronomy 23:12, "you shall have a place outside the camp" — a hand in the sense of an assigned post, a designated spot.
5. A hand can be a visible mark, a sign, or a monument: in Ezekiel 21:24, one must "mark" a sign at the crossroads to indicate the way, a visible and intentional landmark.
H3027M.origine: The word יָד (yad) primarily designates the concrete member of the human body. Its use naturally extends to the notion of strength and action ("the hand does"), then to that of possession and control ("in hand"). From there arises the idea of "what is assigned or marked," of a determined place or a visible sign. This transition from the concrete to the figurative follows the same logic as many biblical words: the bodily image becomes the image of authority, mastery, and a landmark.
H3027M.emploi: The word appears about five times in these biblical excerpts with distinct nuances. In Deuteronomy 23:12, it means an assigned "place," a station. In 1 Samuel 14:34, it designates the place where livestock is brought (literally "by hand"), that is, within reach, the place of action. In Isaiah 56:5, it denotes a lasting "place," an honorable position. In Ezekiel 21:24, it becomes a "mark" or a visible signal — a directional indication drawn on the ground to guide. This range of uses shows how the word enriches from a primary meaning (the concrete member) to secondary meanings (place, position, mark).
H3027M.portee: The word "hand" reminds us that divine and human action is concretized through gestures, decisions, and specific places.
