It is a call to consider that God "acts with His hand" and that He "assigns" each one his place — an invitation to recognize His active authority and His precise plan for our lives.

sens: Transaction, exchange of goods or services
Contact, relationship between people
Intimate or carnal relationship
H3027N.detail:
1. Transaction and exchange of goods: the word primarily designates commercial activity, the merchant exchange, or the business agreement between parties.
2. Contact and relationship: it can mean the relationship or intercourse between people, in a broad sense.
3. Carnal or intimate relationship: in Isaiah 57:8, the prophet uses this word to describe the sensual and idolatrous relationships that the people maintain with false gods, using the language of commerce and alliance to express spiritual infidelity in a veiled form.
H3027N.origine: The Hebrew word yad literally means hand. From the primary image of the hand arises the idea of power, strength ("to lay hands on something"), then of contact, exchange (what hands do together). This same root produces place names and nouns designating everything that the hand grasps, controls, or shares. The transition from a physical meaning to figurative or specialized meanings is characteristic of biblical language, where the concrete becomes the vehicle of the spiritual.
H3027N.emploi: This word appears only once in the Segond in the sense of "commerce." In Isaiah 57:8, Jeremiah uses this term to denounce the impious alliances and idolatrous relationships of the people of Israel. By the context ("you make an alliance with them, you love their commerce"), the prophet designates the carnal exchanges and spiritual transactions — true bargains of the soul — that the people maintain with pagan deities. The use of the word "commerce" rather than a more explicitly carnal term reinforces the prophetic irony: Israel treats its infidelity as a business matter, an ordinary transaction, while it is a betrayal of the Lord.
H3027N.portee: This passage reminds the Christian reader that idolatry is not a trivial personal matter, but a breach of covenant, a true "unfaithful commerce" with what distances us from God. The commitments we make, the "alliances" we enter into through our choices and relationships, do not escape divine judgment. The Word invites us to examine our spiritual "transactions": do we serve the Lord with integrity, or do we widen our bed by seeking elsewhere what can only come from Him?

sens: Member of the human body located at the end of the arm, used for grasping and acting
Force, power, ability to act
Side, region, portion of a territory
H3027O.detail:
1. The hand is primarily the member of the body with which one grasps, holds, and strikes. It is the concrete instrument of work and action. In Numbers 35:17-18, "to hold in hand" a stone or a wooden instrument literally means to have it in hand to strike: it is the image of the weapon one wields to kill.
2. By extension, the "hand" represents power, strength, the ability to act or dominate. This figurative meaning is very common: the hand of God signifies His powerful intervention, protection, or judgment.
3. The word also designates a portion, a region, a side — as when one says "to the right" or "to the left," "the hand of the north." It is the idea of sharing or delimiting a space.
H3027O.origine: The Hebrew word yad comes from an ancient root designating the member of the body that acts. In Greek, this word is often translated as chèir (χείρ). The hand is the quintessential tool of humanity: it grasps, shapes, executes. Throughout the Bible, the image of the hand symbolizes action, responsibility, and power.
H3027O.emploi: The word appears very frequently in the Hebrew Bible — hundreds of times — in very varied contexts: daily actions (grasping, holding, striking), legal responsibility (having blood on one's hands), divine protection ("in Your hand"), and possession or power ("delivered into the hands of"). The two occurrences in Numbers 35 emphasize the instrument held in hand as evidence of voluntary crime. The meaning nuances: sometimes the hand is the physical instrument of the crime or work, sometimes it represents divine authority or protection.
H3027O.portee: Understanding that the "hand" in Hebrew is both the physical member and the symbol of responsible action helps grasp the depth of biblical promises ("I am in the hand of God") and calls to obedience ("do not lift your hand against the innocent"). It is a word that anchors faith in the real: God acts concretely, and man is responsible for his actions.

sens: Organ of the human body with five fingers, located at the end of the arm
Strength, power, ability to act
Side, edge, region of a territory or a bank
Part, portion, fraction
H3027P.detail:
1. The hand is the concrete organ of the body, the one that grasps and acts: this is the most common meaning of the word in biblical Hebrew, as in all ancient texts.
2. By natural extension, the word designates strength or power — what the hand can accomplish. When we speak of "the hand of God" or "the hand of the king," we evoke His power, His authority over events.
3. The word is also used to designate a side, a bank, or a region: "along the Jordan" (Numbers 13:29) or "the banks of the Arnon" (Judges 11:26) use this same word for the banks or areas bordering the watercourse.
4. Finally, it can mean a part, a portion, a fraction of a whole — each one receives their "share" or their "turn."
H3027P.origine: The word יָד (yad) is an ancient root, probably related to the idea of carrying or extending. In biblical Hebrew, it is at the heart of many common expressions. Through its multiple meanings, it reveals how antiquity thought: the hand, a concrete instrument of power and action, becomes the image of all forms of authority, mastery, or territorial possession. The same process occurs in neighboring Middle Eastern languages.
H3027P.emploi: The word יָד appears about 1600 times in the Old Testament, making it one of the most frequent words. It primarily refers to the human hand or that of animals. Very often, especially in narratives and psalms, it evokes the hand of God — His action, His judgment, His protection. In the three provided usages, the word is translated as "long" or "edges," showing a geographical nuance: it describes adjacent areas, regions that line a river. This metaphorical use of "hand" for "side" or "bank" is common in Hebrew: the hand is what delineates, what borders.
H3027P.portee: Understanding that "hand" can mean strength and authority enriches the reading of passages where God acts "by His hand" or where we speak of the "hand of the Lord." It helps us see that God is never distant, far away, or passive: He intervenes, He acts, He protects His people. Conversely, being "in the hand" of an enemy means being under their power. This vocabulary of the hand speaks to the heart: it makes concrete God's governance over events and our lives.

sens: That extends over a large area, spacious
That offers a lot of space, breadth
That contains or can contain a lot
Considerable extent, width of a territory or a body of water
H3027Q.detail: 1. The word primarily describes a physical space that extends widely. When the Israelites spy out the land of Canaan, they are told: "The land is vast" (Judges 18:10), indicating that there is plenty of room, territory to occupy. 2. It qualifies a city or a wide and spacious place. Nehemiah describes Jerusalem as "spacious and great," despite its small population (Nehemiah 7:4), highlighting the extent of the buildings and streets. 3. The word applies to impressive natural expanses. The "great and vast sea" (Psalms 104:25) and the "vast rivers" (Isaiah 33:21) show immense bodies of water that strike with their extent. 4. The image also evokes the freedom and abundance provided by an open space: a vast place offers room, resources, and a lack of narrowness.
H3027Q.origine: The Hebrew word יָד (yad) means primarily "hand" (the limb of the body), an image of what extends, reaching far. In its rare adjectival use, it literally designates a "wide hand" or "spacious hand," hence the meaning of "vast, spacious" — as if the space extends generously. This metaphor reflects the idea that what is wide has amplitude and depth.
H3027Q.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Segond, always to qualify physical spaces: lands, cities, waterways. In Judges 18:10, it emphasizes that Canaan offered a great place for the new occupants. In Nehemiah 7:4, it describes Jerusalem as a vast urban center. In the Psalms and Isaiah, it magnifies the greatness of divine creation — the sea, the rivers — to celebrate God's generosity. The word remains always concrete: it speaks of real dimensions, never abstract.
H3027Q.portee: This word reminds us that God generously provides for His children: He gives them a vast land, spaces to settle and prosper. It awakens wonder before the immense creation — the sea, the rivers — and invites the believer to meditate on divine greatness. It is also an invitation not to feel cramped: God gives abundantly.

sens: To fill someone's hand, to entrust them with the exercise
To ordain someone for the service of worship, to make them sacred for God
To invest with a charge, an official responsibility
H3027R.detail:
1. Originally, the verb literally means "to fill the hand": one places in a person's hand the objects or responsibilities that now belong to them. It is the image of an official installation, as when someone is handed the tools or insignia of their office (Exodus 28:41).

2. In a religious context, to consecrate means to set someone apart for the service of divine worship: they are anointed with holy oil, dressed in sacred garments, and separated from the profane to be made holy. The sons of Aaron and every priest called to sacrifice on the altar are consecrated in this way (Leviticus 16:32, Numbers 3:3).

3. The word can also refer to the act of ordaining a person to a specific function: Micah consecrates the young Levite, meaning he recognizes and establishes him as his personal priest (Judges 17:12).
H3027R.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from the root yad which means "hand." The basic image is that of filling or putting into possession: to fill someone's hand is to entrust them with something, to invest them with a responsibility. It is a strong and concrete metaphor: the hand receives, holds, exercises. The Greek of the Septuagint often translates this term with verbs meaning "to ordain" or "to consecrate."
H3027R.emploi: This verb appears about sixteen times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in contexts of religious consecration. It is particularly frequent in the books of Moses (Exodus and Leviticus) to describe the ordination of priests Aaron and his sons according to the prescribed ritual. It is also found in Judges, Kings, and Chronicles, whenever it involves setting apart a person or object for the service of the Lord. The passage in Exodus 29:35 shows that consecration is a process that extends over seven days, a period of initiation and separation. The context is always official and solemn: it is God who ordains, or one who acts in His name.
H3027R.portee: For the biblical reader, this word teaches that serving God requires true consecration: one does not approach the Lord lightly, but is set apart, transformed, separated for Him. This consecration is not merely a personal or intimate matter; it is a public, ritualized act that acknowledges that the person now belongs to God. For every believer, this term reminds us of the call to a consecrated life: the first recipients (the priests of Israel) foreshadow what every Christian is called to be — a servant set apart for the Lord.

sens: Organ of the human body, member used to grasp and act
Power, strength, authority, mastery over something or someone
Solemn promise made by raising the hand to heaven
Side, portion, part of a territory
Support or grip used to hold or retain
Mark, sign, or monument
H3027S.detail:
1. The hand is primarily the member of the human body: it is with the hand that one grasps, acts, and makes gestures. Leviticus 9:22 shows Aaron raising his hands to bless the people — a simple and concrete gesture.
2. Figuratively, the hand represents power, authority, the ability to act. Saying "the hand of God" or "my hand" refers to the dominion, the effective power one exercises over someone or something. This allows God to hold and control events.
3. Raising the hand to heaven is the gesture of a solemn oath: it is to swear, to promise while taking God as a witness. Deuteronomy 32:40 shows the Lord raising His hand to heaven to swear an oath. It is an irrevocable commitment: "I have raised my hand" means "I have sworn".
4. By extension, the hand can refer to a portion of territory, a side or part of a place, as when speaking of the left or right bank of a river.
5. In constructions, the hand can be a technical support: the tenons or rods that hold a structure in place.
6. The hand can also be a visible sign, a mark, or a monument reminding of an event.
H3027S.origine: The word yad comes from a root that originally designates the grasping organ, the hand itself. It is a very ancient and fundamental word in Hebrew. The family of this word includes derivatives related to the ability to act, control, and hold. The central image is that of grasping, concrete power: one holds something in their hand, one masters it. From this arise the figurative meanings: the hand as a symbol of power, promise (through the gesture of an oath), sharing (a hand, a portion). This is a word that the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) often renders as "cheir", which has the same range of meanings.
H3027S.emploi: The word yad appears 17 times in the provided usages, mainly in the prophetic books and the Psalms. Its most frequent use is in the sense of an oath or solemn promise: it is notably seen in Ezekiel (20:5, 20:6, 20:15, 20:23, 20:28, 20:42, and 36:7), where the Lord "raises His hand" towards Israel or the nations to swear what He will do. It is the expression of an irrevocable divine promise. The word also retains its concrete meaning of hand as a member of the body (Psalms 28:2: raising hands in prayer), and also figures divine power or action (Exodus 6:8, where the Lord says "I will bring you in" by His hand, that is, by His sovereign action). The passages show that "raising the hand" is the ritualized and solemn gesture that expresses the irrevocable commitment of an oath.
H3027S.portee: Understanding that the hand symbolizes both concrete power and solemn commitment helps the reader grasp the strength of divine promises. When God "raises His hand" and swears, it is not an empty word: it is an act of will engaging His power and honor. The Christian can also consider that their own hands — what they do and what they master — are the visible reflection of their heart and commitments to God and to others.

sens: the hand
strength, power
capacity, means, what the hand can accomplish
H3027T.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the physical hand of the human body, the organ with which one acts and works. This is the literal and primary meaning of the Hebrew term.

2. By extension, it expresses strength and power — what one can do with the hand, the ability to act. When one says "the hand of the Lord", they are speaking of His power, His action in the world.

3. The word takes on the meaning of resource, financial or material capacity — what someone can afford according to their means. In Leviticus 14:22, a poor man offers two turtledoves "according to his resources", that is, according to what his hand and means allow him. It is what one can give, accomplish, or acquire with what one possesses.
H3027T.origine: The word יָד (yad) comes from the root that fundamentally means "the hand". The image of the hand — instrument of work, grasping, and strength — naturally extends to the ideas of power, capacity, and possession. The hand opens and closes, it grasps and gives: it symbolizes therefore mastery, action, and available resources.
H3027T.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the provided passages, all in the sense of "resource" or "capacity". It is regularly encountered in the law of Leviticus concerning offerings and vows: divine law takes into account real poverty. A leper too poor should only bring one bird instead of two (Leviticus 14:22). A man who has made a vow to the Lord but does not have the means to fully fulfill it can adapt his offering "in relation to his resources" (Leviticus 27:8). This flexibility of divine law shows that the Lord expects from each person only what they can accomplish, according to their condition.
H3027T.portee: This word teaches that God never asks for the impossible: He considers our true abilities and real limits. The law of Moses, far from being merciless, recognizes poverty and adjusts accordingly. This reveals the practical goodness of God, who hears the prayers and offerings even of the poorest, provided they come from the heart. For the believer, this is a liberation: God looks at what one can truly give, not what one does not possess.

sens: Action of putting the hand to something, undertaking it
Work, task that one undertakes
Business, chore, project that one carries out
Accomplishment, success of an action
Force, power put into action
H3027U.detail:
1. The word first evokes the concrete image of the hand — the one that is extended to grasp, to act, to do. It is the idea of taking something in hand, putting it in motion. In Deuteronomy 15:10, when one "gives" to someone in need, it is a "blessed undertaking": one acts with their own hands with generosity.
2. The word then designates the work done with one's hands: everything one "undertakes", that is, begins and pursues. In Deuteronomy 28:8, God promises to bless all your "undertakings" — your harvests, your constructions, all your works.
3. It is also the business, the project, the action one commits to carry out. Every concrete task of the farmer, merchant, artisan is an "undertaking".
4. Finally, the word can evoke the force, the power necessary to accomplish: to have "enterprise" is to have the power to do, the ability to act and succeed.
H3027U.origine: The Hebrew word יָד (yad) literally means "the hand". It is one of the most concrete and common words in biblical Hebrew. By natural extension, what comes from the hand, what one undertakes with the hand, has come to designate action, work, task. The hand is everywhere in the Old Testament: it grasps, it gives, it strikes, it builds. Saying "my undertaking" is saying "the work of my hands."
H3027U.emploi: This word appears mainly in Deuteronomy, the book of law and covenant. It is used in a context of divine blessing: God promises to bless the work of the faithful, their undertakings, their granaries, their harvest. It is always the business one carries out with their own hands, the concrete work of daily labor. The promised blessing does not concern a vague success: it pertains to each specific work, each project, each undertaking of the believer.
H3027U.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reminds an important truth: God is interested in our works, in our daily undertakings. There is nothing too small, nothing too ordinary to attract the Lord's attention. When you put your hand to a work, you are not working alone: you are under divine blessing or curse, depending on your faithfulness to His covenant. This elevates daily work and attention to the practical details of obedience.

sens: strong affirmation of a truth
inevitable certainty
H3027V.detail:
1. The word expresses a strong and solid affirmation, as if one were putting strength, figuratively speaking, behind their word. It means: "without a doubt," "certainly." In Proverbs 11:21, "Certainly, the wicked will not go unpunished" asserts with a quiet strength that God's justice will be fulfilled.
2. More specifically, it introduces an inevitable truth: something that cannot not happen. It is less a simple affirmation than a certainty that imposes itself, a judgment that allows no exception. In Proverbs 16:5, "Certainly, he will not go unpunished" asserts that pride will inevitably attract punishment.
H3027V.origine: The Hebrew word יָד (yad) means first and simply "hand." From there comes its figurative use to denote strength, power ("the hand of God"). The adverb "certainly" comes from this image of the hand: to say something "with a sure hand" or "with a firm hand" is to affirm it with certainty and strength. The word is thus used to reinforce an affirmation, just as one would reinforce a gesture by raising the hand with authority.
H3027V.emploi: The word יָד appears about 1,600 times in the Old Testament, first in the literal sense of "hand." Here, in Proverbs, it appears only twice, in Proverbs 11:21 and 16:5, where it functions as an adverb meaning "certainly." It introduces a judgment of wisdom: in both cases, it is the assurance that evil receives its punishment and that divine justice will be fulfilled. This usage is particular to the style of Proverbs and gives the text a quiet and undeniable authority.
H3027V.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that God's promises and threats are not pious wishes, but realities that will be fulfilled. The biblical "certainly" invites us to base our trust not on the appearances of the moment, but on the certainty that divine justice triumphs. It is an invitation to wisdom: to recognize that God truly watches over us, and that evil receives its due.

sens: Organ of the human body that grasps and acts
Power, strength, domination of a person or a nation
Authority, governing power
What is nearby, what one has at hand, what is available
Side, region, part of a territory
H3027W.detail:
1. The hand is primarily the physical organ of the body (Exodus 18:10 speaks of the "hand of the Egyptians," the instrument of their oppression).
2. By extension, the hand denotes the power and strength of someone, the ability to act upon others: one escapes from the "hand" of an enemy just as one escapes the power of someone who wants to dominate us (2 Kings 13:5, where Israel "escaped from the hands of the Syrians").
3. The hand also signifies political authority, the right to govern: Edom revolts "against the authority of Judah" (2 Kings 8:20), meaning it refuses to remain under its power.
4. What one has "at hand" means what one possesses, what is immediately available: the priest replies to David that he has no "ordinary bread at hand" (1 Samuel 21:4), meaning accessible, available bread.
5. The hand can also designate a side, a region, a part of a territory, but this meaning is rare in the provided usages.
H3027W.origine: The Hebrew word yad (יָד) is very ancient, common to Semitic languages. It comes from a root that evokes the action of grasping, taking. In the Old Testament, it is the fundamental word for designating the physical hand, but it quickly enriches itself with figurative meanings: from the organ that acts, it moves to the force that acts, then to the power that controls. This progression from the concrete to the spiritual is characteristic of biblical thought.
H3027W.emploi: The word yad appears thirteen times in the provided usages, mainly in two senses. The primary sense (physical hand, then strength and power) is the most common: it denotes the power of an enemy that one endures or escapes from (Exodus 18:10; 2 Kings 13:5; 2 Kings 17:7). The sense of political authority is attested in passages where a king "reigns" or loses his power (2 Kings 8:20; 2 Chronicles 21:8; 2 Chronicles 21:10; Isaiah 3:6). A third sense, that of what one has "available" or "nearby," appears in domestic passages (1 Samuel 21:3-4). The nuance is always that of a grasp, a capacity to possess or dominate.
H3027W.portee: Meditating on "the hand" in the Bible is a reminder that God controls history. His hands accomplish His will, while human hands, even powerful ones, remain under His authority. This word also invites the reader to reflect on power: the Bible describes it without idealizing, showing that true power belongs to the One who can deliver from oppressors. For the believer, this is a source of confidence.

sens: Part of the body at the end of the arm
Power, strength, mastery
Portion, part, side of a region
Weight (unit of measure)
H3027X.detail:
1. The primary and most concrete meaning: the hand, the limb of the human body. Abraham asks his servant to put his hand under his thigh as a sign of solemn oath (Genesis 24:2, 24:9); it is a gesture of commitment that engages one's entire life.
2. Figuratively, the hand represents the power, strength, or mastery that someone exercises: it is the instrument of action and power. When the Bible speaks of the hand of God or that of a powerful man, it denotes their authority and ability to act.
3. By extension, a hand or a portion designates a part, a portion of a territory or property, what belongs to someone as a share.
4. In commercial and legal contexts (Genesis 24:22), the word can also refer to the weight itself, the unit of measure used to weigh gold, making it a technical term for measuring.
H3027X.origine: The Hebrew word יָד (yad) is very ancient and appears in all Semitic languages. Its basic image is that of the physical limb: the hand that acts, grasps, creates, makes a promise. This is why it naturally extends to the idea of power and mastery: the hand is what executes the will. The gesture of putting one's hand under the thigh in swearing reflects an ancient practice where the body engaged the honor of the one swearing.
H3027X.emploi: The word yad appears about 1,600 times in the Old Testament, making it one of the most frequent words. It is found in all textual genres: narratives, laws, prayers, prophecies. Its meaning varies according to context. In the provided passages, it first denotes the gesture of the oath (Genesis 24:2, 24:9, 47:29): it is a legal and moral act where one puts their life at stake. It also appears as a unit of weight (Genesis 24:22), where it measures the substance of gold. Each usage shows how the concrete (the physical hand) enriches itself with symbolic meanings: commitment, power, divine action.
H3027X.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that our hands and our strength do not completely belong to us: they are subject to God's will. Putting one's hand under another's as a sign of oath expresses voluntary submission and a commitment to fidelity. Moreover, this word invites us to meditate on the hand of God: His acting power, His support, His protection towards those who obey Him. It is also a call to honesty in our commitments and an awareness of what binds us to others.

sens: Member of the human body that is used to take, hold, act
Authority, power, control over someone or something
Possession or mastery
H3028.detail:
1. The hand is the member that allows one to do: hold, build, act. In Ezra 5:8, it is literally in the hands of the workers that "the work goes quickly."
2. The hand represents the power one exercises over someone. Nebuchadnezzar says in Daniel 2:38 that God "has given into your hands" all the peoples for him to dominate. It is by the hand that one strikes, holds back, or releases: in Daniel 3:15, he asks which god will deliver from his hand, that of the mighty king.
3. To possess something "in hand" means to have mastery over it, to be its owner. Ezra 7:25 speaks of the wisdom that Ezra "possesses": it is the knowledge and power he holds and can transmit.
H3028.origine: The Hebrew word יַד (yad) primarily designates the organ of the body. Its basic image — the concrete means of acting and dominating — naturally extends to the notion of power and control. This is why the hand becomes a symbol of authority in Hebrew: to have something in hand is to possess and command it.
H3028.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Greek Old Testament, mainly in the historical and prophetic writings of Ezra and Daniel. It is first used literally to designate the physical organ (Ezra 5:8), then figuratively to express power: the power of the king over his subjects (Daniel 2:38), the power of the living God that no one can resist (Daniel 4:35). The expression "to stretch out the hand" means to threaten or act against someone (Ezra 6:12). The word also nuances into possession or mastery: "to possess" by the Segond translation corresponds to "to have in hand" (Ezra 7:25).
H3028.portee: The word teaches that true power belongs to God alone: His hand dominates kings and empires, and no one can escape it. For the Christian, this reminds us that our lives are not in the hands of chance or the powerful of the world, but in the hands of a sovereign and good God. It is an invitation to trust rather than fear.

sens: Expressing gratitude and admiration towards God
Celebrating God's blessings and power
Giving glory to God through prayer and worship
H3029.detail:
1. To praise is to express gratitude to God for what He has done. When Daniel says "I praise you," he thanks God for giving him wisdom and strength to interpret the king's dream (Daniel 2:23). It is an act of gratitude that acknowledges that everything comes from God.

2. To praise also means to celebrate and magnify who God is — His power, wisdom, goodness. This is why one can praise God "for revealing to me the secret": it emphasizes that only God can do what is impossible. Thus, to praise is to declare the greatness of God.

3. In practice, praising is an act of prayer and worship. Daniel "kneeled down, prayed, and praised his God" (Daniel 6:10): praising is part of the believer's prayer life, kneeling before God to pay Him homage.
H3029.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew verb yada (יָדָה), which literally means "to give the hand" or "to extend the hand." This image evokes the idea of turning towards someone, signaling to them, hence the meaning of "to recognize" and "to thank." To praise God is to extend a hand in recognition, to face Him with gratitude. The Aramaic verb yeda captures this sense of gratitude and acknowledgment.
H3029.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Daniel, and always in Daniel's own words. In Daniel 2:23, Daniel praises God after receiving the interpretation of the dream: he acknowledges that this wisdom comes entirely from God. In Daniel 6:10, praising God is part of Daniel's daily prayer routine, three times a day, even when the king has forbidden prayer. These two uses show that praising is a form of deep prayer, an act of recognition and faithfulness towards God.
H3029.portee: Praising God is an act of faith that acknowledges His power and goodness. For the Christian, it is a reminder that praise is not primarily an emotion, but a conscious decision to recognize what God has done and who He is. Daniel's example also shows that praise persists even in trial: it does not wait for perfect circumstances, but springs from the heart of one who trusts in God.

sens: City in the territory of Zebulun
H3030.detail: Jideala is a small city located in the territory that the tribe of Zebulun received as an inheritance at the time of the division of the promised land. It was situated between Shimron and Bethlehem in the region of Galilee (Joshua 19:15), among a list of twelve cities assigned to this tribe.
H3030.origine: The name Jideala literally means "memorial of God" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: the root meaning "to recall" or "to commemorate" and the divine name El, suggesting that this locality bore a name expressing the memory or honor of God.
H3030.emploi: Jideala appears only once in the Bible, in the list of cities in the territory of Zebulun enumerated in Joshua 19:15. It is among the twelve main cities assigned to the tribe of Zebulun during the division of the promised land under Joshua. This brief mention shows that it was a real but minor locality in the region of Galilee.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah living in the time of Egypt and the desert
H3031.detail: Jidbasch is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is presented as one of the three sons of Abi-Etham, who is himself a descendant of Judah. His brothers are Jizreel and Jischma, and they have a sister named Hatselelponi. He lived in a distant time in the history of Israel, probably during the Egyptian and desert period.
H3031.origine: The name Jidbasch literally means "stout" (robust, stocky). It is a compound Hebrew proper name that likely reflects a physical characteristic or quality attributed to this ancestor. This name belongs to the genealogy of Judah and fits within the tradition of family names of the people of Israel.
H3031.emploi: Jidbasch appears only once in the entire Bible, in chapter 4 of the book of Chronicles. He is mentioned in a genealogical list of the descendants of Judah, a text that enumerates the successive generations and family lines of God's people. This unique mention in 1 Chronicles 4:3 places him among the important ancestors of Judah, although we know nothing else about his life or actions.

sens: Throw dice or small objects to make a decision or randomly designate someone
Divide or share something by drawing lots
Drop something by throwing it forcefully
H3032.detail: 1. Casting lots means throwing dice or numbered objects to leave a decision to chance — a common practice in antiquity to designate someone, share spoils, or settle a matter. The context of the three biblical uses shows this meaning: in Obadiah 1:11 and Nahum 3:10, the enemies plundering Jerusalem and Nineveh "cast lots" on the riches or people, meaning they distribute them by drawing lots — the very act of the soldier casting dice for Christ's garments. 2. By extension, "casting lots" also means making a decision by leaving it to chance (or divine providence), or assigning a share to someone without deliberate choice. In Joel 3:3, the prophet denounces those who "cast lots" on God's people: they share it like spoils.
H3032.origine: The Hebrew verb yadad comes from a root that expresses the idea of throwing or projecting. It is specialized to designate the act of casting lots or dice: yadah means "to throw," and yadid (which shares the same root) means "friend" — perhaps because the lot was also called to settle disputes between friends. The biblical context shows that this is not a profane act: it is an implicit appeal to divine will, as Proverbs 16:33 states (not provided here, but in the background): "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord."
H3032.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the sense of "casting lots." It is used to describe the sharing of spoils after conquest: in Obadiah 1:11 and Nahum 3:10, the victors cast lots on the spoils of Jerusalem and Nineveh. In Joel 3:3, the enemy nations cast lots on the people of Israel itself, treating it like merchandise. The act is presented as an act of plunder and desecration: the lot is no longer an appeal to wisdom, but a practice of oppression.
H3032.portee: This word reminds the reader that the lot, in the Bible, is never a surrender to blind chance: it is an act that recognizes (often unwittingly) the sovereignty of God. When Israel's enemies cast lots on His people, they ignore that it is ultimately the Lord who governs the outcome. This invites the believer to trust in divine providence, even in the darkest circumstances.

sens: someone or something that is dearly loved
what one cherishes above all
the person or thing that one loves passionately
H3033.detail:
1. The word designates someone or something that is the object of deep and personal affection. It is one who is tenderly loved, for whom one has a heart inclination. In Jeremiah 12:7, God speaks of His people as the "object of His love" that He had to deliver into the hands of their enemies — which shows that this term expresses a sincere and painful attachment to let go.
2. By extension, it is the person or thing that one cherishes, protects, and holds dear above all. The context of Jeremiah makes this word an expression of the emotional bond between God and His people, a relationship of chosen and preserved love.
H3033.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to love," "to cherish." It is constructed to designate someone who is loved — literally "the beloved," the person toward whom affection is directed. This root is the same that appears in other biblical terms to express personal and elective love, notably God's love for His people or for His elect.
H3033.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 12:7. There, God expresses His love for Jerusalem and His people, but also the pain of having to abandon them to judgment. This unique occurrence shows that the term was used to speak of an intense and personal emotional bond, a relationship of deep attachment — the realm of tenderness rather than mere sentiment.
H3033.portee: This word reveals that God loves His people with a personal and tender love, not just an abstract decision. The mention of the "object of His love" in the hands of enemies shows that God's love is not indifferent to suffering or separation — He suffers in judging what He loves. For the Christian, this is a comfort: our relationship with God rests on a living and affectionate attachment, not on a cold obligation.

sens: Thank God by recognizing His goodness and His saving acts
Celebrate God through word, song, or public worship
Confess one's sins before God or before others
Acknowledge the name, authority, and majesty of God
H3034.detail:
1. To praise is first to thank God wholeheartedly for what He has done. It is not an empty word, but an act of joyful recognition of God's goodness and mercy. In Psalms 107:1, we cry, "Oh give thanks to the Lord, for He is good; for His steadfast love endures forever!" — it is thanking God for who He is and what He does.
2. Praising includes the public and joyful celebration of God: singing, playing instruments, uniting to magnify His name. In 2 Chronicles 5:13, the musicians and singers "praised the Lord" in unison, and the house of God was filled with His presence.
3. The verb can also mean to confess one's sins, that is, to admit one's faults before God. In Leviticus 5:5, the one who has sinned must confess the sin he has committed — this admission is a form of recognition of God's rightful authority.
4. To praise also means to acknowledge and proclaim the name of God, His power and majesty. In Psalms 54:8, the psalmist says, "I will give thanks to Your name, O Lord!" — he publicly proclaims and honors the Lord.
H3034.origine: The Hebrew verb yadah comes from a root that originally evokes the idea of projecting or throwing (like an arrow or a blow). This image has gradually extended to the meaning of manifesting, showing, publicly recognizing. In Aramaic, the related word yeda means "to praise." The family of the word also includes the name Judah (Yehoudah), which comes from this verb: in Genesis 29:35, Leah gives this name to her son, saying, "I will praise the Lord," expressing her gratitude for the child received.
H3034.emploi: This verb appears 111 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Psalms (over 70 occurrences) and in the historical and poetic books. It carries several nuances depending on the context. In its most common sense, to praise denotes the act of giving thanks publicly: the psalmists praise God alone or invite the assembly to praise Him together (Psalms 107:1). It is a duty of worship (1 Chronicles 16:4: David appointed Levites "to praise the Lord"). The word also means to confess one's faults or admit one's sin: in Leviticus 5:5, the sinner "shall confess the sin" — this admission acknowledges God's holiness. Finally, to praise can emphasize the act of proclaiming or publicly recognizing the name and majesty of God, as in Psalms 54:8.
H3034.portee: This word reminds the believer that praise is a natural and joyful response to the discovery of God's goodness and mercy. It is not a burdensome obligation, but the expression of heartfelt recognition. Praise also unites the people around God and turns their gaze toward His greatness. Confessing one's sins, understood in this same verb, shows that true praise passes through honesty: recognizing our faults before God is also a form of worship and submission to His justice.

sens: son of Zechariah, chief of the tribe of Manasseh during the time of King David
H3035G.detail: Jiddo is a figure from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:21, where he is identified as the son of Zechariah and as the leader of the tribe of Manasseh, specifically the half of this tribe that lived east of the Jordan, in Gilead. His role seems to have been administrative or military under the reign of King David.
H3035G.origine: The name Jiddo means "opportune" or "lovable" in Hebrew. It is derived from a root that expresses the idea of what is suitable or pleasant. This name reflects the Hebrew conventions of the time when names often carried a positive meaning or a blessing.
H3035G.emploi: Jiddo appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 27:21. He is listed in an administrative record from the time of King David, establishing the tribal leaders of Israel. This list enumerates the appointed chiefs responsible for administering each of the twelve tribes. Jiddo thus represents a figure of local authority, likely an administrator or military leader in charge of the half-tribe of Manasseh located east of the Jordan.

sens: Man from the time of the exile and the return to Jerusalem
H3035H.detail: Jaddaï is a man mentioned only once in Scripture, at the time when the Israelites returning from exile in Babylon had to purify themselves by sending away their foreign wives. He is among those who had contracted these mixed marriages and who separated from them to obey the order to restore the purity of the people (Ezra 10:43).
H3035H.origine: The name means "opportune" or "lovable" in Hebrew. It belongs to the family of common Israelite names, with no known direct genealogical link to the other Iddo mentioned elsewhere in Scripture (notably the prophet and governor of Manasseh during David's time).
H3035H.emploi: Jaddaï is cited only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:43, in the list of men who, upon returning from exile (around 458 BC), sent away their foreign wives. This moment in Israel's history marks a major crisis: the people, freshly returned from captivity, must take drastic measures to preserve their religious and cultural identity. The name of Jaddaï, among many others, testifies to the extent of this problem and the personal cost that this rectification required.

sens: A Jewish family leader during the exile and return
A builder of the walls of Jerusalem
H3036.detail:
1. Jadon is a Jewish man from Meronoth, a town in Judah, who lived during the time of the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 3:7).
2. He actively participated in the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem under the leadership of Nehemiah, working alongside other family leaders and their men to restore the city's fortifications (Nehemiah 3:7).
H3036.origine: The name Jadon means "thankful" or "one who gives thanks," derived from the Hebrew root yadah which expresses the act of giving glory or acknowledging. This name reflects the piety of the Jews of that time, where fathers would give their children names expressing their faith in God.
H3036.emploi: Jadon appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:7. He is mentioned among the family leaders and workers who were rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem. This collective work, led by Nehemiah, took about 52 days and represented a key moment in the restoration of the Jewish people after the Babylonian exile.
H3036.portee: The mention of Jadon reminds us that the reconstruction of Jerusalem was not the work of one or two individuals, but of an entire community mobilized. His commitment and that of his men testify to the determination of the Jews returned from exile to rebuild their city and their religious life. It is an example of personal involvement in a communal work for the glory of God.

sens: Leader of the people who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah
High priest, son and successor of Johanan
H3037G.detail:
1. Jaddua is one of the leaders of Israel who, upon returning from exile, affixed his seal to the renewed covenant document with God under the leadership of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:21). He represents the families that solemnly committed to observing the Law of the Lord.
2. Jaddua also served as high priest of Israel, succeeding his father or predecessor Johanan. He is probably the last high priest mentioned in the Old Testament, and he would have lived during the time of Alexander the Great, thus marking the end of the period of the Second Temple described in the biblical texts.
H3037G.origine: The name Jaddua means "knower" or "one who knows," derived from the Hebrew root expressing knowledge. This name reflects an important characteristic in biblical culture: knowledge, particularly of God and His Law, was considered a major quality for a spiritual leader and a responsible person of the people.
H3037G.emploi: Jaddua appears only once in the Old Testament, in Nehemiah 10:21, where he is listed among the leaders and Levites who signed the covenant at the time of the restoration of the temple and Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. According to later Jewish tradition, he was also the high priest who knew Alexander the Great. His presence in Nehemiah's document testifies to his religious and civil authority in Israel in the century following the return from exile.
H3037G.portee: Jaddua embodies the faithfulness of the people returned from exile to their commitment to God and His Law. His role as high priest reminds us that the restored community life of Israel rested on men who committed to transmitting and keeping the divine revelation. For the Christian reader, this renewal of the covenant illustrates the biblical principle that each generation must renew its decision to follow God.

sens: High priest of Jerusalem, son and successor of Johanan
H3037H.detail: Jaddua is the name of a Jewish high priest from the Levitical lineage, mentioned in the records of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 12:11). He was the son and successor of Johanan in the supreme charge of worship at the Temple. Biblical sources place him during the time of Darius the Persian and probably during the time of Alexander the Great. He is the last high priest mentioned by name in the Old Testament (Nehemiah 12:22).
H3037H.origine: The name Jaddua means "one who knows" in Hebrew, derived from a root evoking knowledge or recognition. This name was borne by the descendants of Levi, the tribe dedicated to the service of the Temple, reflecting the religious importance of this family in Jerusalem after the Exile.
H3037H.emploi: Jaddua is mentioned twice in the Bible. First in Nehemiah 12:11, where he is named as the son of Johanan in the genealogy of the high priests. Then in Nehemiah 12:22, where he appears among the Levitical leaders of his time, alongside Eliashib, Jojada, and Johanan, during the reign of King Darius of Persia. These references place Jaddua in the period of the restoration of the Temple and the reorganization of the Jewish community after the return from the Babylonian Exile.

sens: A Levite from the family of Merari
The leader of one of the three choirs of the temple
The one whose name appears at the beginning of certain psalms
H3038G.detail:
1. Jeduthun is a Levite, a member of the tribe of Levi who served God during the united monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Kishi and the father of several children, including Obed-Edom. He is also known by the name Ethan (1 Chronicles 6:44).
2. Jeduthun leads one of the three major choirs of the temple in Jerusalem, alongside Asaph and Heman. His sons and descendants also perform the choir service and guard the temple gates (1 Chronicles 16:38; 2 Chronicles 5:12).
3. The name Jeduthun appears at the beginning of three psalms (Psalms 39, 62, and 77), likely indicating that this choir leader directed the singing of these psalms in glory to the Lord (Psalms 62:1).
H3038G.origine: The name Jeduthun means "the one who praises" or "praise." It is the name of a Levitical musician who plays a major role in organizing temple worship. His sons and grandsons continue his musical service before the Lord.
H3038G.emploi: Jeduthun appears about fifteen times in the Bible, mainly in the Book of Chronicles (16, 25) and in the titles of the Psalms. He is mentioned as a prominent choir leader during the time of King David (1 Chronicles 16:42) and as one of the three recognized masters of sacred music, alongside Asaph and Heman (2 Chronicles 5:12). During the time of King Hezekiah, his descendants continue this role (2 Chronicles 29:14). In the psalms, his name marks the musical notation or the choir leader responsible for singing the psalm.
H3038G.portee: Jeduthun reminds us that biblical worship of God is not a matter of solitary individuals, but an organized, collective, and joyful service. His life shows how sacred music and singing hold a central place in worship; this is why the Lord chose to appoint musicians as His servants to lead the people in praise. His legacy—perpetuated by his descendants—also illustrates how the service of God can be passed down from generation to generation within the same family.

sens: Levite from the family of Merari
Choir leader of the temple
H3038H.detail: Jeduthun is a Levite from the tribe of Levi, belonging to the family of Merari. He is the father of Galal (see 1 Chronicles 9:16). He led one of the three major choirs of the temple in Jerusalem, responsible for conducting the songs and praises during worship (Nehemiah 11:17 mentions him as the leader of praise in prayer).
H3038H.origine: The name Jeduthun means "who praises" or "the one who praises," evoking praise and sacred music. It is a typical Hebrew name for Levitical musicians of the temple.
H3038H.emploi: Jeduthun is mentioned twice in the Hebrew Bible. First in 1 Chronicles 9:16, where he appears in the genealogy of the Levites who returned from exile and settled in Jerusalem, as the father of Galal. Then in Nehemiah 11:17, he is named again in a list of Levites with a major role: the one who "sang praise in prayer." He was one of the three choir leaders of the temple whose descendants continued the liturgical service.
H3038H.portee: Jeduthun illustrates the crucial role of music and praise in Israelite worship. Entrusted to experienced Levites, this service of song and prayer shows that praise was not a spontaneous individual act, but an official and organized function at the heart of the religious life of the people. His name, "the one who praises," reminds everyone of the importance of leading and cultivating collective praise.

sens: The one who is tenderly and preferentially loved
The one who is cherished with a particular affection
That which is charming, pleasant, worthy of love
H3039A.detail:
1. The beloved is one who is cherished with a special affection, above others. He is the object of tender and preferential love. In Deuteronomy 33:12, Benjamin is called the "beloved of the Lord," expressing the tenderness and special protection that God grants him.
2. The word also designates one whose deliverance is sought or whom one desires to see safe: the "beloved" of God that must be saved (Psalms 60:7 and 108:7). It is a term of affection and closeness.
3. That which is lovable, charming, and attracts affection. The dwellings of the Lord are described as "lovely" in Psalms 84:2: they inspire desire and reverence through their beauty and holiness.
H3039A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses love and affection. It is related to terms that denote friendship and tenderness. It is a typically biblical word to express elective and preferential love, especially in contexts where God chooses someone or where a particular affection is manifested. The word also evokes what is sweet, pleasant to the heart.
H3039A.emploi: This word appears seven times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and in texts of blessing or praise. In Deuteronomy 33:12, it characterizes Benjamin as especially loved by God. In the Psalms, it designates the faithful whom God loves and protects (60:7, 108:7, 127:2). It also qualifies the divine dwellings as lovely and desirable (84:2). In Isaiah 5:1, it appears in the famous parable of the vineyard, where the beloved (the owner) represents God Himself. Jeremiah 11:15 uses it to evoke what is dear to the heart. The word always carries an emotional weight: the beloved is one who is cared for, cherished.
H3039A.portee: This word reminds the believer that God loves His own with an elective and personal love. It is not a fleeting sentiment, but a persistent affection that protects and provides. Meditating on this divine tenderness invites trust and gratitude. The word also encourages the faithful to recognize what is lovable about God and to cultivate affection for the Lord and for those He loves.

sens: Deep and tender affection between two people
Personal attachment and tenderness
Desire for good and union with the one loved
H3039B.detail:
1. The word designates love in the sense of a deep feeling of affection and personal tenderness. It is the love that unites two beings, filled with sweetness and intimacy. Psalm 45 is described as a "Song of Love": it celebrates the joy of union and the tender attachment between husband and wife (Psalms 45:1).
2. It is also love as an ardent desire for the one loved, an affinity of the heart that seeks union and the good of the other. In this nuptial poem, this love is manifested in the beauty and joy of marriage.
H3039B.origine: The Hebrew word yedidah comes from a root meaning "to cherish," "to love tenderly." It shares a family with yedid, which means "beloved" or "cherished"—the one who is the object of this affection. In Hebrew poetry, this word evokes personal and tender love, distinct from other forms of love: it is the affection that binds two hearts.
H3039B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible. It is found in the title of Psalm 45, which is a nuptial poem celebrating royal marriage. This psalm describes the beauty of the bride, her magnificence, and the love that unites the spouses. The word "love" in the title indicates the tone and subject of the song: it is a song of affection and marital tenderness.
H3039B.portee: This word reminds us that personal love—the tender affection between two beings—is a divine and poetic gift. The Bible does not shy away from celebrating the joy of marriage and the attachment of the heart. For the believer, this affirms that human tenderness and marital union are beautiful and noble realities worthy of being sung.

sens: woman from the divided monarchy period, wife of King Amon
mother of King Josiah
H3040.detail:
1. Jedida is a woman mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when her son Josiah becomes king (2 Kings 22:1). She is the wife of King Amon and thus belongs to the royal family of Judah.
2. She is best known as the mother of King Josiah, one of the most significant kings of Judah, who reigned for 31 years and undertook a major religious reform.
H3040.origine: Her name means "beloved" in Hebrew. It is a name that expresses affection and suggests that she was dear to her family. She is the daughter of Adaiah, from the city of Botskath.
H3040.emploi: Jedida appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 22:1, where she is presented as the wife of King Amon and the mother of Josiah. This brief mention indicates her role in the royal succession of Judah, although no details about her life or actions are provided by the Bible.

sens: Name given to Solomon by the prophet Nathan, meaning "beloved of the Lord"
H3041.detail: 1. This is the name that the prophet Nathan gave to Solomon shortly after his birth, as a sign of divine favor upon this child born to David and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:25). This name expresses that God particularly loved this son and had chosen him for a special destiny in the divine plan.
H3041.origine: The name Jedidja comes from the Hebrew yedîd (beloved, dear) and yah (abbreviation of the name of God, Yahweh). It literally means "beloved of the Lord" or "the one whom the Lord loves." It is a theophoric name — a name that includes a reference to God — common in Israel to express the feelings of gratitude and trust of parents towards the Lord.
H3041.emploi: Jedidja is another name for Solomon, the son that David and Bathsheba had after their first son died a few days after birth (see 2 Samuel 12). The prophet Nathan gave this name to the child on behalf of God, indicating that despite the serious sin of his parents, God granted His grace to this child and destined him for a great role. Solomon retained his original name (Solomon, which means "the peaceful one") throughout his life, but this prophetic name of Jedidja reminded that his life was marked by the special love of the Lord.
H3041.portee: This name reveals that even when God's servants fail, His mercy towards their children remains intact. For the believer, Jedidja teaches that we are all "beloved of the Lord" if we belong to God: not by our merits, but by His free grace that chooses and adopts us.

sens: man from the tribe of Simeon during the divided monarchy
H3042G.detail: Jedaja is a man from the tribe of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah are divided. He appears in the genealogy of Ziza, as an ancestor of this Simeonite family (1 Chronicles 4:37).
H3042G.origine: The name Jedaja means "praised by Jehovah" or "Jehovah praises" — a theophoric name that evokes the praise that God grants. It is a compound form of the Hebrew verb meaning "to praise" and the divine name Jehovah. Such names expressed the hope of parents that their child would be blessed and praised by God.
H3042G.emploi: Jedaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:37, where he appears in the genealogy of the tribe of Simeon. He is presented as the son of Shimei and the father of Allon. He is a distant ancestor of Ziza, who belongs to this same tribe. His name indicates that his family honored the God of Israel and hoped for His blessing.

sens: Man from the time of the Exile and the Return, son of Harumaph
H3042H.detail: Jedaja is a man living during the time of the Exile and the Return to Jerusalem, son of Harumaph. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:10, where he is presented as one of the men who participated in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from Exile.
H3042H.origine: The name Jedaja means "praised by the Lord" or "the one whom the Lord has praised." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: yedid ("beloved, dear") or a form of the verb yada ("to know, to praise") and Yah ("the Lord"). This name reflects the parents' trust in God and their acknowledgment of His kindness.
H3042H.emploi: Jedaja appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:10. He is mentioned among the workers who rebuilt a section of the walls of Jerusalem under the leadership of Nehemiah, after the return from Exile in Babylon. His work was "opposite his house," indicating that he was responsible for repairing the portion of the wall adjacent to his own dwelling. This participation demonstrates the commitment of the Judeans who returned from Exile to restore their city and its defenses.
H3042H.portee: The account in Nehemiah 3, which lists the workers on the wall, reminds us that the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the Exile was not the work of an elite, but that of the entire community — ordinary men, entire families, each working "opposite their house." Jedaja represents these nameless faithful whose obedience and labor contributed to the restoration of God's people. It is an invitation to see the value of humble and communal service in God's purpose.

sens: Son of Benjamin, family chief in the tribe of Benjamin during the patriarchs' time
H3043G.detail: Jediaël is a man from the tribe of Benjamin whose name means "God makes known." He is presented in 1 Chronicles 7:6 as one of the three sons of Benjamin, alongside Bela and Beker. His descendants formed an important house: his son Bilhan had several children (Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Kenaana, Zethan, Tarsis, and Ahishachar), and all these men of the house of Jediaël were valiant warriors, numbering seventeen thousand two hundred fighting men (1 Chronicles 7:10-11).
H3043G.origine: The name Jediaël comes from two Hebrew terms: "Yah" or "El" (God) and a verb meaning "to make known." It expresses the idea that God makes Himself known or makes His will known. This type of theophoric name, where a person's name proclaims an action of God, was common among ancient Israelites.
H3043G.emploi: Jediaël appears three times in the Bible, all occurrences found in 1 Chronicles 7. He is first listed as one of the three major sons of Benjamin (verse 6), indicating that he was a founding ancestor of a clan within the tribe. Verses 10 and 11 complete the genealogical picture by listing his children and emphasizing that his descendants produced a large and powerful lineage of warriors — seventeen thousand two hundred men able to fight. This presentation in a genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin shows the importance of this family in the history of Israel.

sens: Warrior of David
Son of Shimri
H3043H.detail: Jediaël is a warrior among the valiant men of David. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:45, where he is presented as the son of Shimri, with his brother Jocha alongside him. This passage lists the military heroes who served King David, and Jediaël occupies a place among these men renowned for their courage and strength in battle.
H3043H.origine: The name Jediaël means "God makes known" in Hebrew (from "yada," to know, and "El," God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name, expressing the belief that God reveals or makes known His will. This type of name was common in Israel to express the relationship of the bearer with the divine.
H3043H.emploi: Jediaël appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 11:45. He is a warrior during the divided monarchy, son of Shimri and brother of Jocha. He is listed among David's warriors, indicating that he distinguished himself by his courage and dedication to the king. This unique mention places him in the context of David's faithful military servants, without the Bible providing further details about his life or particular exploits.

sens: Military leader of Manasseh who rallied to David at Ziklag
H3043I.detail: Jediaël is a chief of thousands (that is, a military leader commanding a thousand men) from the tribe of Manasseh. He is among those who joined David upon his return to Ziklag, before David became king of Israel (1 Chronicles 12:20). His name means "God makes known" in Hebrew, reflecting the trust that his parents placed in divine revelation.
H3043I.origine: The name Jediaël is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Yah" (God) and "yadaʿ" (to know, to make known). It is a theophoric name, formed like many Israelite names to express a religious conviction: that God reveals or makes known His purpose. This type of name was particularly common among the leaders and warriors of the chosen people.
H3043I.emploi: Jediaël appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:20. He is presented as one of the military leaders of Manasseh who rallied to David when he withdrew to Ziklag, before his reign. He is mentioned among other warriors and officers who recognized David as their leader, indicating that he belonged to the military elite of his time and was a trustworthy man worthy of commanding a thousand men.

sens: Gatekeeper of the temple in Jerusalem, son of Meschélémia
Man from the tribe of Levi, from the family of Korah
H3043J.detail:
1. Jediaël is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:2. He is the second son of Meschélémia, a Levite responsible for guarding the gates of the temple in Jerusalem. He is part of the Korahite lineage, a family of Levites with special responsibilities in worship.

2. His name means "God makes known." Like the other sons of Meschélémia, Jediaël holds an important position in the temple service: that of a gatekeeper. This role required trust and faithfulness, as the gatekeepers controlled access to the holy place and ensured the security of the temple.
H3043J.origine: The name Jediaël comes from Hebrew and combines two elements: "Yod" (God) and "diaël" (makes known). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God, which was common for children of Levitical families dedicated to divine service.
H3043J.emploi: Jediaël appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:2, in the list of the sons of Meschélémia. This passage enumerates the descendants of Meschélémia who served as gatekeepers of the temple. This shows that Jediaël was part of a family of worship servants and had been given the responsibility of overseeing one of the entrances to the sanctuary. His inclusion in this genealogy highlights the importance of his role in the organization of the religious service of the kingdom of Judah.

sens: A son of Nahor and Milcah
A grandson of Abraham through the younger branch of the family
H3044.detail:
1. Jidlaph is a character from the patriarchal period, son of Nahor and Milcah. He appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:22, in a genealogy listing the descendants of Nahor.
2. He represents the family lineage of Abraham through his uncle Nahor — the branch that settled in Mesopotamia while Abraham went to Canaan. His brothers include Buz (from whom Job is said to descend according to tradition) and Kemuel (ancestor of the Arameans). This enumeration shows how God blessed Abraham's descendants beyond just the covenant line.
H3044.origine: The name Jidlaph means "he who weeps" in Hebrew, derived from the root dalap (to flow, to drip, to weep). It is a meaningful name, like many ancient Hebrew names, that expresses a feeling or circumstance. The narrative context does not explain why this name was given to him.
H3044.emploi: Jidlaph appears only once in Genesis 22:22, in the list of Nahor's children mentioned after the sacrifice of Isaac. This enumeration serves to remind that God made promises not only to Abraham but also to the extended family: Nahor had twelve sons, a number that evokes abundance and the fulfillment of divine promises. Jidlaph is mentioned among his full brothers, Buz, Kemuel, Késed, and Bethuel, thus forming the generation that settled in Aram.
H3044.portee: Jidlaph reminds us that God's blessings extend beyond just the heir of the promise. Although he is not in the direct line of Abraham (which passes through Isaac and then Jacob), Jidlaph and his brothers also receive offspring and prosperity. It is an invitation to see that God generously provides for all members of His family according to His purposes.

sens: To have knowledge of something, to learn
To know someone, to recognize, to identify
To understand, to discern, to distinguish
To know carnally (intimate union)
To master, to be skilled in
To reveal, to make known
H3045.detail: 1. To possess knowledge of a fact or reality: to understand what is happening or what is hidden. When God says to Adam, "God knows that on the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil" (Genesis 3:5), He speaks of the knowledge of good and evil that humans do not yet have. It also means to learn something: in Exodus 16:6, Moses tells the people, "you shall know that it is the Lord who brought you out." 2. To recognize someone, to personally identify: "How will we know the word that the Lord has not spoken?" (Deuteronomy 18:21) means to know, to distinguish the true prophetic word from the false. 3. To understand and discern nuances: to perceive the difference between things. The wise man in Ecclesiastes 9:11 possesses knowledge, but this does not guarantee success. 4. Intimate union between two people (specific sense in biblical Hebrew): "Adam knew Eve his wife" (Genesis 4:1) refers to the marital act. 5. To master a field, to be competent: "Joseph was a wise and intelligent man" implies a form of know-how. 6. To make known, to reveal: "I will charge you with your ways... And you shall know that I am the Lord" (Ezekiel 7:9) means that God will make Himself known through His acts.
H3045.origine: This Hebrew root is very ancient and very common in the Old Testament. It primarily expresses the idea of perceiving through the senses, then retaining that perception in the mind. It is akin to the image of knowledge acquired through direct experience: one knows because one has seen, observed, or been close to. The same root appears in many biblical contexts, from the simplest (to recognize someone) to the deepest (to know God means to have a personal relationship with Him). Biblical Aramaic has an equivalent word.
H3045.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, with over 870 occurrences. It constantly appears in Genesis to describe what characters learn or discover: Adam knows he is naked (Genesis 3:7), Abraham knows that Sarah will have a son (Genesis 18:21). In Exodus, God repeatedly states that He will make Himself known through His plagues (Exodus 7:5, 7:17, 14:4). The word thus covers a wide range: daily knowledge (Exodus 3:7: "I have seen the suffering of my people"), recognition (Genesis 24:14: to recognize the one who will be Isaac's wife), marital intimacy (Genesis 4:1), and divine revelation (Exodus 6:7: "you shall know that I am the Lord"). Its meaning varies according to the context, but it always denotes knowledge that is acquired or communicated.
H3045.portee: This word reveals a biblical theology of knowledge. To know is not merely an abstract mental operation, but a concrete experience: one knows God by seeing Him act, by experiencing the consequences. For the believer, to "know" that the Lord is sovereign and that there is a difference between good and evil is not theoretical — it is the foundation of obedience. The word also invites discernment: in a world of lies, knowing the truth requires an openness to God's revelation.

sens: To have knowledge of something, to be informed of a fact
H3046.detail: 1. The fundamental meaning is that of "to know" or "to be acquainted with": to acquire or possess knowledge of something. It is to understand a fact, information, or reality. For example, in Ezra 4:12, the king must "know" that the Jews are rebuilding Jerusalem — this involves having precise information about an action. In Daniel 5:21, Nebuchadnezzar must "acknowledge" (in the sense of becoming aware and accepting) that the supreme God reigns — this is coming to knowledge and acceptance of a fundamental truth.
H3046.origine: The Hebrew verb יְדַע (yada) expresses the action of knowing, of having knowledge. Its root primarily denotes concrete and direct experience: to know someone means to have met and experienced them. The word then extends to all forms of knowledge, information, and understanding. It often carries the idea of knowledge that is acquired or received, not just innate.
H3046.emploi: This verb appears 42 times in the provided usages, concentrated in the books of Ezra and Daniel, especially in official and solemn situations. In Ezra, it expresses the transmission of official information: the king must be informed of a decree, a law, a fact. In Daniel, the context is that of divine revelation and mysterious knowledge: Daniel must know the secrets of the king (Daniel 2:23), Nebuchadnezzar must "acknowledge" or become aware that God reigns (Daniel 4:26, 5:21). The verb thus takes on a nuance of progressive revelation, of increasing awareness.
H3046.portee: For the Christian reader, this word shows that knowing God or a divine truth is not a simple intellectual act: it is receiving a revelation, experiencing it, and particularly — as in the story of Nebuchadnezzar — recognizing His sovereignty. This word invites us to pray that God makes His will known to us, while reminding us that this knowledge transforms the one who receives it.

sens: Member of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H3047.detail: Jada is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the tribe of Judah, living during the time of the divided monarchy (after the reign of Solomon). He appears only in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, son of Hezron. Jada was the son of Onam and the brother of Shammai (1 Chronicles 2:28); he had two sons, Jether and Jonathan (1 Chronicles 2:32).
H3047.origine: The name Jada means "He knows" or "The one who knows," derived from the Hebrew root yadaʿ (יָדַע), which means "to know." This name expressed assurance or certainty, qualities valued in Israelite culture. The name belongs to a family where each generation bears a name recalling a divine action or quality: Onam (father of Jada), Shammai (brother of Jada), Nadab and Abishur (nephews of Jada) follow this same pattern of significant names.
H3047.emploi: Jada appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the first book of Chronicles, chapter 2, which lists the genealogies of Judah. In 1 Chronicles 2:28, he is presented as the son of Onam and brother of Shammai. In 1 Chronicles 2:32, we learn that he had two sons: Jether, who died without children, and Jonathan. These two verses constitute the only biblical mention of Jada; he is a secondary figure, known only by his place in the genealogical chain of Jerahmeel.

sens: Levitical priest mentioned in the lists of the temple reconstruction after the exile to Babylon
Son of the priest Jojarib
Name meaning 'The Lord has known'
H3048G.detail:
1. Jedaeja is a Levitical priest whose name appears in the official documents of the return from exile in Judah. He is listed among the priests who resumed service in the temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity, as indicated in the list of 1 Chronicles 9:10 where he is named alongside other important priests.

2. He is identified as the son of Jojarib (Nehemiah 11:10), placing him in a prominent priestly family: Jojarib is himself a chief of a Levitical family.

3. His Hebrew name literally means "The Lord has known," reflecting his parents' trust in God and expressing the certainty that God knew him and had chosen him for priestly service.
H3048G.origine: The name Jedaeja is composed of two elements: "Yah" (the Lord, abbreviated as "Yah") and "daah" which means "to know." It is a typical theophoric name among the Hebrews, where the divine name is associated with an action or attribute of God. The form "Jedaeja" appears in genealogical and administrative lists of the temple, showing that this name was borne by recognizable and respected priestly families in the reconstituted Jewish community.
H3048G.emploi: Jedaeja is mentioned four times in the official records of the post-exilic restoration: in 1 Chronicles 9:10 in the context of the initial establishment of temple worship, then in Nehemiah 11:10 among the priests living in Jerusalem, in Nehemiah 12:6 in the genealogy of the heads of priestly families, and in Nehemiah 12:19 as the head of a family represented by his descendant Uzzi. These mentions clearly designate him as an important figure in the Jewish clergy of the early post-exilic period, responsible for the organization and continuity of worship in the rebuilt temple. Several individuals bearing this name may be attested, but all belong to the same priestly elite.

sens: Priest of Jerusalem during the divided monarchy
Head of a family of priests who served in the temple
H3048H.detail:
1. Jedaeja is primarily a priest of Jerusalem mentioned under King David, to whom the second lot in the rotation of priests serving in the temple is assigned (1 Chronicles 24:7).
2. His descendants formed an important priestly family: nine hundred sixty-three sons of Jedaeja returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and resettled in Jerusalem (Ezra 2:36 and Nehemiah 7:39).
H3048H.origine: The name Jedaeja means "Jehovah has known" or "Jehovah knows": it associates the divine name Jehovah (YHWH) with the idea that God knows the one who bears it. It is a typical theophoric name of ancient Israel, expressing the personal relationship between God and man.
H3048H.emploi: Jedaeja appears three times in the biblical texts, always in relation to temple worship. He is first a priest in the organization established by King David during the monarchy (1 Chronicles 24). Then, his descendants are mentioned during the return from Babylonian exile in the fifth century BCE, showing the continuity of the Israelite priesthood. The lists in Ezra and Nehemiah (which are almost identical) attest to the numerical importance and authority of this family of priests in Jerusalem.

sens: Priest of Jerusalem at the time of the return from exile
H3048I.detail: 1. Jedaeja is a priest mentioned in the book of Nehemiah as one of the leaders of the priests at the time when Joshua led the people back from exile (Nehemiah 12:7). His name appears among the important names of those who led worship in Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity.
H3048I.origine: The name Jedaeja means "Jehovah has known" in Hebrew: it is composed of the divine name Jah (Jehovah) and the verb yada, which means "to know." It is a theophoric name, meaning it bears the name of God, which was common among priestly families in Israel.
H3048I.emploi: Jedaeja appears twice in the book of Nehemiah, both passages mentioning the priests and their responsibilities in the temple of Jerusalem at the time of the return from exile. In Nehemiah 12:7, he is cited among the leaders of the priests and their brothers at the time of Joshua. In Nehemiah 12:21, he is mentioned again, this time in connection with Nethaneel, possibly his descendant or successor. These references show that Jedaeja was a prominent figure among the clergy who reorganized temple worship after the Babylonian exile.

sens: Man who returned from the Babylonian exile
Donor in the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem
H3048J.detail:
1. Jedaeja is a man who lived during the time of the return from exile, after the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. He appears in the book of Zechariah as one of the people who returned from Babylon (Zechariah 6:10).
2. Along with Heldai and Tobijah, Jedaeja brings valuable gifts to the prophet Zechariah, gifts that will be used to make a crown intended for Joshua the high priest. These crowns will then be kept in the temple of the Lord as a memorial of these generous donors (Zechariah 6:14).
H3048J.origine: The name Jedaeja means "the Lord has known" or "the Lord knows." It is composed of the divine name Yah (the Lord) and the verb yada (to know), expressing the certainty that God knows and watches over the one who bears this name. It is a typical name from the time of exile and return, reflecting trust in God's knowledge and benevolence towards His people.
H3048J.emploi: Jedaeja is mentioned twice in the book of Zechariah, during the prophetic vision that accompanies the return of the exiles from Babylon. He is among the men who went to Jerusalem after the captivity and who support the reconstruction of the temple.
