Zechariah designates him as one of the three bearers of gifts (along with Heldai and Tobijah) who bring silver and gold to the prophet. These exceptional gifts will be transformed into honorary crowns, and the name Jedaeja will be preserved as a memorial in the temple, thus marking the prominent role of these men in the spiritual and material restoration of the Jewish community.
H3048J.portee: Jedaeja embodies the faithfulness of the exiles who returned to God and their willingness to contribute to the reconstruction of the temple, the center of Israel's spiritual life. His act of generosity reminds us that the return from exile is not only a political restoration but also a spiritual one, where everyone contributes their part to God's work. His name, which means that the Lord has known, assures that God recognizes and honors those who work for His glory.

sens: Person who claims to communicate with the dead or consult spirits
Person who claims to be in contact with a "familiar spirit" supposed to reveal the future or hidden secrets
Diviner or magician who practices necromancy (evocation of the dead)
H3049.detail:
1. It is primarily a person who claims to be able to speak to the dead or to contact invisible spirits. They assert that these spirits speak to them and confide secrets. In 1 Samuel 28:3, Saul "had removed from the land those who consult the dead": these individuals formed a recognized class in Israel, but were forbidden by the Law.

2. The term also refers to one who possesses or claims to possess a "familiar spirit" — an invisible force or supposedly benevolent spirit that whispers in their ear. This "spirit" is supposed to enable them to predict the future or reveal hidden things. It is an occult companion, in a sense.

3. More broadly, it is a diviner or magician who practices divination and necromancy. In Deuteronomy 18:11, this character is listed among those who "consult spirits or inquire of the dead": they are part of a set of occult practices that the Law of Moses strictly forbids.
H3049.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to know" or "to have knowledge." The one who evokes spirits is therefore literally "the one who knows" — but a knowledge obtained through occult means, by consulting the dead or spirits, not through the wisdom of God. It is a false knowledge, a counterfeit of true knowledge.
H3049.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in a context of strict prohibition. It is mentioned in the Law of Moses (Leviticus 19:31; 20:6-27; Deuteronomy 18:11) where God commands Israel not to turn to these practitioners. The histories of Israel report that righteous kings expelled them (1 Samuel 28:3; 2 Kings 23:24), while unfaithful kings tolerated or consulted them (2 Kings 21:6; 2 Chronicles 33:6). The prophets Isaiah denounce them as impostors (Isaiah 8:19; 19:3). The word therefore never has a positive connotation in the Bible.
H3049.portee: This word reminds that the people of God should not seek to know the future or mysteries through occult practices or communication with the dead. The Bible offers a clear path: to hear God through His prophets, His Law, and His wisdom. Addressing spirits diverts attention from God and submits to hostile powers. For the Christian, this word warns: true knowledge and true security come from God alone, not from occult sciences.

sens: The complete divine name of God, Yahweh, in its short and poetic form
In praises and prayers, the direct invocation of the God of Israel
The Lord as the source of salvation, strength, and protection
H3050.detail:
1. "Yah" is a brief and concentrated form of the complete divine name Yahweh (יהוה): it is like saying "the Lord" instead of pronouncing His full name. The Hebrews used this short form especially in songs and acclamations, where it sounded powerful. In Exodus 15:2, Moses sings: "The Lord is my strength," and this name alone summarizes all the power and identity of God.
2. This name often appears at the beginning of the Psalms as an invocation — a direct call to God to listen. Psalm 94:12 says: "Blessed is the man whom you chasten, O Lord!" The name alone is sufficient to address God; it is an intimate and passionate way to pray.
3. In most usages, "Yah" is the God who hears distress, who saves, and who restores life. Psalm 118:5 testifies: "Out of my distress I called on the Lord; the Lord answered me and set me free." The divine name there summarizes alone the God who responds to the cries of His people.
H3050.origine: "Yah" comes from the root of the complete divine name Yahweh (יהוה, H3068), which means "The One who is" or "The One who exists." This short form was the one shouted in liturgical acclamations and fervent prayers. It often appears in composition in Hebrew proper names (Jeremiah, Isaiah, etc.), where it carries the weight of the sacred name in a more compact space. The short form retained all the authority of the complete form while being lighter and more melodic for hymns.
H3050.emploi: "Yah" occurs 46 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, and almost exclusively in the Psalms, as well as a few poetic passages from Isaiah and the Song of Songs. The Segond always translates it as "Lord." This name appears especially at the beginning of the Psalms of praise (Psalms 146-150) as a call to celebrate God, and in prayers of supplication or thanksgiving (Psalms 118, 135). Generally placed in apostrophe — one speaks directly to God — it marks the intimacy of the dialogue with the Lord. It is a name for living prayer, not for historical narration; that is why it is rarely found elsewhere than in songs and laments.
H3050.portee: For the believer who prays and praises, "Yah" is a call to intimacy with God: by pronouncing this short and powerful name, one turns directly to Him as to a Father who listens. These verses teach that living prayer — whether a cry of distress or a song of joy — does not need elaborate discourse: a single divine name, cried from the heart, is enough for God to hear and respond.

sens: To hand something to someone, to gift or entrust its use to them
To place, arrange, put in position
To provide, supply, procure what is necessary
To attribute, acknowledge in words (honor, glory, praise)
To allow, grant, consent to
To go away, depart, move (specific usage)
H3051.detail:
1. To hand something to someone: the most common and straightforward meaning. Rachel says to Jacob, "Give me children" (Genesis 30:1), she is asking him to provide her with offspring. It is the act of transmitting, entrusting, giving access to something.

2. To place, arrange, put in position: the word can mean "to put" or "to place" something somewhere. When it says, "Let us make bricks and burn them thoroughly" (Genesis 11:3), we are placing the brick in the fire.

3. To provide, supply, procure: to give someone what they need. One can give food, drink, or provide the necessary resources to accomplish a task.

4. To attribute, acknowledge in words honor and glory: a specific usage where "to give" means "to attribute" or "to render." Psalm 29:2 says, "Give to the Lord the glory due to His name" — this is to recognize and proclaim His majesty.

5. To allow, grant, consent: to grant permission, to give the right to do something. This is a meaning close to "to consent."

6. To go away, depart, move: a less common usage where the verb means to head, to go somewhere. Genesis 11:3 can also be translated as "Let us go!" expressing the movement or action of departing together.
H3051.origine: The Hebrew verb יָהַב (yahab) comes from a very ancient root that expresses the action of transmitting, handing over from hand to hand. It is found in other Semitic languages, notably in Aramaic where it has the same form and meaning: יְהַב (yehab). In Hebrew, the word family includes derivatives designating the one who gives or the gift itself. The basic image is that of the hand gesture that transmits, entrusts, places something in the possession or hands of another.
H3051.emploi: The verb יָהַב appears 29 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is used mainly in Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, and in the historical books. Its primary meaning is always "to give" or "to hand over," but it nuances according to the context: giving a material object (giving children, giving food), placing or arranging something (putting bricks in the fire), attributing or acknowledging something in words (giving glory to God), granting permission or the right to do something. In religious contexts, it often expresses the act of rendering honor or glory to God; in narrative contexts, it describes the everyday action of giving or placing. The translation varies according to the nuance: "to give," "to render," "gives," "to go," "to take," "to consult."
H3051.portee: The verb יָהַב enriches the understanding of generosity and honor in biblical faith. When the Bible speaks of "giving," it reminds us that all transmission of good, power, or life comes from God and must be recognized as such. The use of the verb for "rendering glory" shows that worship and praise are a form of recognition: we create nothing, but we return to God what belongs to Him. It is an invitation to active gratitude and generosity imitated from that of God.

sens: To hand something to someone, to present or entrust its use to them
To grant, bestow upon someone power, a function, an authority
To deliver, hand someone or something over to the mercy of another
To place, establish in position (a foundation, a base)
To pay, disburse what is owed
H3052.detail:
1. To give means to transfer the possession of something to someone else: the simple act of handing over. God "gave" wisdom and strength to Daniel (Daniel 2:23).
2. To grant or bestow refers to conferring dignity, power, responsibility to someone. God "gave" greatness to Nebuchadnezzar, so that the peoples trembled before him (Daniel 5:19).
3. To deliver means to hand someone or something over to someone else, often to be destroyed or enslaved. The three young men "delivered their bodies" rather than worship another god (Daniel 3:28); the animal was "delivered" to the fire to be burned (Daniel 7:11).
4. To place or establish concerns the setting up of foundations or structures. The elders of the Jews were commanded to build the house of God (Ezra 6:4).
5. To pay or disburse expresses the settlement of a financial obligation. The expenses will be "paid" exactly to these men (Ezra 6:8).
H3052.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from a root that fundamentally means "to give" or "to place into the hands of." It appears in the Aramaic texts of the books of Daniel and Ezra, portions written in this language in the Old Testament. The primary notion is that of a voluntary handing over or a concrete placing.
H3052.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears 28 times in the Old Testament, exclusively in the Aramaic sections of Daniel and Ezra. In Ezra, it describes the order given by the Persian authorities regarding the financing and reconstruction of the temple (Ezra 6:8). In Daniel, it takes on various meanings: God gives wisdom and strength to Daniel (2:23), He confers power and authority to kings (2:37-38, 5:19), and the word also expresses handing over to suffering or destruction (3:28, 7:11). The nuance varies according to the context: sometimes an act of generosity or grace, sometimes a cession of power, sometimes a delivery to misfortune.
H3052.portee: This word reminds us that all power, all authority, all wisdom ultimately comes from God. Even great kings have only what God "gives" them (Daniel 5:19). It also teaches us that giving one's life, one's body for a conviction or for God is an act of supreme dignity: the three young men who "deliver" their bodies to not renounce their God illustrate the voluntary sacrifice in favor of faithfulness.

sens: what one carries on oneself, heavy load
lot, portion assigned to someone
what one entrusts to someone else, confidence
concern, worry of the heart
H3053.detail: 1. The burden is primarily a concrete load, something heavy that one carries — like a weight on the shoulders. But in this Hebrew word, it also designates what weighs morally: a responsibility, a duty. 2. It is also the share, the portion that fate or God assigns to each in life. 3. And finally, it is what one entrusts to someone else, what one "hands over" into their hands. In Psalms 55:23, the psalmist says: "Cast your burden on the Lord" — it is the same word: it is about depositing one's burden, one's load of worries and fears, at God's feet so that He may carry it for us. 4. The word thus evokes the concerns and anxieties that weigh on the heart, the emotional and spiritual weight that one drags along.
H3053.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew-Aramaic root that means "to give, to yield." The burden is therefore what is "given" to someone, what "weighs" on them and that they must carry or entrust. This same root is found in the Aramaic name of King Nebuchadnezzar, which means "Nabu gives an heir." The central image is that of the act of giving: one receives a burden, and one can entrust it to another.
H3053.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 55:23. It is very rare, which underscores its importance. In this context, the psalmist calls for a concrete and urgent action: faced with persecution and betrayal (the psalm depicts someone fleeing from enemies), the believer must not keep the weight of his anxiety within, but hand it over to God. It is a call to trust: God who has borne this burden will "never allow the righteous to be shaken." The sense of "to hand over" prevails here: it is an act of faith.
H3053.portee: This word speaks directly to the heart of the Christian who suffers or worries. It teaches us that the burdens we carry — fear, guilt, stress, injustice suffered — are not meant to remain within us, but to be entrusted to God. Handing over and trust are inseparable: one can only "hand over" if one believes that the one to whom they hand over is capable and willing to help us. It is a word of comfort and hope.

sens: To adopt the Jewish faith and practices
To enter the Jewish community by conviction or interest
H3054.detail: 1. This verb describes the action of becoming a Jew, not by birth but by choice: adopting the faith, customs, and identity of the Jewish people. In Esther 8:17, after the king restores the rights of the Jews who were in danger of death, "many people from the provinces of the land became Jews," drawn by the sudden power and royal favor now enjoyed by the Jews. 2. The word can evoke both a sincere conversion and a self-interested or superficial adherence: the text remains open regarding the true motives of these new "Jews," between religious conviction and political calculation or fear.
H3054.origine: This verb comes from a Hebrew root meaning "Jew" (Yehudi), which is derived from "Judah." By taking the reflexive form (Hithpael), the verb indicates a voluntary action: "to make oneself a Jew." It is a rare term, appearing only once in the Hebrew Bible, at this pivotal moment in the book of Esther when the status of the Jews shifts.
H3054.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Esther 8:17. It occurs at the heart of the resolution of the book: King Ahasuerus has just signed a new edict granting the Jews the right to defend themselves against those who were persecuting them. This spectacular turnaround in the fate of the Jews triggers a chain reaction: "many people from the provinces of the land" of the Persian kingdom decide to "become Jews." The unique usage of the term underscores the exceptional nature of the situation and the sudden appeal of an identity that had previously been despised or ignored.
H3054.portee: This verse reminds us that Jewish identity is not only a matter of genealogy but also of choice and practice. For the believer, it shows how a reversal of fortune can attract others to the faith of God's people — not only through deep conviction but also through recognition of His divine protection. It is an invitation to seek the Lord first, knowing that His people will ultimately be honored.

sens: City in the territory of the tribe of Dan
H3055.detail: Jehud is a small city located in the region that God assigned to the tribe of Dan during the division of the land of Canaan. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:45, among the cities listed as part of Dan's inheritance. Its name means "beauty" in Hebrew.
H3055.origine: The name Jehud literally means "beauty." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of something beautiful or remarkable. It was an ordinary place in Israel, without any particular sacred character, geographically situated between Baalath and Bene-berak, about 13 kilometers east of Jaffa.
H3055.emploi: Jehud appears only once in the Scriptures, in Joshua 19:45. It is listed among the cities that constituted the territorial inheritance of the tribe of Dan after the conquest of Canaan. This enumeration was important for establishing the exact boundaries of each tribe's territory and for each family of Israel to know precisely the limits of their possession.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Judah
Wife of Caleb
Mother of six sons
H3056.detail: 1. Jahdai is a woman belonging to the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:47. She lived during the time of Egypt and the desert, a formative period for the people of Israel. 2. She is the wife of Caleb, one of the twelve spies sent to explore the promised land and one of the two most faithful figures to God during the Exodus (the other being Joshua). 3. She is the mother of six sons named in the Bible: Rehu, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph, who are part of Caleb's lineage listed in the genealogical record of Israel.
H3056.origine: The name Jahdai comes from the Hebrew root meaning "he/she whom God will place" or "whom God will establish." Her name expresses the idea that her existence and place in Caleb's lineage are established by God. This name reflects trust in divine providence, characteristic of names from that era.
H3056.emploi: Jahdai is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:47, in the genealogy of Caleb. The text simply lists her sons, without providing further details about her life or role. Her presence in this genealogical record shows that the Bible honors women by including them in the narrative of the transmission of the promised lineage, even when they are not at the center of the faith narratives.
H3056.portee: Jahdai reminds the reader that behind every man of faith whose story is told in the Bible stand often invisible women. Her inclusion in the genealogical record testifies that God sees and records the role of mothers in passing down faith from one generation to another. It is a quiet call to recognize the forgotten women of biblical history as actors in God's plan.

sens: woman belonging to the tribe of Judah
H3057.detail: 1. A woman of the tribe of Judah. The word designates a woman from the people of Judah, as opposed to other tribes of Israel. In 1 Chronicles 4:18, this term is used to identify a woman without giving her proper name: she is simply "the Jewess," the wife of Mered, and mother of three sons (Jared, Heber, and Jekuthiel).
H3057.origine: The word comes from Judah (יְהוּדָה), the son of Jacob and founder of the southern tribe. The feminine suffix -ה (-ah) and the definite article "the" indicate gender and specificity: "the Jewish woman." It is the feminine equivalent of "Judean" or "Jew."
H3057.emploi: This name appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:18, in a genealogy of the tribe of Judah. The text uses it to qualify the wife of Mered, whose proper name is unknown but whose tribal affiliation is noted. This mention emphasizes her tribal identity in the context of an important family lineage for the genealogies of Judah.

sens: Prophet during the time of Baasha and Jehoshaphat, son of Hanani
H3058G.detail: Jehu is an Israelite prophet who serves during the reigns of Baasha, king of the north, and Jehoshaphat, king of the south. He is the son of Hanani. At the time of Baasha, the Lord entrusts him with a message of condemnation against this king and his house because of the evil committed (1 Kings 16:1-7). Later, he meets Jehoshaphat to rebuke him for aiding the wicked Ahab (2 Chronicles 19:2). His writings, recorded in his memoirs, are cited as a source for the book of the Kings of Israel (2 Chronicles 20:34).
H3058G.origine: The Hebrew name יְהוּא (Yéhou) means "the Lord is He," expressing that God alone is the true Lord. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, proclaiming the divinity of the one true God. This Jehu is to be distinguished from King Jehu, son of Nimshi, who reigned over Israel several generations later.
H3058G.emploi: Jehu is an active prophet during the period of the divided kingdom. He first appears as the spokesperson of the Lord against Baasha, communicating the consequences of his unfaithfulness. Under the reign of Jehoshaphat, he plays the role of moral advisor and critic of the king: he reproaches Jehoshaphat for his alliance with Ahab, the idolatrous king of the north. Biblical tradition recognizes him as a reliable witness of Israel's history, as his memoirs are explicitly cited as a written source of the royal archives. He embodies the prophet's vocation: to proclaim the Word of God without fear, even to kings.
H3058G.portee: Jehu shows that the prophet is one who, in all faithfulness, addresses the Word of God to the powerful, without complacency. His rebuke to Jehoshaphat reminds us that compromise with idolatry provokes the Lord's anger: the king, despite his religious reforms, must not ally with the unfaithful. His example invited the Israelites to honor the prophets who speak in the name of the Lord and not to reject their correction.

sens: king of Israel who overthrew the dynasty of Omri
army general sent to anoint this king
H3058H.detail:
1. Jehu is the king of the northern kingdom, Israel, who was anointed by the prophet Elisha to bring down the house of King Ahab and his wife Jezebel. He succeeded by force: he killed Joram (the son of Ahab), Jezebel herself, and all the survivors of the house of Ahab at Jezreel, leaving not one (2 Kings 10:11). He also exterminated the worship of Baal from the midst of Israel (2 Kings 10:28).
2. Before becoming king, Jehu was a military leader, son of Nimshi. It was in this capacity that Elisha anointed him through a young prophet (1 Kings 19:16).
H3058H.origine: The name means "Yahweh is He" or "Jehovah is He" in Hebrew: it expresses that God alone is God. It is a theophoric name, constructed from the divine name YHVH (the Lord) and the Hebrew pronoun of affirmation, a profession of faith that one would give to a child to place him under the protection of the one true God.
H3058H.emploi: Jehu appears 46 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost entirely in 2 Kings 9—10, where his military coup that overthrows Joram and kills Jezebel is recounted. These two chapters form a dramatic and detailed narrative of his march on Jezreel, his confrontation with the king, his systematic murders, and his establishment of the strict worship of Yahweh. He is mentioned at the beginning of this story (1 Kings 19:16) as the one whom God has designated for this mission. He reappears in 2 Kings 13:1 when his son Joash becomes king. The prophet Hosea will later recall this bloodshed (Hosea 1:4), showing that God also judges Jehu's violence despite his apparent piety.
H3058H.portee: Jehu illustrates the biblical tension between obedience to God and the manner in which one obeys Him: sent to eliminate idolatry and injustice from the house of Ahab, he fulfills his mission with a brutality that God will not fully approve. It is an invitation to reflect: does serving God require killing all His enemies mercilessly? The biblical answer is nuanced: Jehu is right to pursue idolatry, but his method falls into carnal vengeance that God will condemn.

sens: Descendant de Juda de la maison de Hetsron
Fils d'Obed et père d'Azaria
H3058I.detail: This Jehu is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 2:38. He appears in the lineage of Hetsron, between his father Obed and his son Azaria, as a link in a genealogical chain that traces back to the origins of God's people.
H3058I.origine: The name means "Jehovah is He" or "This is Jehovah", expressing the affirmation of God's divinity. This name carries a clear spiritual heritage: it proclaims that the Lord alone is God. Several characters bear this name in the Scriptures, including the warrior king of the northern kingdom and a prophet, but this Jehu belongs to the tribe of Judah.
H3058I.emploi: This Jehu is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 2:38. He is among the descendants of Judah from the house of Hetsron, an important lineage of the tribe. Although little documented, his place in this genealogy shows that he was part of the recognized ancestors of the people of Judah, passing on the name of the Lord through the generations.

sens: Homme de la tribu de Siméon à l'époque de la monarchie divisée
H3058J.detail: 1. Jehu is a man belonging to the tribe of Simeon, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is presented as the son of Joshibiah and is part of a genealogy of tribal leaders (1 Chronicles 4:35). He is a minor character in biblical history, known only through this genealogical list.
H3058J.origine: The name Jehu means "Jehovah is He" or "Yahweh is He", composed of the divine name Jehovah (Yahweh) and a verb meaning "to be". It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God within it, which was common in Israel to express faith or commitment to the Lord.
H3058J.emploi: This man named Jehu appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:35. He is listed in a genealogy of the tribe of Simeon during the divided monarchy period. He is the son of Joshibiah and is part of a succession of leaders or important figures of his tribe. Although the same name Jehu is borne by other more famous biblical characters (particularly a king of Israel), this man is a minor genealogical figure whose lineage is all we know.

sens: Le chef Jéhu d'Anathoth, guerrier de David
H3058K.detail: 1. Jehu of Anathoth is a military officer mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time he joins David before David becomes king (1 Chronicles 12:3). He is part of the list of valiant warriors who rally to David at Ziklag, and he is designated as the leader of his troop.
H3058K.origine: The name Jehu means "Jehovah is He" or "He is Jehovah" in Hebrew. It derives its strength from two elements: the divine name Jehovah (Yahweh) and a pronoun affirming divine identity. It is a theophoric name, very common in Israel, expressing trust in God. Several people bear this name in the Old Testament, each with their own role in the history of Israel.
H3058K.emploi: Jehu of Anathoth is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 12:3. He is a warrior from Benjamin, originally from the city of Anathoth (known to be the birthplace of the prophet Jeremiah). He appears in the list of officers and valiant men who come to join David at Ziklag, before David is recognized as king. This context shows that he was a figure of some military importance in David's circle, although the Bible provides no further details about his life or actions.

sens: Roi du royaume d'Israël, fils de Jéhu et père de Joas
Personnage historique de l'époque de la monarchie divisée
H3059G.detail: Joachaz is a king of Israel (the northern kingdom) who reigned after his father Jehu. His name means "the Lord has seized". He is first mentioned in 2 Kings 10:35, where he succeeds his father. Joachaz experienced a difficult period: he suffered oppression from the king of Syria, but when he cried out to the Lord, God answered him (2 Kings 13:4). Although oppressed by his enemies, he left a legacy to his son Joash, who achieved victories against Syria and reclaimed cities that Hazael had taken from Joachaz (2 Kings 13:25).
H3059G.origine: The name Joachaz comes from two Hebrew elements: Yah (a short form of the name of God "the Lord") and the verb "to seize" or "to take". It thus means "the Lord has seized". This king bears a name that affirms God's action, even though his life was marked by the struggle against the Syrian invasion.
H3059G.emploi: Joachaz appears thirteen times in the books of Kings and Chronicles, with all occurrences found in the second book of Kings and the second book of Chronicles. He is presented as a weak king in the face of the power of Syria, but who turned to God in his distress. The text reports that his actions and exploits are recorded in the book of the Chronicles of the kings of Israel (2 Kings 13:8). His reign is framed by that of his father Jehu and that of his son Joash, both also kings of Israel.
H3059G.portee: The life of Joachaz shows that even a weak king can find help from God when he cries out to Him in oppression. His story reminds the reader that sincere prayer is heard, and that God does not refuse His help to those who ask for it, despite difficult circumstances.

sens: king of Judah, son of Josiah
sovereign briefly enthroned after his father's death
H3059H.detail:
1. Joachaz is a king of Judah mentioned in 2 Kings 23:30, son of King Josiah and Hamutal. After Josiah's death, the people established him as king in his place, anointed him, and crowned him (2 Chronicles 36:1).
2. His reign was extremely short: he ruled only three months in Jerusalem before Pharaoh Necho deposed him (2 Kings 23:31-34). The Pharaoh sent him to Egypt, where he died, and placed his brother Eliakim on the throne, changing his name to Jehoiakim.
H3059H.origine: The Hebrew name Jehoahaz literally means "Jehovah has seized" or "Jehovah has taken." It is composed of "Jehovah" (the God of Israel) and the verb "to seize" or "to take." This name, borne by several kings in the history of Israel and Judah, expresses God's sovereignty over the throne and the authority entrusted to the king.
H3059H.emploi: Joachaz appears four times in the Bible, all in passages recounting his brief kingship. The first mention (2 Kings 23:30) reports his enthronement by the people after the death of his father Josiah at Megiddo. The second passage (2 Kings 23:31) provides his personal details: twenty-three years at his accession, three months of reign, his mother Hamutal of Libnah. The last two passages (2 Kings 23:34 and 2 Chronicles 36:1) describe how Pharaoh Necho deposed him, exiled him to Egypt where he died, and replaced his power with that of his brother Jehoiakim. His historical role is that of a king intercepted by Egyptian politics.
H3059H.portee: The story of Joachaz illustrates the political instability of Judah at the end of the monarchy and the domination of foreign powers over God's people. His brief kingship shows how human plans can be quickly overturned by external forces, reminding believers that it is God who establishes and overturns kingdoms, even when circumstances seem determined by men.

sens: King of Judah in the 9th century B.C., son of Jehoram and Athaliah
H3059I.detail: Joachaz is a king of Judah, also known as Ahaziah. He is the son of King Jehoram and Queen Athaliah. In 2 Chronicles 21:17, he is referred to as "the youngest" of the king's sons, indicating that he had older brothers. He is the father of Joash, who will become king after him. His reign occurs during the period of the Divided Monarchy, when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah existed side by side.
H3059I.origine: The name Joachaz (in Hebrew יְהוֹאָחָז) is composed of two elements: "Yaho" or "Jehovah" (the name of God) and "achaz" (to seize or retain). It thus means "the Eternal has seized" or "the Eternal retains." This name belongs to a family of royal names that express God's action in the life of the king. The same man is also called Ahaziah (אֲחַזְיָהוּ), a slightly different form of the same name.
H3059I.emploi: Joachaz appears twice in Chronicles. In 2 Chronicles 21:17, he is mentioned as the youngest son of King Jehoram, the only one who survives when invaders pillage the royal palace and take the other sons and the king's wives. In 2 Chronicles 25:23, he is named as the father of King Joash (also called Amaziah in this context), confirming his place in the genealogy of the kings of Judah. These two passages constitute the only direct mentions of Joachaz in the Old Testament.

sens: king of Judah during the Divided Monarchy
son of King Ahaziah and Zibiah
husband of Jehoaddan
father of King Amaziah
H3060G.detail:
1. Joash is a king of Judah who became king at seven years old after the death of his father Ahaziah (2 Kings 11:21). He reigned forty years in Jerusalem and is known as the eighth king of the kingdom of Judah during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two.

2. Joash was the son of King Ahaziah and his mother Zibiah, originally from Beer-sheba. He was raised and advised by the priest Jehoiada, who had a significant influence on his religious policy during his reign.

3. Joash did what was right in the eyes of the Lord as long as he followed the directions of the priest Jehoiada (2 Kings 12:2). He notably organized the collection of funds dedicated to the repair of the temple (2 Kings 12:4).

4. Joash was the father of King Amaziah. The biblical text also mentions that Joash was married to Jehoaddan.
H3060G.origine: The name means "given by the Lord," combining the idea of divine gift with the notion of God's will for the king. It is a classic theophoric name in Judah's royalty, testifying to God's place in the dynastic succession.
H3060G.emploi: Joash appears 7 times in the Segond, exclusively in 2 Kings, in chapters 11 and 12 (and referenced in 14:13b). The passages show his accession to the throne at seven years old (2 Kings 11:21), the beginning of his reign in the seventh year of Jehu (2 Kings 12:1), his piety as long as he followed Jehoiada the priest (2 Kings 12:2), and his willingness to finance the repairs of the temple (2 Kings 12:4, 6, 7, 18). The biblical accounts emphasize his dependence on the counsel of the priest and his commitment to worship in Jerusalem.

sens: son of Joachaz and twelfth king of the Northern Kingdom of Israel
king who fought against King Amaziah of Judah
sovereign who reigned sixteen years in Samaria
H3060H.detail:
1. Joash is the son of Joachaz, king of the Northern Kingdom of Israel during the period of the Divided Monarchy. He reigns in Samaria, the capital of the north (2 Kings 13:10). His name means "given by the Lord."
2. During his reign, Joash achieved significant military victories: he recovered from Ben-Hadad the cities that Hazael had previously taken from his father Joachaz, and he defeated Ben-Hadad three times (2 Kings 13:25).
3. Joash came into conflict with Amaziah, king of Judah. Instead of heeding Amaziah's challenge, Joash sent a parable (the thornbush of Lebanon and the cedar) to dissuade him (2 Kings 14:9), but they still confronted each other at Beth-Shemesh (2 Kings 14:11). Joash defeated Amaziah, captured him, and breached the walls of Jerusalem (2 Kings 14:13).
H3060H.origine: The Hebrew name יְהוֹאָשׁ literally means "Yah has given" or "the Lord has given." It combines the divine name Yah and the verb "to give." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude to the Lord. Do not confuse with Joash (יוֹאָשׁ), the king of Judah who bears a similar name but is a different person.
H3060H.emploi: Joash of Israel appears nine times in the texts of 2 Kings 13-14. He is presented as the son of Joachaz and as an active military king. The Bible first shows him as a restorer of Israel's forces, reclaiming cities lost to the Arameans. Then, it depicts him as a victor over Amaziah, king of Judah, highlighting the military power of the Northern Kingdom at that time. The accounts also reveal his character: he refuses peaceful mediation and chooses direct confrontation, revealing the pride characteristic of his foreign policy.
H3060H.portee: The story of Joash illustrates how military victory and political success, even when they seem inevitable, do not mean that all is well for a kingdom. Although he temporarily restores Israel's power, the broader context of the books of Kings shows that Israel continues its spiritual and political decline. For the Christian reader, the narrative invites reflection on the vanity of trust in arms and human strategy, and on the importance of remaining humble before God.

sens: son of Jacob and Leah, ancestor of the people of Israel
the tribe descended from this son
the territory inhabited by this tribe
H3061.detail:
1. Judah is one of the twelve sons of Jacob and Leah, born during the time of the patriarchs. He becomes the ancestor of a great lineage and plays a key role in the history of Israel.
2. The tribe of Judah, composed of all the descendants of this son, forms one of the twelve tribes of Israel with its own territories and responsibilities.
3. The territory or region occupied by the tribe of Judah, called the province of Judah, where the inhabitants of the kingdom live. It is here that Daniel and other captives were taken into exile (Daniel 2:25, Daniel 5:13), and it is to Judah that the king sends an inspector (Ezra 7:14).
H3061.origine: The name Judah means "praise" or "let him be praised" in Hebrew. It comes from the root that expresses the action of thanking and acknowledging. It is also the name of the southern region of ancient Israel, the largest and most powerful of the tribes after the division of the kingdom.
H3061.emploi: Judah appears 7 times in the provided usages, exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel. These passages date from the period of the Babylonian exile and return. The word first designates the captives from Judah (Daniel 2:25, Daniel 5:13, Daniel 6:13), that is, the inhabitants of the kingdom of Judah deported to Babylon. It also designates the province itself, the territory that the Jews inhabit or from which they come (Ezra 5:1, Ezra 5:8, Ezra 7:14). In these contexts, Judah is always a place or a community of exiles awaiting restoration.
H3061.portee: Judah reminds the reader that the story of faith in God is that of a promise made to a particular family and people. For the Christian, Judah symbolizes God's faithfulness to His people even in exile, and the hope of return and restoration. It is also the name of the Messiah Himself according to Revelation: Jesus is the "Lion of the tribe of Judah."

sens: Inhabitant of the kingdom of Judah or his descendants
Member of the people and religious community of Israel returned from exile
H3062.detail:
1. The word first designates someone from Judah, the southern kingdom, or descended from this people. After the exile in Babylon, this term applies to the Israelites who returned to rebuild the temple and the city of Jerusalem (Ezra 5:1: "the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem").
2. It then characterizes religious and community identity: to be a Jew is to belong to the people who keep the covenant with God, observe the Law, and worship the Lord in the restored temple. The "elders of the Jews" lead this people in its reconstruction (Ezra 6:7).
H3062.origine: The word comes from Judah (יְהוּדָה), the son of Jacob and the name of the southern kingdom. The Aramaic יְהוּדַי takes the same term as the Hebrew יְהוּדִי (Jew): both derive from the name of Judah, ancestor and founder. After the exile of 586 B.C., the survivors and their descendants are called "Jews," as most came from the territory of Judah.
H3062.emploi: The word appears nine times, only in the books of Ezra and Daniel, and takes on an Aramaic form. It reflects the Persian and Babylonian period of writing. Ezra uses it to refer to the workers and religious leaders who rebuild the temple (Ezra 4:12; 5:1; 6:7). The meaning remains constant: it is the people of Israel after the exile, recognizable by their faith, their dwelling in Jerusalem or in the territory of Judah, and their commitment to restore the house of the Lord.
H3062.portee: For the Christian reader, this word shows how the identity of the people of God refocused after the catastrophe of exile. Being a "Jew" no longer depends on political power, but on belonging to the religious community attached to the Law and the temple. It is a lesson in faithfulness: the people of God subsist not by force, but by their living connection with God, even in the heart of the land of exile.

sens: Son of Jacob and Leah, ancestor of the Judean people
Tribe of Israel descended from this figure
Territory occupied by this tribe in the south of Canaan
Southern kingdom after the division of the kingdom of Israel
Inhabitants of this kingdom or region
H3063G.detail:
1. Judah is first the fourth son of Jacob and Leah. Leah names him thus saying, "This time I will praise the Lord" (Genesis 29:35), for the name means "he who is praised." He is a key figure in the patriarchal cycle: husband of Tamar, father of Perez and Zerah, and brother of Joseph.

2. The name then designates the entire tribe that descends from him. During the census in the desert, the tribe of Judah was the most numerous (Numbers 1:26-27).

3. After the conquest of Canaan, the territory of Judah was the mountainous region in the south, which Joshua assigned to this tribe (Joshua 15:1-12).

4. After the death of Solomon, the united kingdom divided: Judah became the small southern kingdom, comprising the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, governed by the descendants of David (2 Kings 23:24; 2 Chronicles 25:23).

5. By extension, the term also designates the inhabitants or citizens of this kingdom (2 Samuel 19:42: "the men of Judah" oppose the men of northern Israel).
H3063G.origine: The Hebrew name יְהוּדָה (Yehoudah) comes from the root יָדָה (yadah), which means "to praise" or "to give glory." Leah, the mother of Judah, chose this name in thanksgiving to God for his birth (Genesis 29:35). The word thus expresses praise and acknowledgment towards the Lord. From this founding figure flows an entire genealogy: his sons, his descendants, the tribe, the territory, and then the kingdom.
H3063G.emploi: Judah appears 746 times in the Bible. First as a living character during the patriarchal era: he plays an important role in the cycle of Joseph and Benjamin (Genesis 37-50), where he shows himself to be a leader and responsible for his brothers. Then, the word designates the tribe throughout the Old Testament, from the census in the desert (Numbers) to the conquest (Joshua, Judges) and establishment in the territory. From 1 Kings onward, after the split of the kingdom, Judah becomes the name of the southern kingdom: the texts then speak of the "king of Judah," the "men of Judah," the "land of Judah" (2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, etc.). The prophets Jeremiah and Isaiah address their oracles to Judah and Jerusalem.
H3063G.portee: Judah represents a perpetuation of the promise made to Jacob and David. The very name, "he who is praised," reminds us that God deserves all praise. The story of Judah and his kings shows how faithfulness to God brings blessing and stability, while unfaithfulness leads to catastrophe and captivity. For the Christian reading the Gospel, Judah is also the province from which Jesus comes, born in Bethlehem: it is in Judah that the remainder of the messianic promise is fulfilled. The name remains a symbol of identity, responsibility, and praise.

sens: Man of the Levitical tribe at the time of the return from exile
Levite among those who had taken foreign wives
H3063H.detail:
1. At the time of Ezra, after the return from captivity in Babylon, a Levite bore this name. He appears in the list of men who, at Ezra's command, had to send away the foreign wives they had married, which shows that he was among those who had strayed from the Law. He is an ordinary Levite, distinct from the priests, tasked with serving in the temple.
2. His only mention in Ezra 10:23 places him among the members of the community returned from captivity who participated in the restoration of Israelite worship, but who had committed a transgression by taking wives from pagan nations.
H3063H.origine: The name "Juda" means "praised" or "one who praises," derived from the Hebrew root "Yadah" which means "to praise, to celebrate." It is a name of great importance in biblical history, first borne by one of Jacob's twelve sons. Here, it simply designates a man from this people at the time of restoration.
H3063H.emploi: This Juda appears only once in Scripture, in Ezra 10:23, in the context of the religious crisis caused by mixed marriages upon the return from exile. The prophet Ezra seeks to purify the community by sending away the foreign wives. This Juda, although a Levite and thus called to holiness, had allowed himself to be drawn into this practice. His inclusion in this list shows that even those who held a religious function could fail, and that no status exempted one from obeying the Law.
H3063H.portee: This brief mention reminds us that authentic faith requires a conversion of the heart and actions, even among those who hold a religious position. It also shows that God remains faithful to restore His people: despite infidelities, Ezra calls for repentance and restoration, and God accepts this return.

sens: Leader of Jerusalem at the time of Nehemiah
Son of Senua
H3063I.detail: 1. Juda is a leader of Jerusalem who lived at the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. He is designated as the second leader of the city (Nehemiah 11:9), tasked with helping to direct and organize the life of the restored community. 2. His father was Senua, which confirms his identity in the genealogical records of the returning community.
H3063I.origine: The name Juda means "praised" or "one who praises" in Hebrew, a meaning of the utmost importance since the same name designates the patriarch son of Jacob, founder of the tribe and the southern kingdom. This minor leader thus bears the glorious name of a lineage and a spiritual identity fundamental to Israel.
H3063I.emploi: Juda is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:9, where he is presented as the second administrative leader of Jerusalem after Joel. He appears in the list of leaders who helped to repopulate and rebuild the capital after the return from Babylonian exile in the 5th century BC. His role is clearly administrative and civil: supervising the life of the city alongside Joel.

sens: Levitical musician at the time of Nehemiah
H3063J.detail: Juda is one of the Levitical musicians who participate in the consecration of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile, under Nehemiah's leadership. He is mentioned alongside other Levites such as Benjamin, Schemaiah, and Jeremiah during this great religious ceremony (Nehemiah 12:34).
H3063J.origine: The name Juda means "praised" or "one who is praised," coming from a Hebrew root that expresses the action of giving thanks or proclaiming the glory of God. It is a common name in the Bible, borne by several different characters — the son of Jacob, an entire tribe, a kingdom — but here it designates a simple Levite from the time of the Temple restoration.
H3063J.emploi: This Juda appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:34, where he is named among the Levitical musicians who take part in the consecration of the wall of Jerusalem, probably in the fifth century BC. He represents those Temple musicians who played an essential role in the worship of God after the return from Babylonian exile.

sens: Levitical musician at the time of Nehemiah
singer in the dedication procession of the wall of Jerusalem
H3063K.detail:
1. Juda is a musician belonging to the tribe of Levites, who lived at the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile to Jerusalem. He appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:36, where he is named among the musicians who participated in the religious ceremony.
2. He played a role in the dedication procession of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem: he was one of the singers or musicians who accompanied this solemn procession with the traditional temple instruments, alongside his brother Hanani and seven other Levite brothers.
H3063K.origine: The name Juda means "praised" or "one who praises," formed from a Hebrew root expressing praise. It is a widely held name in Israel, particularly by the direct descendants of the son of Jacob named Juda, from whom the tribe and kingdom of the same name are derived.
H3063K.emploi: This Juda is a Levitical musician mentioned only in Nehemiah 12:36 at the time of the return from exile. He appears in the list of musicians and singers who participated in the grand ceremony of dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, alongside his brothers Hanani, Nethanel, Maai, Gilalai, Milalai, Azarel, and Shemaiah. He represents one of the Levitical families responsible for music and singing in the worship of the Second Temple.

sens: A Levite from the time of Ezra and Nehemiah, bearer of the name of the patriarch Juda
H3063L.detail: 1. Juda is here a Levite (member of the tribe dedicated to temple service) who lived during the time of the Exile and the return to Jerusalem. He appears in Ezra 3:9, where he collaborates with Joshua and Kadmiel to oversee the workers who are rebuilding the temple. He is a man charged with an important responsibility in the restoration of worship after the Babylonian exile.
H3063L.origine: The name Juda means "praised" or "one who praises," derived from a Hebrew root expressing praise. It is the name of the patriarch founder of the tribe whose spiritual heritage this Levite bears. Several people bear this name in Scripture — the most well-known is Juda son of Jacob — but here it designates a servant of the temple in the post-exilic period.
H3063L.emploi: This Juda is mentioned only once in Ezra 3:9, where he is among the Levite leaders responsible for overseeing the reconstruction of the temple. He is also called Hodaviah in Nehemiah 7:43 and Juda in Ezra 3:9 — probably the same person designated by two names. He represents those Levites returned from captivity who dedicated their efforts to restoring worship and the religious institutions of Israel.
H3063L.portee: This character illustrates the role of the Levites in the restoration of the Israelite community after the exile. His commitment to overseeing the temple work shows how faithful believers, even after trials, mobilize to rebuild divine worship and restore community order.

sens: A Levite musician during the time of Nehemiah
One of the names for the son of Jacob and his descendants
The tribe descended from Judah son of Jacob
The territory occupied by this tribe
The southern kingdom after the division of Solomon's kingdom
H3063M.detail:
1. Judah is the name of a Levite musician who lived during the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. He was responsible for leading the songs of praise with his brothers during the ceremonies of the restored temple (Nehemiah 12:8).

2. Judah is the name of the son of Jacob and Leah, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. All members of this tribe descend from him.

3. The tribe of Judah was one of the twelve tribes of Israel, formed by all the descendants of Judah son of Jacob.

4. The territory of Judah refers to the region that this tribe occupied in the south of Canaan, after the land was distributed among the tribes.

5. After the death of Solomon, the kingdom of Israel was divided into two: the northern kingdom (Israel) and the southern kingdom (Judah), composed of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.
H3063M.origine: The name Judah comes from the Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehoudah), which means "praised" or "he who will be praised." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing praise and acknowledgment towards God. This name evokes the act of thanking and celebrating the Lord. The name gave rise to the term "Jew" which designates the descendants of Judah.
H3063M.emploi: In the provided usage (Nehemiah 12:8), Judah is a Levite musician who leads the songs of praise with his brothers during the ceremonies of the temple. He appears as an important figure in the religious service after the return from exile. Beyond this specific Levite, the name Judah in the Bible also refers to the son of Jacob and Leah, the founder of the major tribe of the people of Israel. The territory and kingdom of Judah are central geopolitical realities in the history of Israel, especially after the schism of the united kingdom under Solomon.
H3063M.portee: For the Christian reader, Judah reminds us that God has guided and preserved His people through the most difficult times, including exile and return. The role of the Levite Judah as a musician shows that praise and song are essential acts of worship at the heart of the restored community. The name meaning "praised" invites everyone to an attitude of gratitude towards God.

sens: territory occupied by the tribe of Judah in the south of Canaan
southern kingdom formed after the division of Solomon's kingdom
region of settlement and refuge for the Judeans
H3063N.detail:
1. Judah primarily refers to the region occupied by the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan, located in the southern part of the country. It is the territorial inheritance assigned to this tribe during the land distribution.
2. After the death of Solomon, the united kingdom divides into two: Judah in the south (also including Benjamin and Jerusalem) and Israel in the north. Judah becomes an independent kingdom with its own dynasty and temple.
3. In exile or after the return from exile, Judah remains the home of the descendants of Judah, the place where they can regroup and rebuild. In Ezra 9:9, the people returned from exile seek a "refuge in Judah," a safe shelter to rebuild their lives and the temple.
H3063N.origine: The name Judah comes from the son of Jacob, Judah (יְהוּדָה in Hebrew), whose name means "Praised" or "He who praises." This name expresses the act of praising God. The tribe founded by this son gave its name to the entire southern region, and this name persists to designate the territory, the kingdom, and then the province, even after the destructions and exiles.
H3063N.emploi: Judah frequently appears in the Bible, designating the southern territory and its inhabitants. In the accounts of the kings (1 and 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles), it is the heart of the southern kingdom in contrast to the northern kingdom (Israel). After the Babylonian exile, Judah remains the name of the region where the exiles return and the community is rebuilt. In Ezra 9:9, Judah is the refuge where the people can settle and rebuild the temple. In Jeremiah 40:15, it is the land where those who survive the destruction of Jerusalem gather.
H3063N.portee: For the believer, Judah reminds us that God remains faithful to His people even after political divisions and exiles. It is from Judah that the Messiah will come (Genesis 49:10), and the name becomes a symbol of hope: the scattered people can return, regroup, and rebuild around the temple of the living God.

sens: Place in Judah where the ark of God rested before David transported it to Jerusalem
H3063O.detail: 1. Baalé-Judah is a city or sanctuary in the territory of the tribe of Judah, in Israel. It is where the ark of the covenant was located before King David solemnly brought it to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:2). The name "Baalé" means "lords" or "masters" and likely refers to the place where the ark was kept or venerated.
H3063O.origine: The name "Judah" (Judah in French) comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to praise" or "to celebrate" — hence the gloss "praised." It was the name of Judah, the fourth son of Jacob, from whom the royal tribe descended. The tribe of Judah bore this same name and dominated the southern kingdom after the division of Israel. "Baalé-Judah" combines this term with "Baalé," the plural of Baal (master, lord), to designate a specific place in the region.
H3063O.emploi: Baalé-Judah appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 6:2, during a decisive moment in Israel's history: the transport of the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. David gathers all the people and sets out from Baalé-Judah to bring the ark to the heart of the kingdom, thus acknowledging the presence of the Lord among Israel. This sanctuary was therefore an ancient and important place of worship in Judah.
H3063O.portee: This passage shows David seeking to place the ark — the supreme symbol of divine presence — at the heart of his kingship and nation. For the believer, this reminds us that seeking to place God at the center of our lives and community is an act of authentic praise and faith, and that the presence of God transforms and unifies a people.

sens: Royal palace officer during the time of the divided kingdom
H3065.detail: Jehudi is a man who lived during the time of the divided kingdom of Judah and Israel, serving King Jehoiakim. His name means "Jew" in Hebrew, but it refers here to a particular person. He appears in the book of Jeremiah as an officer tasked with royal missions: he is the one the king sends to fetch the prophetic scroll that Baruch had written under Jeremiah's dictation (Jeremiah 36:21). Jehudi reads this text to the king and his advisors, then witnesses its dramatic destruction when Jehoiakim cuts the scroll and burns it piece by piece in the fire (Jeremiah 36:23). He is presented as a servant of the king, executing orders without intervening, which shows him as a courtier attached to his sovereign rather than to the Word of God.
H3065.origine: The name Jehudi comes from the Hebrew root meaning "Jew," derived from the name Judah. It is a patronymic indicating origin or belonging to the tribe of Judah. The source definition specifies that he is the son of Nethaniah, who himself belongs to a lineage of palace servants.
H3065.emploi: Jehudi is mentioned only in chapter 36 of the book of Jeremiah, three times. He is first sent by the leaders to summon Baruch, then dispatched by King Jehoiakim to fetch the scroll. His role is that of a royal intermediary, a trusted officer tasked with conveying the monarch's orders. He reads the prophetic text to the king without apparent comment, playing a passive but necessary role in this decisive moment when the king rejects the word of the Lord delivered by Jeremiah.
H3065.portee: The story of Jehudi illustrates how men in power can remain indifferent or hostile to the Word of God. Jehudi executes his duties without resistance, without interceding: he embodies the complacency of the servant in the face of his master's iniquity. This scene reminds the believer that proximity to the powerful of the world does not guarantee an audience for the divine message, and that sometimes obedience to human authority can distance us from God's justice.

sens: wife of the patriarch Esau
daughter of Beeri the Hittite
H3067.detail: Judith is a woman mentioned only once in the Bible. She is the daughter of Beeri the Hittite (that is, a man from the people of Heth, a Canaanite nation) and she becomes the wife of Esau, the firstborn son of Isaac, when he is forty years old (Genesis 26:34). Thus, she represents one of Esau's marital alliances with Canaanite women.
H3067.origine: The name Judith comes from Hebrew and means "Jewish" or "she who is praised." It is a feminine name formed from the root related to Judah and divine praise. Although Judith herself is a Canaanite Hittite and not a Jew in the ethnic sense of the word, the name reveals how biblical tradition has designated her: as a woman associated with God and blessing.
H3067.emploi: Judith appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 26:34. She is presented as one of Esau's wives in a context where Esau chooses wives from the daughters of the land of Canaan. This marriage of Esau with a Hittite is recounted without detail and without particular approval, but it fits into the narrative of family tensions between Isaac and his sons: Isaac desired that Esau only marry women from his own household (descendants of Abraham), which makes these Canaanite marriages significant for God's plan.
H3067.portee: The character of Judith, although very little known, symbolizes Esau's choice to stray from the path of divine blessing by taking a wife from the Canaanite peoples. Her existence reminds us that our choices, particularly in family and personal alliances, reveal our spiritual priorities. The very name Judith — "praised" — creates a tension: is the heart of man turned toward the praise of God or toward something else?

sens: The proper name of the one true God of Israel
The One who exists by Himself, the living and eternal God
The Lord creator of heaven and earth
The One who acts, speaks, and reveals Himself to His people
H3068G.detail:
1. It is the proper name of the true God revealed in Israel. When we read "the Lord" in the Segond, it is always this Hebrew word: the personal name of God, distinct from simple titles like "Lord" or "God". (Genesis 2:4)
2. Its primary meaning is "the One who exists", "the One who is": it designates a being who exists fully, without depending on anything else. That is why the name suggests eternity and constancy.
3. He is the living God who acts, who speaks, who creates, and who meets His people. He is not an abstract idea, but a person who intervenes in history and in the lives of men. (Genesis 3:8, Jeremiah 28:6)
4. He is the One who made the heavens and the earth and who masters creation. (Genesis 2:4, Psalms 118:24)
H3068G.origine: This name comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to be" or "to exist". The word includes the idea of permanence and eternity: the One who was, who is, and who will always be. Traditionally, the Jews did not pronounce it aloud out of respect and substituted the word "Adonai" (Lord) in its place. The consonants of the name (YHVH, often written YHW) inspired the Greek term "Yahweh" or "Jehovah" in modern translations.
H3068G.emploi: This name appears more than 5,500 times in the Old Testament: it is the most frequent word in the Hebrew Bible. It appears massively in Genesis from the creation of the world (Genesis 2:4 and following), where the Lord creates, orders, and converses with man. It constantly returns in historical narratives, psalms, and prophecies. The name is used to emphasize that God is the sovereign Lord who acts, judges, promises, and saves. It is the name by which God reveals Himself to Moses, to Abraham, and to all the prophets: a personal God, engaged with His people, not an impersonal force.
H3068G.portee: To know the name of the Lord is to recognize His deep nature: He is the God who truly exists, who does not pass away, who keeps His promises. For the believer, it is a source of trust and security. This name also reminds us that God is not a theoretical notion, but a person with whom one can speak, whom one can know, and to whom one can confidently entrust oneself.

sens: God Himself, the God of Israel
That which remains unchanging, without end
The permanent presence of God with His people
H3068H.detail:
1. The Lord is the proper name of the God of Israel, revealed to Moses at the burning bush. It is the most sacred name, one that the Jews do not pronounce aloud out of reverence. It designates God in His divine nature, His absolute authority, and His sovereignty over the world.
2. The name evokes eternity and immutability: God does not change, has no beginning or end. While everything that exists passes and transforms, the Lord alone remains always identical to Himself.
3. In Ezekiel 48:35, the restored city of Jerusalem itself bears this name of the Lord as a future name: "the name of the city will be: the Lord is here." This indicates that the presence of God with His people becomes its defining reality, its eternal glory.
H3068H.origine: This name comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to be". The Lord is the One who IS, who exists by Himself, while everything else receives its existence from Him. In Exodus 3:14, God says to Moses: "I AM WHO I AM," revealing that His essence is absolute being and independence. The Hebrew name יְהוָה (Yahweh) has given in French the word "Eternal" to respect the inexhaustible and unchanging character of the living God.
H3068H.emploi: The Lord is the most frequently used proper name throughout the Bible to designate God. It appears thousands of times, from the Book of Genesis to Revelation, notably in the Psalms and the prophets. In Ezekiel 48:35, this name crowns the vision of the restoration of the temple and the city: the future Jerusalem will be defined by the permanent presence of the Lord. This name emphasizes that God is not distant or remote, but remains with His people eternally, guaranteeing His faithfulness and protection.
H3068H.portee: For the believer, invoking the Lord is turning to the One who never fails, who endures when all else passes. This name reminds us that God is not subject to time as we are, but dominates it. It assures that God's promises are stable, that His presence does not abandon us, and that His plan will be fulfilled without failure. It is a source of hope and unwavering trust.

sens: The name of God revealed to Israel, designating His eternal and unchanging being
In composition: the holy city placed under the lordship of God
H3068I.detail:
1. In the Bible, the word "Eternal" is the French translation of the Hebrew divine name, the one that God gave to Moses at the burning bush. This name expresses that God exists without beginning or end, that He is the living God who remains forever, unlike the gods of the nations who are silent and perishable idols. It is the name that God desires to be called by His people.
2. When it says "city of the Eternal" in Isaiah 60:14, it designates Jerusalem as the city that the Eternal has chosen, His dwelling on earth, the center of His plan of salvation for the nations. The peoples who had despised Zion will then recognize that this city belongs to the living and eternal God, not to a transient human power.
H3068I.origine: The divine name יְהֹוָה (YHWH) comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to be" or "to exist." It is revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14, where God says: "I AM WHO I AM." It is the only personal and incommunicable name of God, which the Jews considered so holy that they did not pronounce it aloud and instead read "Adonai" (Lord) in its place. Translators chose "Eternal" to signify His timeless and unchanging character.
H3068I.emploi: The name "Eternal" (YHWH) appears more than six thousand times in the Old Testament, primarily in the books of the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets. It designates the God of Israel in His personal and covenantal relationship with His people. In Isaiah 60:14, in an eschatological passage of comfort for Zion, this name is associated with Jerusalem itself: the city becomes "city of the Eternal," meaning that the nations will finally recognize the sovereignty of the true God over the holy city, and those who had oppressed it will bow before it.
H3068I.portee: For the Christian reader, this name reminds us that God is not an abstract force, but the living and personal God who has made Himself known in the history of Israel and who fulfills His promises in time. The promise that Isaiah 60 addresses to Jerusalem—that the nations will recognize its glory and the reign of the eternal God—shows that the history of the world converges toward the public manifestation of the Kingdom of God.

sens: The God of Israel, whose revealed name is Yahweh, the only true God
He who exists by Himself and from all eternity
The Lord who governs history and manifests His power
He who speaks to the prophets and intervenes in human affairs
H3069.detail:
1. This word designates the God of Israel in His covenant relationship with His people, particularly when He acts in power and judgment. He is the personal God who reveals Himself to Abraham, Moses, and the prophets, the one who made a covenant with Israel. In Genesis 15:2, Abraham calls Him "Lord God" while imploring His promise of descendants.
2. The eternal image of the word evokes the one who exists from all eternity, without beginning or end, unlike the gods of the nations who are perishable. That is why it is translated as "the Eternal": He is the only one who does not pass away.
3. In the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel), He is seen as the Lord who governs empires, who punishes and restores. Jeremiah 2:19 reminds the people: "It is a bad and bitter thing to forsake the Eternal, your God."
4. He is the God who speaks directly to the prophets and whose judgment is executed on earth: "Thus says the Lord, the Eternal of hosts" in Ezekiel 23:22 seals His words with absolute authority.
H3069.origine: This Hebrew word is formed by combining the divine Name YHWH (Yahweh, "the Lord," which literally means "He who is") with the vowels of the word Elohim ("God"). The Name YHWH is the Name of God revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14: "I AM WHO I AM." This blend of consonants and vowels reflects the dual nature of the biblical God: He is both the sovereign Lord (YHWH) and the all-powerful God (Elohim). The Jews read this word with reverence by using Adonai ("Lord") or Elohim to avoid pronouncing the sacred Name.
H3069.emploi: This word appears about 296 times in the Hebrew text, almost exclusively in the prophetic books and the Psalms. It is particularly frequent in Ezekiel, where it introduces the oracles: "Thus says the Lord, the Eternal" (Ezekiel 5:5, 5:7). In the Psalms, believers invoke it in supplication (Psalm 71:5, 73:28). In Jeremiah, it emphasizes divine authority in judgments against Judah and the nations (Jeremiah 2:19, 46:10). The context always shows a God who speaks, who acts, who judges, and who comforts, never a distant or silent God.
H3069.portee: Understanding this Name is crucial for the believer: it reminds us that God exists from all eternity, that He is not subject to any power, and that He is the absolute Lord of history. He is the personal and powerful God who commits Himself to His people and keeps His promises. The respect for this Name expresses an attitude of reverence before the sacred character of God: it is not pronounced lightly; it is revered.

sens: Servant of King Joash who participated in his assassination
Murderer of a king of Judah
H3075G.detail:
1. Jozabad, son of Shomer (a Moabite woman), was one of the servants of King Joash of Judah. Along with his accomplice Jozacar, he struck the king and killed him (2 Kings 12:21). This is an example of betrayal at the very heart of the royal court.
2. The two accounts of this event (2 Kings and 2 Chronicles) name him together among the conspirators, confirming his role in this act of regicide that marked the reign of Joash.
H3075G.origine: The name Jozabad means "God has endowed" or "Jehovah has endowed": it combines the divine name (Jah or Yaho-) with a verb meaning "to give" or "to endow." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the belief that God provides for our needs. The name of the father, Shomer, means "guardian," creating a bitter irony: son of a guardian who should have protected the king, Jozabad became instead his murderer.
H3075G.emploi: Jozabad is mentioned twice in the Bible, in two parallel accounts of the same event (2 Kings 12:21 and 2 Chronicles 24:26). He appears as one of the two main conspirators who assassinated King Joash of Judah during his reign. Scripture expressly designates him as a servant of the king, highlighting the depth of the betrayal. His name appears alongside that of Jozacar in the Kings account, and alongside that of Zabad in the Chronicles account (a variant of the same name). This criminal act had lasting consequences for the kingdom.
H3075G.portee: The story of Jozabad reminds us that proximity to power and responsibilities does not guarantee loyalty. It serves as a warning about the dangers of betrayal and rebellion, even within established structures. For the Christian reader, it illustrates how sin corrupts the soul and leads to acts contrary to the order that God has established.

sens: Levite porter of the temple, son of Obed-Edom
H3075H.detail: Jozabad is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe dedicated to the service of the temple. He is the second son of Obed-Edom, who is himself an important figure in worship in Israel. Jozabad serves as a porter of the temple and also as a guardian of the temple treasury during the time of King David. He is a man of service, responsible for access to and the guarding of the holy places (1 Chronicles 26:4).
H3075H.origine: The name "Jozabad" combines two Hebrew elements: the divine name (Jehovah) and a verb meaning "to provide, to supply." It thus means "Jehovah has provided" or "Jehovah has endowed," expressing a blessing or gift from God. It is a typical theophoric name from ancient Israel, where parents gave their children names that recalled God's saving and benevolent acts.
H3075H.emploi: Jozabad appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:4, where he is listed among the sons of Obed-Edom. This passage lists the children of Obed-Edom who serve as porters and guardians of the temple during the reign of King David. His role is part of the organization of the cultic worship established by David, reflecting the importance of managing the temple and its entrances for the preservation of the holiness of the place.
H3075H.portee: This character reminds us that the service of the temple was not reserved for the priests, but involved a whole organization of faithful Levites fulfilling essential functions. Jozabad symbolizes the humble and constant work of those who serve God in ordinary places, often overlooked but fundamental to the faith life of all the people.

sens: Military officer of the kingdom of Judah
Commander of an army under King Jehoshaphat
H3075I.detail: 1. Zozabad is a military leader of the kingdom of Judah, living during the time of King Jehoshaphat (around 870-850 B.C.). His name means in Hebrew "The Lord has enriched" or "The Lord has endowed." He is mentioned as one of Jehoshaphat's chief officers, responsible for a significant army.
H3075I.origine: The name Zozabad is composed of the divine Hebrew name Yahu or Yeho ("the Lord") and the verb zabach which means "to enrich" or "to endow." It belongs to the family of theophoric names, that is, names that incorporate the name of God. The form "Zozabad" in French follows the transliteration of the Segond version, which transforms the Hebrew Yéhozabad.
H3075I.emploi: Zozabad is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:18. He is an officer commanding a powerful military force of one hundred eighty thousand armed men for battle, placed under the orders of King Jehoshaphat. He appears in the list of generals and captains who strengthened the military power of Judah at the time when Jehoshaphat consolidated the kingdom and organized its defense. His presence in this role shows the importance of the organized army of the kingdom of Judah.

sens: Warrior of Israel during the time of King David
H3076G.detail: 1. Jochanan is a warrior mentioned only once in Chronicles. He is among the valiant soldiers who joined David at Ziklag, before he became king (1 Chronicles 12:4). He was a man recognized for his military bravery.
H3076G.origine: The Hebrew name Yehohanan literally means "Yahweh has granted favor" or "Yahweh has shown grace." It is composed of the divine Yahweh and the verb "to grant, to show grace." This name expresses the belief that a child is a gift from God and the fruit of His kindness towards his family.
H3076G.emploi: Jochanan appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:4, among the list of valiant warriors who came to join David at Ziklag. These men were elite warriors who supported David before his accession to the throne. Although we know of Jochanan only from this one verse, his presence in this enumeration honors his reputation as a courageous fighter.

sens: One of David's mighty warriors
H3076H.detail: 1. Jochanan is one of the renowned warriors who joined David at Ziklag before he became king. He is named eighth in a list of leaders who came to him (1 Chronicles 12:12), which shows his military importance and his place of honor among the faithful fighters who supported David.
H3076H.origine: The name Jochanan means "The Lord has shown grace": it combines the divine name (Yah) and a verb meaning to give or to show grace. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by several characters at different periods of biblical history, including priests, Levites, and military leaders.
H3076H.emploi: Jochanan appears only once in the Bible in the strict sense we are discussing here: 1 Chronicles 12:12. He is listed as eighth among the mighty warriors who gathered around David at Ziklag, before he was recognized as king of Israel. This mention shows that he was a prominent military figure among David's faithful.

sens: Man from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel
Porter of the tabernacle, son of Meshelemiah
H3076I.detail: 1. Jochanan is a man who lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel and Judah. The name means "the Lord has shown grace." In 1 Chronicles 26:3, he is mentioned as the sixth son of Meshelemiah, a Levite responsible for guarding the doors of the tabernacle during the time of King David. He had several brothers: Zechariah, Jediah, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Elam, and Elihoenai (1 Chronicles 26:3).
H3076I.origine: The name Jochanan is formed from two Hebrew elements: Yah ("the Lord") and chanan ("to show grace, to grant favor"). This is why it literally means "the Lord has shown grace." This type of theophoric name, which includes the divine name, was common in Israel to express trust in divine blessing. The family of porters of the tabernacle, of which Jochanan was a part, descended from Korah and was responsible for access to the holy place.
H3076I.emploi: Jochanan appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:3, where he is designated as the sixth son of Meshelemiah. He was a Levite of the Korahite class, a porter at the tabernacle during David's reign. The text essentially gives us his name and his place in his family, without recounting other details of his life. His role was to guard one of the sanctuary doors, an honorable responsibility entrusted to the Levites.

sens: Military captain in the service of King Judah Jehoshaphat
H3076J.detail: 1. Jochanan is a military leader who appears among the commanders of the army of King Jehoshaphat of Judah in the 9th century B.C. According to 2 Chronicles 17:15, he was the first of these captains and commanded a force of two hundred eighty thousand men — making him one of the most important military officers in the kingdom.
H3076J.origine: The name Jochanan comes from Hebrew and literally means "the Lord has shown grace" or "God has favored." It results from the combination of "Yah" (the divine name) and "chanan" (to show grace, to show favor). This theophoric name, which places divine favor at the heart of identity, was common among officers and religious leaders in Israel.
H3076J.emploi: Jochanan appears only once in the French translation of the Bible (Segond 1910): in 2 Chronicles 17:15, where he is designated as the chief of the captains of Jehoshaphat. His positioning at the head of the list of military commanders indicates his prominent status in the military hierarchy of Judah. The context shows that Jehoshaphat had established a powerful military organization throughout the kingdom, with Jochanan at its head.

sens: Military officer of the kingdom of Judah under King Jehoshaphat
H3076K.detail: Jochanan is the father of Ishmael, a captain in the army of Judah.
