He appears in the account where the priest Jehoiada organizes a coup to overthrow Queen Athaliah and restore the young king Joash to the throne (2 Chronicles 23:1). Ishmael, his son, is one of the military leaders who participate in this decisive action to save the Davidic dynasty.
H3076K.origine: The name Jochanan means "the Lord has been gracious" or "the Lord has shown favor": it is composed of the divine name (Jehovah) and the Hebrew verb meaning "to be gracious." It is a very common theophoric name in Israel, borne by several important figures at different periods in the history of the people.
H3076K.emploi: The Jochanan mentioned here is a military officer during the time of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. His son Ishmael is cited as one of the captains who gather around the priest Jehoiada to carry out a crucial military and religious action: the overthrow of the usurping queen Athaliah and the safeguarding of the young king Joash, the legitimate heir of the house of David.
H3076K.portee: This passage shows how God preserves His promise to the house of David, even in times of political crisis. Leaders like Jochanan and his son embody the faithfulness of the officers and the people toward the dynasty that God has established. It is a reminder that human leaders, when they align with God's plan, become instruments of His providence.

sens: Man of the time of the Divided Monarchy
Father of Azaria
H3076L.detail:
1. Jochanan is a chief of Ephraim mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Judah are divided. He is known as the father of Azaria, who, along with other leaders, opposes soldiers returning from campaign (2 Chronicles 28:12).
2. His name literally means "God has been gracious" or "Jehovah has granted favor." This meaning expresses the belief that this child was a gift from God.
H3076L.origine: The name Jochanan comes from Hebrew: it combines the divine name Yahweh (often written "Jehovah") and the verb meaning "to be gracious" or "to show favor." It is a very common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the trust that parents placed in divine benevolence. Several biblical figures have borne this name, reflecting its popularity in the history of Israel.
H3076L.emploi: Jochanan appears only once in the biblical texts, in 2 Chronicles 28:12, during an episode of the Divided Monarchy. He is mentioned as the father of Azaria, one of the chiefs of the sons of Ephraim who take a stand against soldiers returning from campaign. Although Scripture provides no further details about his life or role, this mention indicates that he belonged to a family of influential leaders. The historical context places this event during the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah.

sens: a priest from the family of Eliashib at the time of the return from exile
son of Eliashib
H3076M.detail:
1. Jochanan is a priest mentioned in the book of Ezra at the time when the Jewish people return from exile in Babylon. He belongs to the priestly family of Eliashib, which means he is from a lineage of priests responsible for the worship at the temple.
2. The text of Ezra 10:6 shows him welcoming the scribe Ezra into his chamber, an act that reveals his status and authority among the priests of the time. It is there that Ezra withdraws, distressed by the marriages contracted with foreign women, refusing food and drink in his sorrow.
H3076M.origine: The name Jochanan comes from Hebrew יְהוֹחָנָן and literally means "Yahweh has been gracious" or "the Lord has shown compassion." It is formed from two elements: יְהוֹ (Jého-, abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh) and חָנַן (chanan, which means "to be gracious, to show pity"). This name expresses the faith that the Lord has granted His grace to the one who bears it.
H3076M.emploi: Jochanan appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:6. He is a high-ranking priest at the time of Ezra, a member of the family of Eliashib who played a major role in the temple worship after the return from exile. His appearance in this passage highlights the importance of priests in the spiritual guidance of the people during the period of reconstitution of the Jewish community. The fact that Ezra withdraws into his chamber underscores his respect and authority.
H3076M.portee: This passage reminds us that even in times of crisis and disobedience, there are faithful men of God who welcome prophets and help them intercede. Jochanan embodies the committed priest who supports the spiritual restoration of the people at the time of the return from exile.

sens: Israelite who married a foreign woman at the time of Ezra
H3076N.detail: 1. Jochanan is a man of Israel who, upon returning from exile in Babylon, had married a non-Israelite woman. Ezra 10:28 mentions him among those who had to repudiate these foreign wives to remain faithful to the law of Israel and to the covenant with the God of Israel.
H3076N.origine: The name Jochanan (יְהוֹחָנָן) means "the Lord has been gracious" or "the Lord has shown favor." It is formed from two elements: the divine name "Yaho" (the Lord) and "chanan" (to be gracious, to show favor). This name expresses gratitude to God for His blessings. Several important figures in the history of Israel have borne this name, including a military leader during the reign of King Jehoshaphat and a Judean officer after the fall of Jerusalem.
H3076N.emploi: In the passage of Ezra 10:28 that concerns us, Jochanan appears in the list of Israelites who acknowledged their guilt in having married foreign women during the exile or after the return. Ezra, as a scribe and religious leader, gathered the people and urged them to separate from these mixed marriages to preserve the purity and religious identity of Israel. Jochanan is among the sons of Bebai who accepted this correction and conformed to the Law.
H3076N.portee: The case of Jochanan illustrates the tension, during the return from exile, between divine mercy (as his name testifies) and obedience to God's Law regarding separation from foreign peoples. For the Christian reader, this passage reminds us that faithfulness to God may require difficult separations and that the spiritual restoration of God's people involves a conscious separation from evil and idolatry.

sens: Man of the time of exile and return
Son-in-law of Tobias, a character from Judah
H3076O.detail: Jochanan is a Jewish man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Israelites return from exile in Babylon. He was the son of Tobias, an important figure of this period, and he had married the daughter of Meshullam, son of Berechiah (Nehemiah 6:18). His name means "God has been gracious" or "the Lord has shown favor." He appears in the context of the intrigues and marital alliances that marked the reconstruction of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership, when several influential figures of Judah were striving to oppose the restoration of the people.
H3076O.origine: The name Jochanan comes from Hebrew and is composed of two parts: "Yah" (God, the Lord) and "hanan" (to be gracious, to show favor). It is a theophoric name, common among the Israelites, which expresses gratitude toward the Lord and His benevolence. Several important biblical figures bear this name, including the priest Jochanan of the time of Ezra and Nehemiah.
H3076O.emploi: Jochanan appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 6:18, where he is presented as the son of Tobias and the son-in-law of Meshullam. In this passage, the author mentions the family ties and oaths that united several influential figures of Judah, complicating Nehemiah's task in the reconstruction of Jerusalem. This context reveals how marital alliances played a political and social role in the Jewish community upon returning from exile.

sens: priest at the time of the return from exile
H3076P.detail: 1. Jochanan is a priest who served during the return from exile, at the time of the temple's reconstruction. He appears in the list of priests of Jerusalem established upon the return from Babylon. In Nehemiah 12:13, he is mentioned as the head of the priestly house of Ezra, which means he was responsible for a family of priests among those who resumed the temple worship.
H3076P.origine: The name Jochanan means "the Lord has shown grace" or "the Lord has favored." It is composed of the divine name Yah (God) and the verb chanan (to show grace, to grant favor). It is a classic theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude to God for His kindness. Several other individuals bear this name in the Old Testament, but the provided usages refer only to this particular Jochanan.
H3076P.emploi: Jochanan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:13. He is listed in the solemn roster of priests who returned with Zerubbabel from Babylon and resumed service in the restored temple. This mention highlights the importance of his priestly family in the organization of worship upon the return from exile.

sens: Priest at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem during Nehemiah's time
H3076Q.detail: 1. Jochanan is a priest who participated in the dedication ceremony of the wall of Jerusalem, rebuilt after the exile to Babylon. His name appears in the list of singers and priests who celebrated this significant event under the leadership of Jizrachja (Nehemiah 12:42).
H3076Q.origine: The name Jochanan means "the Lord has shown grace" (Jehovah has graced): it combines the divine name "Yaho" (Jehovah) and the verb "chanan" (to show grace, to show kindness). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by several figures at different periods in biblical history, particularly during the exile and return.
H3076Q.emploi: Jochanan appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:42, where he is cited among the priests and singers who participated in the grand dedication ceremony of the wall of Jerusalem. This event took place during Nehemiah's time, after the return from the Babylonian exile, likely in the mid-fifth century B.C. He was part of the religious group responsible for celebrating and sanctifying this major restoration of the holy city.

sens: Father of Benaja, David's mighty warrior
Chief priest who supported David at Hebron
High priest who saved the young king Joash during Athaliah's reign
H3077G.detail: Jehojada is first known as the father of Benaja, one of David's most valiant warriors, who commanded the Cherethites and the Pelethites, an elite unit responsible for the king's personal guard (2 Samuel 8:18). He also appears as an influential priest during the time of David and Solomon, participating in important events of the royal succession, notably during Solomon's anointing (1 Kings 1:32-44). Finally, although not detailed in the provided usages, he is identified as the high priest who played a crucial role during the succession crisis in Judah, hiding the young king Joash for six years under Queen Athaliah's reign, and then restoring him to the throne.
H3077G.origine: The name means "Jehovah knows": it combines the divine name Jehovah with the Hebrew verb "to know." It is a theophoric name, meaning it proclaims a truth about God and expresses the trust of those who bore it.
H3077G.emploi: Jehojada appears 21 times in the Bible, mostly in 1 Kings and 1 Chronicles, where he is presented as a trusted figure in the royal house of David. He is first mentioned as the father of Benaja under David (2 Samuel 8:18 and following), then as a faithful priest supporting Solomon against Adonijah (1 Kings 1:8-44). The references show a man of influence and responsibility in the army and worship, close to royal power during the tumultuous periods of succession.
H3077G.portee: Jehojada exemplifies the faithfulness of a servant of God who places divine order above political interests. His action to preserve the legitimate descendant of David shows how God protects His dynastic promise even in times of crisis. For the reader, it serves as a reminder that faith is often lived out in concrete roles of responsibility and service.

sens: High priest of Judah under Queen Athaliah and King Joash
Chief priest and prominent political figure
Figure of faithfulness to God and religious authority in the kingdom
H3077H.detail: 1. Jehojada is the high priest of Judah at the time when Queen Athaliah usurps the throne and nearly massacres the entire royal family. For six years, he secretly hides Joash, the king's son, in the temple (2 Chronicles 22:11), then organizes his revolution: in the seventh year, he makes a covenant with the military leaders in the house of the Lord and has them swear to support the young king (2 Chronicles 23:1). 2. Jehojada is also a man of political and religious influence: he wisely guides King Joash throughout his childhood and adolescence; the text states that "Joash did what was right in the eyes of the Lord all the days that he followed the instructions of the priest Jehojada" (2 Kings 12:2). He leads the temple reforms and oversees the collection of offerings for repairs (2 Chronicles 24:6-14). 3. A figure of longevity and divine blessing: the text recounts that "he died, old and full of days; he was 130 years old at his death" (2 Chronicles 24:15), which shows God's favor upon his life.
H3077H.origine: The name means "Jehovah knows" or "Jehovah is aware," combining the divine name Yah and the verb "to know" (yada). It is a typical theophoric name in the Israelite context: it expresses the trust that God knows and protects the one who bears it. Jehojada embodies this trust through his bold action to preserve the hidden king and restore faithful worship to the Lord.
H3077H.emploi: Jehojada appears about 25 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in Kings and Chronicles, in chapters 11 to 24. He is a historical figure of the Kingdom of Judah around the 9th century B.C. The usages show his triple role: protector of the child king (he hides him in the temple while his grandmother Athaliah reigns), political organizer (he forms alliances with military leaders to overthrow the usurper), and religious reformer (he restores authentic worship and the temple). After his death, when Joash ceases to follow his counsel, the king deviates and ultimately allows the stoning of the prophet Zechariah, son of Jehojada (2 Chronicles 24:20-22).
H3077H.portee: The life of Jehojada reminds the reader that a man of prayer and courage can, at a crucial moment, preserve the messianic royal line and restore faithfulness to God. His example shows that the spiritual influence of an upright person upon political power can redirect a people. It also invites reflection: when the spiritual guide dies, how do the king and the people keep to the path of God? Jehojada is a model of commitment to righteous action, based on the trust that God knows and supports those who serve Him.

sens: Advisor to King David
Son of Benaja
H3077I.detail: Jehojada is one of the advisors surrounding King David at the end of his reign. According to 1 Chronicles 27:34, after Ahithophel, Jehojada and Abiathar are listed among the king's trusted men, while Joab commands the army. He is the son of Benaja, one of David's mighty warriors, indicating that he belongs to a prominent family in the kingdom.
H3077I.origine: The name Jehojada means "the Lord knows" in Hebrew, composed of Yaho (form of the divine name) and yada ("to know"). It is a theophoric name, very common among the Hebrews, which expresses trust in divine knowledge and providence.
H3077I.emploi: Jehojada appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:34. He is presented as one of King David's advisors, alongside Abiathar, in the list of the royal court. His brief appearance in this administrative context suggests that he was a man of influence and wisdom with the king, although the details of his specific functions are not provided.

sens: Character from the time of the Divided Monarchy, mentioned only once in the provided contexts
H3077J.detail: Jehojada is a proper name referring to a man living during the time of the Divided Monarchy of Israel and Judah. He appears in the correspondence between Jeremiah and the exiles in Babylon, where he is cited as a priest established by the Lord to maintain order in the temple of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 29:26).
H3077J.origine: The name Jehojada means "the Lord knows" or "the Lord is aware," formed from two elements: Jehovah (Yah) and the verb "to know" or "to be aware" (yada). This name expresses the confidence that the Lord knows those who belong to Him and the affairs of His people.
H3077J.emploi: Jehojada is mentioned only once in the Bible according to the provided contexts: in Jeremiah 29:26, the prophet Jeremiah reproaches the priest Zephaniah for having established a certain Jehojada in place of the legitimate priest, to oversee the men who claim to be prophets and to keep them imprisoned. The context of the letter to the exiles suggests a time of turmoil and false prophets in Jerusalem.

sens: King of Judah, son of Jehoiakim
Young monarch who reigned three months before the Babylonian captivity
Figure of divine restoration after the exile
H3078.detail:
1. Jehoiachin is a king of Judah, son of King Jehoiakim, who ascended the throne at eighteen years old (2 Kings 24:8). His reign lasted only three months before he surrendered to the king of Babylon along with his mother and court (2 Kings 24:12).

2. He represents the collapse of the monarchy of Judah in the face of Nebuchadnezzar: the Babylonian king imprisoned him and took him into captivity, along with the king's wives and the nobles of the land (2 Kings 24:15). He remains a symbol of an ephemeral kingship, swept away by enemy power.

3. After thirty-seven years of imprisonment in Babylon, King Evil-Merodach released him and "lifted up his head," meaning he restored him to a certain honor and allowed him to live freely (2 Kings 25:27). This final gesture shows that even in exile, God's hand did not completely abandon him.
H3078.origine: The name Jehoiachin means in Hebrew "Jehovah establishes" or "God establishes." He is also referred to by other names in Scripture: Coniah in Jeremiah, Jeconiah in Matthew, and Shallum in Jeremiah 22:11, reflecting the different ways scribes and prophets designated him according to context.
H3078.emploi: Jehoiachin figures in the history of the kings of Judah as the son of Jehoiakim and the penultimate king before the fall of Jerusalem. Key passages show him first as a young king (2 Kings 24:8), then as a captive delivered to Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 24:12 and 24:15). His name appears mainly in the historical books of Kings and Chronicles, which recount the decline of the kingdom of Judah. Scripture also mentions him during his late release (2 Kings 25:27), emphasizing that even in political ruin, a glimmer of hope remains. His story fits into the broader picture of the fall of Judah and the deportation to Babylon.
H3078.portee: The story of Jehoiachin teaches the believer that political downfall and exile do not mean a definitive abandonment by God. Although his kingship was short and crushed by a superior power, his final release shows that God never completely forsakes His people. Jehoiachin becomes a sign that even in the depths of captivity, the hope of restoration remains alive.

sens: King of Judah in the 7th century B.C.
Son of Josiah, established by Pharaoh Necho
Vassal of Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon
Sovereign hostile to the prophets of the Lord
H3079.detail: 1. Jehoiakim is a king of Judah who reigned eleven years, from his enthronement by Pharaoh Necho around 609 B.C. until his violent death around 598 B.C. He is a key figure in the late history of the southern kingdom, living at the time of the rise of Babylonian power. 2. His real name was Eliakim, son of King Josiah; Pharaoh Necho placed him on the throne in place of his brother Jehoahaz and changed his name to Jehoiakim to mark his authority (2 Kings 23:34). 3. After the battle of Carchemish in 605 B.C., Jehoiakim became a vassal of the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar, to whom he had to pay heavy tribute and accept domination (2 Kings 24:1). 4. He fiercely opposed the prophets that the Lord sent, notably Jeremiah: he sought to kill the prophet Uriah and burned the scroll of God's word that Jeremiah had dictated to his secretary Baruch (Jeremiah 26:21-23 and 36:32).
H3079.origine: The name Jehoiakim means "the Lord raises" or "the Lord establishes" — a typical name of the kings of Judah that expresses the hope that God will elevate and support the reign. At court, he was also called by his first name, Eliakim ("my God establishes"). However, history shows us a tragedy: despite this name carrying divine promise, this king turned his back on the Lord and His messengers.
H3079.emploi: Jehoiakim appears 37 times in the Bible, mainly in the books of Kings, Chronicles, and the prophet Jeremiah, who wrote during and after his reign. He is first encountered as the successor imposed on Judah by Pharaoh Necho (2 Kings 23:34), then as a vassal of Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 24:1). Jeremiah provides a brutal portrait: a king who oppresses his people, rejects the word of the Lord, and violently opposes the prophets. The prophet announces terrible judgments against him — notably that his corpse will not be buried honorably (Jeremiah 22:18-19). Chronicles and Jeremiah together situate this entire context: it is the time of Judah's decline, before the exile of 586 B.C.
H3079.portee: Jehoiakim illustrates the tragic fate of a leader who possesses political power but refuses the word of God. His story teaches that the greatness of a royal title means nothing if the heart turns away from the Lord. For the Christian reader, it also shows how God protects His prophets and His word: despite Jehoiakim's rage in burning the scroll, God commands Jeremiah to write again everything he had dictated, plus other words (Jeremiah 36:32). This is proof that God's judgment and His word cannot be annihilated.

sens: Priest of Jerusalem
Chief of the first course of priests during the time of King David
H3080G.detail: Jehojarib is a priest of Jerusalem mentioned only once in the Bible, during the organization of sacred services at the temple. David divided the priests into twenty-four groups or courses, each taking turns to ensure worship — a prestigious and sacred duty. Jehojarib received the first lot, making him the chief of the first of these priestly courses (1 Chronicles 24:7). This was a considerable honor: being named first in this official enumeration of worship leaders.
H3080G.origine: The name Jehojarib literally means "the Lord contends" or "the Lord disputes." It is composed of the divine name Jehovah (the Lord) and a form of the verb meaning "to contend" or "to plead." It was a common theophoric name in ancient Israel, expressing the faith that God Himself takes a stand for His people or defends their cause.
H3080G.emploi: Jehojarib appears only once in Scripture: in 1 Chronicles 24:7, where David establishes the order of the twenty-four courses of priests. He is named first in this official list, indicating his role as chief of the first course. This enumeration shows how the priestly duties were organized in a hierarchical and regular manner to ensure the continuity of worship at the temple. His unique appearance places him at a key moment in the history of the priesthood of Israel.

sens: Levite priest of Jerusalem
Chief of the first course of priests during the time of David
H3080H.detail:
1. Jehojarib is a priest belonging to the tribe of Levi, living in Jerusalem during the time of the Exile and the Return. His name appears among the priests listed in 1 Chronicles 9:10, alongside Jedaiah and Jakin.
2. He was the chief of the first of the 24 courses of priests established by David to ensure the service of the temple. This organization allowed the priests to serve in turn in the sanctuary.
H3080H.origine: The name means "Jehovah contends" or "Jehovah pleads." It is composed of the divine name Jehovah and the verb meaning "to contend" or "to plead." It is a typical theophoric name in the Old Testament, expressing the relationship between the people and their God. Jehojarib is also referred to as Joiarib elsewhere in Chronicles (see 1 Chronicles 9:10 and parallel references).
H3080H.emploi: Jehojarib is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:10, among the priests who settled in Jerusalem after the Exile and the Return. He is presented there as one of the Levite priests responsible for worship in Jerusalem, and he is identified as the father of Jedaiah. His main role was to lead the first course of priests according to the organization that David had established for the service of the temple.

sens: Servant of King Zedekiah, son of Shelemiah
H3081.detail: Jucal is a man living during the time of the divided monarchy, in the days of the prophet Jeremiah. He is the son of Shelemiah and a servant of King Zedekiah of Judah. The king sends him to the prophet Jeremiah to ask him to intercede in prayer to God (Jeremiah 37:3).
H3081.origine: His Hebrew name means "Jehovah is able" or "God is powerful." It is a common theophoric name (containing the name of God) in Israel, expressing trust in the omnipotence of the Lord. He is also referred to as "Jucal" in biblical texts.
H3081.emploi: Jucal appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Jeremiah 37:3, where King Zedekiah sends him with the priest Zephaniah to Jeremiah to request his prayers and counsel. This is a diplomatic and religious mission during a time of crisis — the prophet was imprisoned during the siege of Jerusalem. This episode reveals that the king still held a formal respect for the prophet, even in captivity.

sens: Son of Rechab, leader of the Rechabite community
Ally of King Jehu in his fight against the worship of Baal
Founder of a community faithful to the commandments of his father
H3082G.detail:
1. Jonadab is a historical figure from the kingdom of Israel, son of Rechab, who lived during the time of the divided monarchy. He meets King Jehu and allies with him (2 Kings 10:15-23), thus becoming the first witness to the destruction of the worship of Baal.
2. He is the leader of a community called the Rechabites, which is distinguished by its strict obedience to the rules he established for his household: not to drink wine, not to sow, not to build a house (Jeremiah 35). Centuries after his death, his descendants continue to faithfully observe his orders, making him a reliable model of teaching that God uses to reproach the people of Judah for their unfaithfulness.
H3082G.origine: His name means "The Lord is willing" or "The Lord is voluntary." It comes from the Hebrew root that expresses goodwill, benevolent intention. Jonadab embodies one who leads with firmness and wisdom, whose commandments are respected by the generations that follow.
H3082G.emploi: Jonadab appears in two distinct contexts: first in 2 Kings as a political and religious ally of King Jehu at the time of the eradication of the worship of Baal in Israel (2 Kings 10:15, 23), and then especially in Jeremiah 35 where he is presented as the founder of a way of life for his descendants. The prophet Jeremiah stages the sons of Jonadab as a people who scrupulously observe their father's commandments "to this day" (Jeremiah 35:14), many centuries later. This faithfulness of the Rechabites stands in stark contrast to the unfaithfulness of Judah to the Lord, and God promises that the house of Jonadab will never lack descendants to serve Him (Jeremiah 35:18-19).
H3082G.portee: Jonadab teaches the power of obedience and the faithful transmission of values. His example shows that a pious leader whose commandments are just can create a spiritual legacy that lasts for generations. For the Christian, he reminds us of the importance of moral consistency and the transmission of faith to children, as well as the contrast between those who obey true principles and those who reject God's calls.

sens: Cousin of David, son of Shimeah, who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel
H3082H.detail: Jonadab is a figure from the Davidic royal family, son of Shimeah (David's brother). He appears in the story of Amnon and Tamar (2 Samuel 13), where he plays a role as an advisor to his cousin Amnon, David's firstborn son. It is he who suggests to Amnon to feign illness to lure Tamar to him — a counsel that will lead to the grave crime committed by Amnon against his sister.
H3082H.origine: The name Jonadab means "Jehovah is willing" or "Jehovah is voluntary," composed of "Jehovah" (the divine name) and the verb "to be willing." There was another famous Jonadab, son of Rechab, leader of the Rechabites during the time of Jehu, but these are two different people. In biblical texts, this same character is sometimes referred to as Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:21).
H3082H.emploi: Jonadab appears only once in the Segond with this name, in 2 Samuel 13:5, during the sinister counsel he gives to Amnon. This is a pivotal moment in the narrative: while Amnon is consumed with obsessive love for his half-sister Tamar, Jonadab, described as "very shrewd" (2 Samuel 13:3), proposes the scheme that will allow Amnon to meet her alone. His intervention reveals a clever man but morally complicit in a criminal intention. The Bible reports nothing else about him, and he disappears after this episode.
H3082H.portee: Jonadab embodies the danger of carnal wisdom used to serve sinful desire. Although clearly intelligent, his counsel nurtures an abominable crime: it shows how intelligence without the fear of God becomes an instrument of evil. For the Christian, this account warns: the ability to find ingenious solutions does not redeem one who uses it to facilitate sin.

sens: Man living before the monarchy in Israel
Son of Gershom and priest of the tribe of Dan
H3083G.detail:
1. Jonathan is a character who lived before kings ruled in Israel. In Judges 18:30, he is mentioned as the one who established idolatrous worship among the Danites, at the time when this tribe settled in the north of the country.
2. Jonathan was the son of Gershom, himself the son of Moses. He and his descendants were priests for the tribe of Dan, maintaining this role until the captivity — that is, until the time when Israel was exiled and this idolatrous worship disappeared with it.
H3083G.origine: The name Jonathan means "Jehovah has given" in Hebrew: it comes from the combination of the divine name Jehovah (Yahweh) and the verb "to give." It is a name that expresses trust in God. Several men bore this name in the Bible, each playing a different role in the history of Israel.
H3083G.emploi: The Bible explicitly mentions this Jonathan only once, in Judges 18:30. He is the one who inaugurated the worship of the "golden calf" among the Danites when this tribe left its territory and settled in the north. He and his sons served as priests for Dan, transmitting this compromising religious practice until the destruction of the northern kingdom. This text shows how a bad religious tradition can perpetuate itself in a family over several generations.
H3083G.portee: This account reminds us that even a prestigious lineage — that of Moses himself — does not guarantee faithfulness to God. Jonathan illustrates how a single bad decision, that of establishing idolatrous worship, can mark an entire tribe and contaminate future generations. It is a call to personal and communal vigilance against anything that distances us from the true God.

sens: Son of King Saul and friend of David
Brave man who fought against the Philistines
He who loved David with a deep friendship
H3083H.detail:
1. Jonathan is the eldest son of King Saul and belongs to the tribe of Benjamin. He is one of the central figures in the books of Samuel, mentioned as early as 1 Samuel 13:2 and omnipresent in the narrative of the rivalry between Saul and David.
2. Jonathan is distinguished by his warrior courage: he single-handedly attacks a Philistine outpost with only his young armor-bearer, showing remarkable confidence in the Lord ("Nothing prevents the Lord from saving by many or by few," 1 Samuel 14:6). He wields the sword and bow with excellence, as celebrated in David's lament (2 Samuel 1:22).
3. Jonathan embodies friendship: he forms an unbreakable covenant with David (1 Samuel 18:3-4), warns him of Saul's threats (1 Samuel 19:1-7), and throughout their separations, remains loyal to his friend at the peril of his life. His love for David is so intense that it surpasses that of a woman (2 Samuel 1:26), according to the funeral song that David composes after his death at the battle of Gilboa (2 Samuel 1:12, 31:2).
H3083H.origine: The name Jonathan (יְהוֹנָתָן in Hebrew) literally means "the Lord has given" or "Jehovah has given." It combines the divine name YHWH and the root "to give" (nathan), expressing a gift from God. A shorter form, Yonatan (יוֹנָתָן), is also attested in the Old Testament.
H3083H.emploi: Jonathan appears in 59 passages, concentrated in 1 Samuel (from chapter 13 to chapter 23), 2 Samuel (chapters 1, 4, 9, 21), and 1 Chronicles (chapters 8 to 9). His role starts as prince and warrior; over the narratives, he becomes David's inseparable friend. After his initial military discernment (14:6-8), the text emphasizes his friendship: the secret conversations with David (20:1-42 notably), his commitment to protect him from Saul, and finally his death at Gilboa with his father, which causes national mourning. The silence of the Word on his later acts suggests that he did not survive the change of reign, unlike Mephibosheth his son, whom Saul had to care for.
H3083H.portee: Jonathan reminds the believer that true friendship is possible in faith: it transcends personal and familial interests (Jonathan chooses David instead of defending his father Saul's honor). His friendship with David illustrates how two hearts united in God strengthen each other in the face of adversity. His simple courage against the Philistines, based on trust in the Lord rather than in the multitude, remains a model of bold faith.

sens: Son of the high priest Abiathar
Companion of David during his flight from Absalom
Secret messenger of King David
H3083I.detail:
1. Jonathan is the son of Abiathar, the high priest who accompanies David. He is a member of the priestly class of Israel, linked to the king's house by the bonds of religious duty (2 Samuel 15:27).
2. During Absalom's revolt against David, Jonathan plays an active and courageous role: he risks his life to stay with the exiled king, alongside his companion Ahimelech, son of the priest Zadok. He represents the faithfulness of worship towards the legitimate David (2 Samuel 15:36).
3. Jonathan becomes a secret messenger: hidden at En-Rogel, a spring near Jerusalem, he receives news from the city through a devoted servant and relays it to the king. He symbolizes courage in danger and dedication to David's cause (2 Samuel 17:17, 17:20).
H3083I.origine: The name Jehonathan means "Jehovah has given" in Hebrew: it combines the divine name Jehovah and the verb "to give," expressing gratitude to God for a child received. It was a common name among the Israelites, notably borne by the famous son of King Saul, friend of David. The name here designates the son of Abiathar, marking the religious heritage of the priestly family.
H3083I.emploi: Jonathan son of Abiathar appears in four key passages of 2 Samuel 15-17, all set during the crisis of Absalom's revolt (around 980 B.C.). King David, fleeing Jerusalem, entrusts the high priest Zadok and Abiathar with a secret mission: their respective sons, Ahimelech and Jonathan, will serve as couriers between the priests remaining in the city and the exiled king. Jonathan and Ahimelech position themselves at En-Rogel, an easily accessible spring, from where a servant transmits the information they must carry to David. When Absalom's spies actively search for them, they must hide and cross the brook to escape their pursuers. Jonathan embodies loyalty to David and the crucial role that priests play in maintaining the legitimate king in power.
H3083I.portee: The story of Jonathan illustrates how faithfulness to God and His king manifests through concrete and courageous actions, even in danger. It shows that true loyalty may require personal risk and self-denial. For the believer, Jonathan reminds us that serving God sometimes means supporting legitimate authorities at the cost of effort and peril.

sens: Warrior of Israel during the united monarchy
H3083J.detail: Jonathan is a name borne by several important men in Israel's history. The one mentioned in 2 Samuel 23:32 is one of David's elite warriors, son of Shammah. The name means "God has given" in Hebrew (from Yah, "God," and natan, "to give"), reflecting the blessing represented by the birth of a child in the Bible. This man is listed among David's mighty warriors, highlighting his military importance in the kingdom.
H3083J.origine: The name Jonathan comes from two Hebrew elements: Yah (abbreviation of Yahweh, the name of God) and natan ("to give"). The longer form Yehonatan literally means "Yahweh has given." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude for a child as a gift from God. The Bible mentions several characters bearing this name, reflecting its popularity in Israelite families.
H3083J.emploi: The Jonathan of 2 Samuel 23:32 belongs to the list of David's "mighty men," the elite warriors who supported the king during his reign. He was the son of Shammah. Scripture counts several Jonathans throughout the centuries: the most famous is the son of King Saul, intimate friend of David (1 Samuel); others are mentioned as high priests, Levites, scribes, or royal officers. Each played a role in Israel's religious or political history, from the time of David to that of Nehemiah.
H3083J.portee: The name Jonathan reminds us that even warriors and military leaders are considered gifts from God in the biblical perspective. This man is among those who loyally served David, demonstrating the importance of fidelity and courage in service to the king. His inclusion in the register of David's mighty men emphasizes that true greatness, in the Bible, is measured by devotion and commitment, not by wealth or personal power.

sens: Character from the divided monarchy, son of Ozias
H3083K.detail: Jonathan (or Jehonathan) is a man who lived during the divided monarchy of Israel. In the only biblical mention that has come down to us, he appears as the son of Ozias and is responsible for royal provisions: he oversees the food supplies stored in the fields, cities, villages, and towers of the kingdom (1 Chronicles 27:25).
H3083K.origine: The name Jonathan literally means "Jehovah has given" in Hebrew: it is composed of Jehovah (the God of Israel) and natan ("he has given"). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude to God for a gift received, often the birth of a child.
H3083K.emploi: This Jonathan appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 27:25, in the context of the administration of King David's goods. He is distinguished by his important responsibility: managing the food stocks of the kingdom, which implies great trust and a certain organizational ability. The Bible mentions several other characters bearing the name Jonathan at other times (notably the son of King Saul and friend of David), but this text speaks of a different Jonathan, linked to the Davidic royal court.

sens: A Levite sent by King Jehoshaphat to teach the Law in the cities of Judah
H3083L.detail: 1. Jonathan is one of the Levites chosen by King Jehoshaphat to travel through the cities of Judah and teach the book of the Law to the people (2 Chronicles 17:8). His role was that of a religious educator, tasked with imparting knowledge of the divine Law.
H3083L.origine: The name Jonathan means "Jehovah has given" or "the Eternal has given" — it combines the divine name Jehovah with the verb "to give." This name was very common in Israel, borne by many people at different times in biblical history, including the famous son of King Saul.
H3083L.emploi: Jonathan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:8. He appears in the context of King Jehoshaphat's reign (9th century B.C.), during the time of the divided monarchy. He is cited as one of the Levites sent on a teaching and religious mission to instruct the inhabitants of the cities of Judah in the knowledge of the Law of the Eternal.

sens: Priest from the family of Melicu during the time of Nehemiah
Name meaning "The Eternal has given"
H3083M.detail:
1. Yéhonatan is a priest from the family of Melicu, mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile in Babylon. He appears in the list of priests who returned to Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership (Nehemiah 12:18), where he is noted as the representative of his family for the official priestly register. This brief mention shows that he held a position of responsibility in the reorganization of temple worship after the exile.

2. His name, composed of "Yéhô" (the Eternal) and "natan" (to give), literally means "The Eternal has given." This name expresses gratitude towards God and reflects the faith of the parents who gave him this name, recognizing that every gift comes from the Eternal. It is a common name in the Bible, borne by several important figures, including the beloved son of King Saul and friend of David.
H3083M.origine: The name Yéhonatan comes from the combination of two Hebrew elements: "Yéhô," an abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah (the Eternal), and "natan," which means "to give." This nominal formation reflects a common theology in Israel: giving a child a theophoric name (containing the name of God) to express trust in the Eternal and recognition of His blessings. The same element "natan" is found in other biblical names like Nathanael ("God has given"). The meaning of the name reminds us that, in the faith of Israel, all that is good and useful is a gift from the Eternal.
H3083M.emploi: Yéhonatan from the family of Melicu appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:18. This passage lists the priests who returned from captivity in Babylon and participated in the reorganization of temple worship under Nehemiah's leadership, after the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem (around 445 B.C.). The context shows that this register of priestly families was important for the religious and administrative life of the restored people. Although his mention is brief, it bears witness to his role in the religious community at the time of the return from exile.
H3083M.portee: Although Yéhonatan of Melicu is scarcely mentioned, his presence in the register of priests of the return from exile reminds us that God has not forgotten His people and that He restored worship and the religious life of Israel after the exile. His name, meaning "The Eternal has given," invites the reader to recognize that all restoration, all spiritual renewal, comes from God's gracious gift. Even minor figures in biblical history have their place in God's plan for His people.

sens: Scribe in the service of the king of Judah during the time of the prophet Jeremiah
H3083N.detail: 1. Jonathan is a scribe, that is, a royal official responsible for writing and keeping the kingdom's records. He performs his duties in Jerusalem during the reign of Zedekiah, while Jeremiah prophesies. The leaders of the kingdom, angry with the prophet who announces the city's downfall, have him imprisoned in Jonathan's house, which has been turned into a jail (Jeremiah 37:15). Jeremiah will later plead with the king not to send him back to that place, for fear of dying there (Jeremiah 37:20, 38:26).
H3083N.origine: The name Jonathan literally means "the Eternal has given" in Hebrew. It comes from the root "natan" (to give) preceded by the abbreviated divine name. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, carrying within it an act of divine grace. The most famous Jonathan is the son of King Saul, a close friend of David; however, this one, living several centuries before Jeremiah, is a different character.
H3083N.emploi: Jonathan, the scribe during Jeremiah's time, appears only three times in the Bible, all in the book of Jeremiah (37:15, 20 and 38:26). Each time, he is mentioned in connection with the prison where Jeremiah is held — Jonathan's house. He embodies, alongside the other leaders, the official opposition to the prophetic message. His role as a scribe suggests that he is a man of authority in the royal administration, but it is his participation in the persecution of the prophet that marks him in the Scriptures.
H3083N.portee: Jonathan the scribe reminds us that hostility towards the word of God can come from those who hold power and authority. His imprisonment of Jeremiah shows how the powerful attempt to silence the prophetic testimony. For the believer, it is a call not to fear human authorities when it comes to defending divine truth.

sens: Son of Shimeah, brother of David, who killed a giant from Gath
Uncle of David and counselor to the king
H3083O.detail:
1. Jonathan, son of Shimeah and brother of King David, is known for having fought a giant from Gath and defeated him (2 Samuel 21:21; 1 Chronicles 20:7). This feat brings him close to the military prestige of David himself.
2. Jonathan was also David's uncle and served as a counselor to the king, described as a man of wisdom and discernment (1 Chronicles 27:32). He thus played an important role in the royal administration.
H3083O.origine: The name Jonathan (Jehonathan in Hebrew) means "Jehovah has given." It is formed from "Yah" (God) and "natan" (to give). This theophoric name expresses gratitude towards God for the gift of a son. Several people bear this name in the Bible; this one specifically concerns David's military relative and counselor during the time of the united monarchy.
H3083O.emploi: Jonathan appears three times in the provided biblical texts, always in direct relation to David. Two passages (2 Samuel 21:21 and 1 Chronicles 20:7) report the same event: his victorious battle against a giant from Gath, a remarkable military feat. The third passage (1 Chronicles 27:32) presents him as the king's uncle and influential counselor, esteemed for his practical intelligence. These mentions show his importance in David's royal entourage.
H3083O.portee: Jonathan embodies familial loyalty and service to the king: both a courageous warrior and a wise counselor. His example reminds us that God gives (as his name signifies) diverse talents—military strength, wisdom, the ability to counsel—for the service of God's people.

sens: Son of Jacob and Rachel, patriarch of Israel
Tribe of Israel descended from his descendants
Figure of one whom God elevates despite trials
H3084.detail:
1. Joseph is the eleventh son of Jacob, born of Rachel (Genesis 30:24). His name means "Jehovah has added" or "The Eternal adds" — Rachel named him this, saying that God had given her another child. He becomes the central figure of Genesis 37-50, sold as a slave in Egypt, wrongfully accused, imprisoned, and then elevated by Pharaoh to become governor of the land. He saves his family from famine and reconciles with his brothers who sold him.
2. The name Joseph also refers to the tribe that descends from him, particularly through his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim. In biblical poetry, "Joseph" can evoke the northern tribes (Psalms 81:6 speaks of Joseph as a community that God guides).
3. Joseph embodies divine providence: one who endures injustice and captivity without losing his moral integrity, one whom God protects and exalts, and who generously forgives those who have wronged him.
H3084.origine: The Hebrew name יְהוֹסֵף (Yehoseph) is composed of "Yah" (the Eternal) and the verb "to add." Rachel named him this in recognition that God had granted her an additional child. This name expresses gratitude for divine fertility. Joseph belongs to the lineage of the patriarchs — son of Jacob, the man who received the name Israel — and occupies a pivotal place between the history of the fathers and the establishment of the people in Egypt.
H3084.emploi: Joseph is one of the great characters of the Old Testament. His story occupies a large part of Genesis (chapters 37-50), where it is divided into three acts: his favor with Jacob and the jealousy of his brothers, his sale into slavery and his integrity in Egypt, and finally his exaltation and forgiveness. He marries Asenath and has two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, who become the ancestors of two of the twelve tribes. The name Joseph is also used to refer to the entirety of his tribal descendants, particularly in poems and lists of the tribes (Psalms 81:6 mentions him in a context of deliverance and divine guidance).
H3084.portee: The story of Joseph teaches the believer that God accomplishes His purposes even through the wrongdoing of others, that faithfulness and moral integrity do not go unrewarded, and that authentic forgiveness is possible. Joseph shows how to suffer without losing one's soul, and then how to exercise power with mercy. His journey — from favored son to prisoner to governor — speaks to anyone going through trials.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin living during the divided monarchy
H3085.detail: Jehoadda is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogy of Saul. He is the son of Achaz and the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri (1 Chronicles 8:36). His name also appears in the form Jarah in 1 Chronicles 9:42, in another similar genealogical list. He is a descendant of Saul through the line of Jonathan, recorded in the continuity of the royal house of Israel.
H3085.origine: The name Jehoadda means "Jehovah has adorned" or "Jehovah has decorated." It is composed of the divine name Jehovah and a verb expressing the idea of beautifying or decorating. This theophoric name reflects his family's faith in the protection and blessing of the God of Israel.
H3085.emploi: Jehoadda is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:36, within a detailed genealogy of the descendants of Saul. He also appears under the name Jarah in 1 Chronicles 9:42, in a variant of this same genealogy. These two passages are part of the genealogical lists that trace the history of the tribe of Benjamin after the exile and establish familial ties within the house of Saul.

sens: Woman of Judah during the divided monarchy
Wife of King Joash of Judah
Mother of King Amaziah of Judah
H3086.detail: 1. Joaddan is a Jewish woman who lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two: the kingdom of Judah in the south and that of Israel in the north. She is known for having been a royal mother, which gave her an important role at court. 2. She was the wife of King Joash of Judah, a king who reigned in the 9th century B.C. This was a typical dynastic union of that time. 3. She is best known as the mother of King Amaziah, who became king of Judah after his father Joash. Amaziah reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem from the age of twenty-five (2 Kings 14:2). Her role as the mother of a king conferred a certain influence in the kingdom.
H3086.origine: Her name means "The Eternal delights" or "The Eternal takes pleasure." It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God (Jehovah or the Eternal). Like many Hebrew names of this time, it expresses a religious conviction: the name affirms that God takes pleasure in this person or in her birth.
H3086.emploi: Joaddan appears only twice in the Bible: in 2 Kings 14:2 and in 2 Chronicles 25:1. These two passages recount the same event with the same details: the beginning of Amaziah's reign in Jerusalem. In both cases, it is simply mentioned that Joaddan was his mother and that she came from Jerusalem. She is never described as an active participant in the political or religious events of the kingdom, but only identified as the mother of the king. It was common in the royal annals of the time to name the mother of the reigning king, which attested to the legitimate succession.

sens: Member of the tribe of Levi living during the Exile and Return
High priest in exile in Babylon, son of high priest Seriah
Father of high priest Joshua who restored the temple after the exile
H3087.detail: Jotsadak is a Levite from the priestly lineage, living at the time when Judah and Jerusalem were taken captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar (1 Chronicles 6:15). He is a descendant of high priest Hilkiah and is himself the son of high priest Seriah (1 Chronicles 6:14); despite this prestigious genealogy, he never attains the position of high priest himself, as the exile keeps him in Babylon. He is the father of Joshua (or Jeshua), who becomes high priest and plays a key role in the reconstruction of the temple after the return from exile, alongside the governor Zerubbabel (Haggai 1:1, 1:12, 1:14).
H3087.origine: The name Jotsadak means "Jehovah is just" or "Jehovah has justified" in Hebrew. He belongs to the family of the Levites, that is, the descendants of Levi, one of Jacob's twelve sons, dedicated to temple service and the priestly function. It is a theophoric name — that is, it contains the divine name — which testifies to the piety of this priestly house.
H3087.emploi: Jotsadak appears 8 times in the biblical texts, especially in Chronicles and in the book of Haggai. In 1 Chronicles 6:14-15, he is presented in the genealogy of the high priests, situated just before the exile of Judah. In the book of Haggai (1:1, 1:12, 1:14, 2:2, 2:4), Jotsadak is regularly mentioned as the father of the high priest Joshua, during the restoration of the temple under King Darius and Governor Zerubbabel (around 520 B.C.). These passages show that although Jotsadak himself is exiled in Babylon and does not exercise the supreme priesthood, his son Joshua embodies the continuity and restoration of the priestly order after the exile. In Zechariah 6:11, he is also mentioned in relation to the events of the return. The text of 1 Chronicles 6:14 uses the form "Jehotsadak," while Haggai prefers "Jotsadak."
H3087.portee: Jotsadak symbolizes God's faithfulness to His priestly lineage, even in the midst of exile and punishment: although he himself is held captive in Babylon, God restores the priesthood through his son Joshua. His story reminds the reader that exile does not interrupt God's plan, but prepares for a return and restoration. It also shows that serving God can involve the trial of captivity, without invalidating future service. For the believer, Jotsadak is a testimony that God's promises regarding the restoration and continuity of His people remain certain, even when circumstances seem desperate.

sens: King of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat
H3088G.detail: Joram is a king of the kingdom of Judah who reigns during the period of the divided monarchy. He is the son of King Jehoshaphat and succeeds his father on the throne. According to 2 Chronicles 21:5, he is thirty-two years old when he becomes king and reigns for eight years in Jerusalem. His father Jehoshaphat left him the kingdom because he was the firstborn, despite the considerable gifts given to his other sons (2 Chronicles 21:3). Joram marries Athaliah, a woman of harmful influence who leads him to abandon the God of Israel and restore the worship of Baal. During his reign, the Lord raises against him the Philistines and the Arabs (2 Chronicles 21:16). The name means "Jehovah is exalted."
H3088G.origine: The name Joram is an abbreviated form of Jehoram, composed of two elements: Jehovah (the name of God) and the verb meaning "to exalt." It is a theophoric name typical of the kings of Judah, expressing the hope that God will exalt the sovereign and his reign.
H3088G.emploi: Joram appears in the accounts of the Kings and the Chronicles as a king of Judah during the period of the divided monarchy. He is first mentioned in 1 Kings 22:51 as the successor of Jehoshaphat. The Chronicles provide details about his reign: he receives a royal inheritance, establishes his power by eliminating his brothers (2 Chronicles 21:4), and suffers invasions from neighboring peoples. His name also appears in parallel with other kings, as in 2 Kings 8:25 where the reign of Ahaziah is dated in relation to that of Joram of the north (son of Ahab), thus showing how the two kingdoms coexist.
H3088G.portee: Joram illustrates the danger of the influence of marrying someone who does not share faith in God. His wife Athaliah leads him to renounce the Lord and restore the worship of idols, which brings divine judgment upon him and his people. His story shows that even a king from a faithful lineage can stray from God if he is seduced by alliances contrary to faith.

sens: Priest during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah
H3088H.detail: Joram is a priest who serves during the reign of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. He is mentioned in 2 Chronicles 17:8 as sent by the king, alongside other Levites and priests, probably to teach the Law in the cities of Judah. This is one of Jehoshaphat's measures to strengthen obedience to the Word of God in his kingdom.
H3088H.origine: The name Joram means "Jehovah is exalted" (composed of the Hebrew יְהוֹ "Jehovah" and רָם "exalted"). It is a theophoric name bearing the divine name, expressing the belief that God is high and recognized as sovereign. Several important men have borne this name in the history of Israel, including kings of Judah and Israel, as well as priests and Levites.
H3088H.emploi: This Joram appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:8. He is cited among the envoys of Jehoshaphat tasked with a religious educational mission. The context indicates that the king, wanting to consolidate the faith of his people, dispatched competent priests and Levites to teach the Law to the inhabitants of Judah. Joram thus represents the clergy engaged in transmitting divine teaching to the people.

sens: King of Israel, son of Ahab and Jezebel, who reigned twelve years in the 9th century B.C.
King of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat, who reigned eight years and led the nation into idolatry
H3088I.detail: 1. Joram is first the name of a king of the northern kingdom, Israel. Son of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, he reigned twelve years over Israel starting from the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat's reign, king of Judah (2 Kings 3:1). He fought against Hazael, king of Syria, but was wounded at Jezreel (2 Kings 9:15). He was killed by Jehu in the field of Naboth, thus fulfilling Elijah's prophecy against Ahab (2 Kings 9:24). 2. The name also refers to a king of Judah, son of King Jehoshaphat. Although distinct from the king of Israel, he lived at the same time and is mentioned during their joint encounter at Jezreel to confront Jehu (2 Kings 9:21 and 2 Chronicles 22:5). This Joram of Judah reigned eight years and led his people into idolatry, influenced notably by his wife Athaliah.
H3088I.origine: The Hebrew name יְהוֹרָם (Yehoram) means "the Lord is exalted" or "Jehovah is exalted." It is formed from two elements: Yaho (or Yah), an abbreviation of the divine name of God (Yahweh), and ram, which means "exalted" or "elevated." This name expresses faith in God as the supreme and glorious power. A shortened form, Joram (יוֹרָם), was also used.
H3088I.emploi: Joram is the name of two kings contemporary in the 9th century B.C.: one reigns over Israel (the northern kingdom), the other over Judah (the southern kingdom). The texts of the Kings and the Chronicles distinguish them by their lineage: "Joram, son of Ahab" for the king of Israel, and "Joram, son of Jehoshaphat" for the king of Judah. The former is at the center of accounts of conflict with Syria and his death at the hands of Jehu, who executed Elijah's prophetic vengeance. The latter is noted for leading Judah to the worship of Baal under the influence of his wife Athaliah. Both monarchs are involved in the same military campaign and both die shortly thereafter, killed by Jehu.
H3088I.portee: These accounts of Joram, both in Israel and in Judah, illustrate how kings who deviate from the true worship of the Lord and embrace idolatry, or who ignore prophetic warnings, meet a tragic end. They remind the believer that political power does not protect from God's judgment, and that faithfulness to the Lord is the only lasting foundation.

sens: Daughter of King Joram of Judah and Queen Athaliah
Wife of the high priest Jehoiada
Savior of the young king Joash during Athaliah's persecution
H3089.detail: 1. Josheba is a royal princess of Judah, daughter of King Joram and Queen Athaliah. She lives during the time of the divided kingdom, around the 9th century B.C. 2. She marries Jehoiada, the high priest of the temple, making her an influential woman both by her royal birth and by her marriage to the religious leader of the nation. 3. Her most notable act is saving her young nephew Joash, son of King Ahaziah, from the hands of his grandmother Athaliah, who massacres the royal family to seize power. In 2 Kings 11:2, she takes the child from among the princes who are to be killed and hides him with his nurse in the bedroom of the temple for six years, until Jehoiada proclaims him king legally.
H3089.origine: Her name means "Jehovah has sworn" (Jehovah + verb meaning to swear). It expresses a vow or promise from God. She is also called Jehosheba in 2 Chronicles 22:11, a variant of the same name with a slightly different pronunciation.
H3089.emploi: Josheba appears only once by name in 2 Kings 11:2, although 2 Chronicles 22:11 recounts the same event calling her Jehosheba. She is a secondary but decisive figure: without her courage and loyalty, the lineage of David would have been annihilated and Athaliah would have reigned without a legitimate heir. She symbolizes God's providence that preserves the people through a faithful and courageous woman.
H3089.portee: Josheba shows how God uses the most unexpected people to accomplish His purposes. A woman of the court, married to the priest, hides the future king in the temple: this is an act of faith, not armed rebellion. She teaches us that discreet faithfulness and dedication to God's plans can have major historical and spiritual consequences.

sens: Woman of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy, wife of the high priest Jehoiada
H3090.detail: Joschabeath is a princess of Judah, daughter of King Joram and Queen Athaliah. She is best known for her act of courage: at the moment when her mother Athaliah massacres all the heirs to the throne to maintain power, Joschabeath takes her young nephew Joash, son of her brother Ahaziah, and hides him for six years in the temple with his nurse, saving him from certain death (2 Chronicles 22:11). She is married to the high priest Jehoiada, who shares this secret with her. Thanks to their mutual faithfulness, the child survives and will restore the worship of the true God when he is old enough to reign.
H3090.origine: Her name means in Hebrew "the Lord is an oath" or "the Lord is a covenant." It reflects the Israelite faith in God's covenant with the house of David. Joschabeath is also known by the name Jehosheba (a shorter variant of the same name).
H3090.emploi: Joschabeath appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 22:11. This passage describes her at a critical moment in her life: she is presented as the daughter of King Joram, sister of Ahaziah, and wife of the priest Jehoiada. The text emphasizes her decisive role in preserving the Davidic lineage by hiding the young king Joash when Athaliah seeks to destroy all the heirs to the throne. Her act reveals her courage and loyalty to God and her royal house.
H3090.portee: The story of Joschabeath shows how God preserves His promise made to David, even in the darkest circumstances. It reminds us that discreet faithfulness and quiet courage can save lives and change the course of history. She is an example of a believing woman who acts with discernment and risks her own life to protect what matters: the worship of the true God and the continuity of His dynasty.

sens: Military leader and successor of Moses at the head of Israel
Conqueror of Canaan
Trusted man of Moses and warrior
Leader of the people in the desert and the promised land
H3091G.detail:
1. Joshua, son of Nun, is the great military leader who succeeds Moses after his death. From the Exodus, he appears as Moses' faithful warrior: he is the one sent to fight Amalek when Moses raises his hands (Exodus 17:9). He gradually becomes the designated leader to lead Israel into Canaan.

2. His main role is to conquer the promised land. The book of Joshua recounts how he leads the battles to take the cities: he burns Ai and reduces it to ruins (Joshua 8:28), he defeats enemy kings like Horam of Gezer (Joshua 10:33). The walls of Jericho fall under his command (Joshua 6:12).

3. He is first a trusted man of Moses. The book of Exodus shows him always alongside the prophet: he accompanies him on the mountain, he listens to his instructions. Moses lays his hands on him to fill him with wisdom and authority (Numbers 27:18-22).

4. Once Moses is dead, he guides the people across the Jordan and leads them to map out the conquered land (Joshua 18:8). He is a leader who organizes the division of the land and keeps the people in obedience to the Lord.
H3091G.origine: The name Joshua means "the Lord saves" — it comes from the same Hebrew root as "Yeshoua" (Jesus in Greek). It is a prophetic name that proclaims that it is God Himself who saves His people, not the military strength of the leader. Joshua is first called Hoshea (Numbers 13:8), a shorter name, before Moses renames him Joshua — this name change marks his new vocation. Later, in the Greek Old Testament, this same name appears in the form "Jeshua" (Nehemiah 8:17).
H3091G.emploi: Joshua appears 185 times in the Bible. First in Exodus and Numbers, where he is the servant and faithful warrior of Moses alongside whom he grows. In Deuteronomy, Moses explicitly prepares him to take over (Deuteronomy 31:23). Then, starting from the book that bears his name (Joshua), he becomes the main narrator: we follow his military decisions, his consultations with God, his management of lands and peoples. His role evolves: he goes from fighter to organizer and judge of the people. The acts of Joshua show that he always acts according to the Lord's command, confirming that it is God alone who gives victory.
H3091G.portee: Joshua embodies the leader who trusts God rather than his own strength. His victories do not come from clever tactics but from obedience and faith: he walks around Jericho at the command of the Lord, he waits for His orders before each battle. His example shows that conquering our "promised lands" — realizing what God calls us to do — requires not natural courage, but listening and submission to divine will. Joshua remains for Christians a model of faith-based leadership.

sens: Inhabitant of Beth-Shemesh whose field welcomed the Ark of the Covenant
H3091H.detail: 1. Joshua is an ordinary man from the city of Beth-Shemesh. When the Philistines returned the Ark of the Lord after keeping it, it stopped in his field (1 Samuel 6:14). This place then becomes a memorable place of worship where the cows that pulled the sacred cart were sacrificed.
H3091H.origine: The name Joshua means "the Lord is salvation" in Hebrew. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God within it. Although several important figures in Israel bore this name — notably the successor of Moses — this Joshua is a simple resident of Beth-Shemesh, known only for the miraculous event that occurred on his land.
H3091H.emploi: Joshua is mentioned twice in the book of 1 Samuel, in verses 6:14 and 6:18, always in relation to the return of the Ark of the Lord. He is neither a leader nor a major biblical figure: he is a landowner whose name has been preserved in sacred history because his field became a place of testimony to God's power and holiness. The texts emphasize that the great stone where the Ark was placed "is still today" in his field, indicating that the site had become a visible memorial.

sens: Governor of Jerusalem under King Josiah
H3091I.detail: 1. Joshua is a civil officer who governs Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah (circa 640-609 B.C.). He holds an important administrative position in the capital of the kingdom of Judah. The only mention of him in the Bible is found in 2 Kings 23:8, where he is cited as responsible for a city gate that bears his name — "the gate of Joshua."
H3091I.origine: The name Joshua means "the Lord is salvation" or "the Lord saves" in Hebrew (from Yah, "the Lord," and shûa, "to save"). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name. This name has been borne by several important figures in Israel's history, including the successor of Moses in the conquest of Canaan, but this Joshua is a simple officer from the seventh century B.C., much later.
H3091I.emploi: This Joshua is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 23:8. He appears in the context of the religious reforms of King Josiah, who destroys the high places and cleanses the worship of Judah. A gate of Jerusalem bears his name, indicating his rank and administrative importance at the time. His exact role is not detailed: the Bible simply cites him as an official whose name is attached to one of the gates of the city.

sens: High priest during the time of the temple restoration, after the Babylonian exile
H3091J.detail: 1. Joshua is the high priest who works with the governor Zerubbabel on the reconstruction of the temple after the return from exile (Haggai 1:1). He receives a direct word from God through the prophet Haggai and is encouraged to be strong to fulfill this sacred mission (Haggai 2:4).
H3091J.origine: The name "Joshua" (יְהוֹשׁוּעַ in Hebrew) means "the Lord is salvation." It is the same name as that of the famous successor of Moses who conquered Canaan, but here it is borne by a different character, a priest from the time of the return from exile. The root expresses the deliverance and salvation that God brings.
H3091J.emploi: Joshua, son of Jehozadak, is mentioned exclusively in the prophecies of Haggai and Zechariah, dating from the return from exile in Babylon (around 520 B.C.). He appears as the high priest in charge of directing the reconstruction of the temple alongside Zerubbabel, the civil governor. The prophecies describe his spiritual and messianic role: in Zechariah 3, he is presented before the angel of the Lord, accused by Satan, but justified by God; his filthy garments are removed and replaced with pure garments, symbolizing the spiritual restoration of the people. Zechariah 6:11 reports that two crowns are placed on his head, linking him to the messianic figure.
H3091J.portee: The life of Joshua teaches the believer that God restores and justifies His people despite accusation and condemnation. His role in the reconstruction of the temple shows how God uses His servants to build His work and establish worship. His purification and prophetic crowning place him in the messianic lineage, reminding that ultimate salvation comes from God alone.

sens: Son of Ahilud, archivist at the court of King David and then Solomon
H3092G.detail: Jehoshaphat is a high-ranking official in Jerusalem during the reign of David and his son Solomon. He bears the title of archivist (or "secretary"), meaning he is responsible for the official documents and administrative affairs of the kingdom. His four appearances in Scripture always show him in this same role, alongside the king, working with great figures like Joab who commands the army (2 Samuel 8:16; 1 Kings 4:3). He is a trusted man, holding one of the most important positions in the state.
H3092G.origine: His name, Jehoshaphat, comes from the Hebrew "Jehovah has judged." It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God Himself (Jehovah) and expresses a religious conviction. Jehoshaphat's father, Ahilud, is known only through this famous son, and this recurring mention of the lineage shows his importance.
H3092G.emploi: Jehoshaphat appears four times in the Bible, always in the same role and in the same place: secretary or archivist at the royal court. The four occurrences are found in 2 Samuel 8:16, 2 Samuel 20:24, 1 Kings 4:3, and 1 Chronicles 18:15. He is mentioned under David and Solomon, which attests to a long administrative career. Each mention designates him by the same title and establishes his precise identity and stability in the role through his kinship with Ahilud. Although not detailed by Scripture, he is among the seven or eight high officials of the kingdom.

sens: High-ranking officer at the court of King Solomon
Hebrew name meaning "the Lord has judged"
H3092H.detail:
1. Jehoshaphat is one of the twelve commissioners that Solomon established to provide for the daily needs of his royal household. He represents the class of high-ranking administrators who managed Solomon's prosperous kingdom. He is the son of Paruah and is assigned to the region of Issachar, one of the twelve districts into which Solomon divided the kingdom to facilitate administration and tax collection (1 Kings 4:17).
2. His Hebrew name literally means "the Lord has judged," composed of two elements: "Yah" (Lord) and "shaphat" (to judge or exercise authority). This name reminds us that even earthly authorities act under the watch of God.
H3092H.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew root שׁפט (shaphat) which means "to judge" or "to govern." The first part, יְהוֹ (Yeho), is a short form of the divine name Jehovah (the Lord). Characters bearing this same name appear elsewhere in Israel's history: notably the king of Judah Jehoshaphat, who is much more famous and reigned about a century after this administrative Jehoshaphat. The name conveys the idea that God is the supreme authority who judges and governs all peoples.
H3092H.emploi: Jehoshaphat son of Paruah appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Kings 4:17, where he is listed as one of the twelve officers commissioned to supply and maintain Solomon's royal palace. This context shows the sophisticated administrative organization of Solomon's reign at the peak of political and economic prosperity of the united kingdom of Israel. This brief mention illustrates the governmental structure of Israel under Solomon, where the charge was distributed among twelve regions of Israel.
H3092H.portee: This character reminds us that God works through men in governmental and administrative structures. A name like Jehoshaphat ("the Lord has judged") placed at the head of a region symbolizes the conviction that no human authority escapes God's judgment. Even those who manage temporal affairs operate within the order established by the Lord.

sens: King of Judah, son of Asa, who reigned for about 25 years
One of the best and most pious kings of Judah, prosperous and esteemed
Symbolic figure of a valley near Jerusalem, place of final judgment
H3092I.detail:
1. Jehoshaphat is a king of the tribe of Judah who succeeds his father Asa. He reigns during the period of the divided monarchy, for about 25 years according to 1 Kings 22:42, and is first mentioned in 1 Kings 15:24 when he comes to power. He is a central figure in the accounts of the Kings and Chronicles.

2. Jehoshaphat is distinguished by his piety and justice. He seeks the prophets of the Lord (2 Kings 3:11: "Is there not here a prophet of the Lord, that we may inquire of the Lord through him?"); builds castles and fortified cities (2 Chronicles 17:12); and strengthens his kingdom through the fear of God. Despite some diplomatic missteps, he remains a just king who consults the Lord.

3. Symbolically, the valley of Jehoshaphat is associated with God's final divine judgment on the nations, located near Jerusalem between the city and the Mount of Olives, crossed by the Kidron. His name itself means "the Lord has judged," making it a highly symbolic place in biblical theology.
H3092I.origine: The name Jehoshaphat literally means "the Lord has judged" (יְהוֹשָׁפָט: Yaho = the Lord, shapat = he has judged). It comes from the Hebrew root שׁפט (shaphat), which denotes judgment, and from the divine name יְהוָה (Yahweh). This name expresses the conviction that the Lord exercises His sovereign judgment. The valley of Jehoshaphat likely derives its symbolic name from this theological significance: the place where God will judge the nations.
H3092I.emploi: Jehoshaphat appears 66 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the Kings and Chronicles. The main narrative spans from 1 Kings 15:24 to 2 Kings 8:16, covering his accession to the throne, his reign of religious reforms, and his military campaigns. The Chronicles (particularly chapters 17-20) enrich the portrait by highlighting his efforts in religious teaching and his miraculous victory against an enemy coalition in 2 Chronicles 20. He also appears in genealogies (1 Chronicles 3:10) as the father of Jehoram. His name is also symbolically applied to a valley near Jerusalem, the scene of eschatological judgment.
H3092I.portee: Jehoshaphat embodies the king who sincerely seeks God and prospers through his piety and justice. His example shows that consulting the word of the Lord and fearing God produces peace and stability (2 Chronicles 19:1: "Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, returned in peace to his house"). For the Christian reader, the valley of Jehoshaphat reminds us that God ultimately judges all nations according to His justice, a truth that is a source of hope for believers and a warning for the rebellious.

sens: Man of Northern Israel, father of King Jehu
H3092J.detail: This name refers to Josaphat, son of Nimshi, father of the future king Jehu of the Northern Kingdom of Israel. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy, after the separation between Israel and Judah. Although not well-known, he is mentioned because he is the ancestor of an important dynasty: his son Jehu will establish a new royal lineage in Northern Israel.
H3092J.origine: The name Josaphat means "The Lord has judged" in Hebrew (from "Yah," divine name, and "shaphat," to judge). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, common among the royalty and nobility of Israel.
H3092J.emploi: Josaphat appears twice in the Segond account (2 Kings 9:2 and 9:14), always referred to as the father of Jehu. He is mentioned at the moment when the prophet Elisha sends a messenger to bring Jehu up from among his brothers to make him king. His importance lies entirely in his genealogical role: he is the link in the chain that leads to King Jehu, who will profoundly mark the history of Northern Israel.

sens: Valley near Jerusalem, site of the final judgment of the nations
Biblical symbol of God's judgment on all peoples
H3092K.detail:
1. Josaphat is a valley located near Jerusalem, probably the deep ravine that separates the city from the Mount of Olives, through which the Kidron flowed. It is a real geographical place, identifiable on the ground.
2. In the prophecy of the prophet Joel, this valley becomes the symbol of the final judgment: God will gather all nations there to judge them concerning the people of Israel and the land that God has given them (Joel 3:2 and 3:12). This is not just a local event, but the moment when God will settle accounts with all the nations of the world.
H3092K.origine: The name Josaphat means "the Lord has judged": it combines two Hebrew elements, Yah ("the Lord") and Shaphat ("he has judged"). This prophetic name is particularly appropriate for designating the site of the final judgment, as the verb "to judge" is at the very heart of the name.
