Although it is primarily an authentic geographical place, the Bible makes it a symbolic name loaded with theological meaning.
H3092K.emploi: Josaphat appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of the prophet Joel (Joel 3:2 and 3:12), where it specifically refers to a valley. These two verses constitute a coherent prophecy: God will gather the nations in the valley of Josaphat to enter into judgment with them. The prophet uses this name of a real valley as the symbolic framework for the final judgment, transforming a geographical landmark into the theater of God's final action.
H3092K.portee: For the Christian reader, Josaphat serves as a reminder that God will one day judge all nations and all peoples with justice. This judgment is not arbitrary: it concerns how the nations have treated the people of God and respected His land. This prophecy invites the believer to place all trust in God, who will bring justice and defend His own.

sens: One who believes themselves superior to others and manifests it through their attitude or words
One who acts with arrogance, without humility or respect
One who refuses to submit or take others into account
H3093.detail:
1. The proud person is one who glorifies themselves, believing they are better and greater than others. In Proverbs 21:24, this man "is called a scoffer": he belittles others to elevate himself, speaking with boldness and disdain.
2. It is a way of life: the proud person acts "with the fury of arrogance" (Proverbs 21:24), showing through all their actions their contempt for limits and wisdom. They cannot bear correction or counsel.
3. On a spiritual level, it is to refuse to recognize an authority above oneself, whether that of God or that of men. In Habakkuk 2:5, the proud person "enlarges his mouth like the grave": their insatiable desire for conquest and power drives them to swallow nations, never being satisfied.
H3093.origine: The Hebrew word יָהִיר comes from a root that expresses the idea of rising up, elevating oneself. It is the image of one who stands above others, who exalts themselves. In Hebrew, this term belongs to the same family as other words describing elevation or arrogance, as pride is literally this act of placing oneself above.
H3093.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always to depict a despicable character. In Proverbs 21:24, it qualifies one who acts as a scoffer, losing wisdom through their arrogance. In Habakkuk 2:5, it depicts the Babylonian empire intoxicated with conquests: the proud person does not know when to stop, they consume everything, nations and peoples. In both cases, the Bible shows that this pride leads to downfall, whether through ridicule or through God's judgment.
H3093.portee: Pride is presented in these verses not as mere self-esteem, but as a destructive force that blinds the one afflicted by it and ruins their relationship with others and with God. Recognizing one's own pride within oneself is a step towards humility, the fruit of biblical wisdom.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
Father of Ziph, Zipha, Thirja, and Asareel
H3094G.detail:
1. Jehalléleel is a man from the tribe of Judah, mentioned in the genealogies during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between north and south. He appears in the list of descendants of Caleb, placing him in the lineage of those who received a portion of the promised land.
2. He is primarily identified as the father of four children: Ziph, Zipha, Thirja, and Asareel (see 1 Chronicles 4:16). This genealogical mention shows his role in the transmission of the Judean lineage through generations.
H3094G.origine: The name Jehalléleel means "God is praised" or "let God be praised." It is composed of the divine element "Yah" (God) and the verb "hallel" (to praise, to celebrate), expressing an acclamation of praise directed to the Lord. This type of theophoric name was common in Israel and revealed the religious orientation of the family that bore it.
H3094G.emploi: Jehalléleel appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:16. He is listed in the genealogy of Judah, specifically among the descendants of Caleb, during the period of the divided monarchy (after the schism between Israel and Judah). The Bible designates him solely by his role as the father of his children, without providing further details about his life or deeds. This brief genealogical mention indicates that he was an important link in the genealogical chain of God's people.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Merari during the time of King Hezekiah
Father of Azaria
H3094H.detail: Jehalléleel is a Levite from the lineage of Merari who lived during the time of King Hezekiah of Judah (8th century B.C.). He is mentioned in 2 Chronicles 29:12 as the father of Azaria, one of the Levites who rose up to purify the temple during the religious reforms led by Hezekiah. His name means "God is praised" or "God is celebrated," reflecting the importance of praise in the temple worship of which he was responsible.
H3094H.origine: The name Jehalléleel is formed from two Hebrew elements: "Yah" (God) and "hallel" (to praise, to celebrate), hence the meaning "God is praised." This root "hallel" is the same found in the word "Hallelujah" (praise the Lord) that we know well. The name thus expresses trust in God and the call to praise Him, central values in the worship life of Israel.
H3094H.emploi: Jehalléleel appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 29:12. He is presented as one of the Levites of the tribe of Merari who responded to King Hezekiah's call to participate in the restoration and purification of the temple in Jerusalem. His son Azaria is also mentioned on this occasion, showing that religious responsibility was passed from father to son within the Levitical tribe.

sens: Very hard and brilliant precious stone, used in jewelry
Gem of the Israelite priestly garment
Symbol of divine beauty and wealth
H3095.detail:
1. The Hebrew word designates an extremely hard and durable precious stone, renowned for its brilliance. Among the stones known in antiquity, it could refer to the diamond itself or another very hard stone like onyx or jasper. The Segond translation chose "diamond" to convey this stone of exceptional hardness (Exodus 28:18).

2. This stone appears in the description of the breastplate of the Israelite high priest, alongside sapphire, carbuncle, emerald, and onyx — each stone symbolizing one of the twelve tribes of Israel (Exodus 39:11).

3. In the vision of the prophet Ezekiel, the king of Tyre is described as covered with this stone among other jewels, in the context of original beauty and splendor created by God (Ezekiel 28:13). The enumeration of precious stones evokes divine magnificence and honor.
H3095.origine: The Hebrew word יַהֲלֹם comes from a root expressing the idea of hardness and resistance. The literal meaning of the word is a stone of great hardness — which made it an exceptionally valuable stone in antiquity. The Segond consistently translates this word as "diamond," the hardest and most precious gem known.
H3095.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. Two occurrences are found in the description of the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:18 and 39:11), where it designates one of the twelve precious stones set in the priestly garment. The third occurrence (Ezekiel 28:13) places this stone among the ornaments of the king of Tyre on the day of his creation, in a vision where the abundance of jewels symbolizes the splendor and divine wealth he was granted before his fall.
H3095.portee: This stone reminds the believer that Israel's worship before God was surrounded by splendor and beauty — not out of vanity, but to reflect God's glory. It also invites meditation on the incomparable value of what comes from God and recognizes that all beauty and wealth come from His creative act.

sens: City in the territory of Reuben, east of the Jordan
H3096.detail: Jahats is a city located in the territory of the tribe of Reuben, east of the Jordan, in the land of Transjordan. It is primarily known as the site of the battle between Israel and Sihon, the king of the Amorites: Sihon refused passage to Israel and came to fight at Jahats, where he was defeated (Numbers 21:23; Deuteronomy 2:32; Judges 11:20). Later, after the conquest, Jahats became one of the Levitical cities assigned to the sons of Kohath, descendants of Levi (Joshua 21:36; 1 Chronicles 6:78). It is also mentioned in prophecies against Moab (Isaiah 15:4; Jeremiah 48:21, 34), suggesting its proximity to the Moabite territory. The etymology of the name suggests a land "trampled" or "trod upon," which fits a battlefield.
H3096.origine: The name Jahats comes from the Hebrew verb meaning "to tread, to trample." It thus evokes the image of a place where one walks, where movements unfold — a natural image for a battlefield or a crossroads. The name may also reflect the nature of the terrain or the history of the place, marked by the passage of caravans and armies.
H3096.emploi: Jahats appears nine times in the Bible, primarily in the account of Israel's victory over Sihon (Numbers 21:23; Deuteronomy 2:32; Judges 11:20), where it serves as a geographical landmark to locate this decisive battle. It is then mentioned in the list of cities allocated to the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13:18) and in the list of Levitical cities (Joshua 21:36; 1 Chronicles 6:78). The prophet Isaiah and Jeremiah refer to it in oracles addressed to Moab, placing it on the routes of lamentations and flights (Isaiah 15:4; Jeremiah 48:21, 34). These usages show that Jahats was a well-known and strategically important city.

sens: Commander-in-chief of King David's army
Political figure and strategist at the royal court
Person of great influence and power with the king
H3097G.detail:
1. Joab is primarily the general who leads David's armies. He appears alongside David during the years of fleeing from Saul (1 Samuel 26:6) and officially becomes commander of the army under David's reign (2 Samuel 8:16). He leads battles, organizes troops, and reports victories to the king.

2. Beyond his military role, Joab is an influential statesman. He intervenes in royal family matters: he is the one who arranges Absalom's return to David (2 Samuel 14:1-23), demonstrating his political skill and direct access to the king's power. David recognizes him as someone wise (2 Samuel 14:20).

3. Joab also embodies the man of power who sometimes acts against the king's orders to serve what he believes to be the interest of the kingdom, particularly during the battles against Absalom (2 Samuel 18:2-15), revealing tensions between royal authority and military command.
H3097G.origine: The name Joab means "Yahweh is father" in Hebrew. Joab is the son of Zeruiah, David's sister, making him a close relative of the royal family. He has two brothers: Abishai and Asahel (1 Chronicles 2:16). His status as a relative of the king explains his exceptional position with David.
H3097G.emploi: Joab appears more than 140 times in the books of Samuel and Chronicles, making him one of the most prominent military figures in the Old Testament. His story spans from the time of David's flight from Saul to David's final days. He is first seen as a valiant warrior alongside Abishai (2 Samuel 2:12-32), then as commander-in-chief leading major campaigns against the Ammonites and Arameans (2 Samuel 10:7-14, 12:26-31). He plays a key role in the affair of Uriah: David orders him to place Uriah at the forefront of the battle to have him killed (2 Samuel 11:14-25). Joab also becomes a major political actor, intervening in dynastic conflicts around the throne, notably by bringing back Absalom (2 Samuel 14) and killing him despite David's order (2 Samuel 18).
H3097G.portee: Joab illustrates how political and military power can become an ambiguous force in the history of the kingdom. Loyal to David, he often acts ruthlessly and independently, reminding us that the earthly success of the king does not solely depend on his piety, but also on men of war willing to do what is necessary. His story invites the reader to reflect on the limits of human power and the consequences of the blend between political ambition and loyalty.

sens: A man from the tribe of Judah mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:14
Son of Serajah in the genealogy of Judah
Ancestor of the inhabitants of the valley of workers
H3097H.detail: 1. Joab is a man from the tribe of Judah, cited in the genealogical list of the book of Chronicles. His name means "The Eternal is father," which expresses a confession of faith in God. 2. He is the son of Serajah, who is himself a descendant of Kenaz, placing him within a precise genealogical lineage of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:14). 3. Joab is presented as the founder or ancestor of the valley of workers: this place is named after him and the community of artisans who lived there, suggesting that he was a figure of leadership or a founder capable of organizing a community of workers.
H3097H.origine: The name Joab comes from two Hebrew words: "Yo" (the Eternal) and "Ab" (father), literally meaning "the father is the Eternal" or "the Eternal is father." This type of theophoric name expressed the piety of Hebrew parents and their acknowledgment of God.
H3097H.emploi: Joab appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:14, in the context of the genealogies of the tribe of Judah. He is a minor character in the genealogical records, different from the famous Joab, David's general, who is mentioned much more frequently in the books of Samuel and Kings. This Joab belongs to a later time and is primarily known as the ancestor of a community of artisans established in a region called the valley of workers.

sens: Jewish family returned from exile to Jerusalem
H3097I.detail: 1. Joab refers here to a family (or clan) of Judeans who participated in the return from exile to Jerusalem after the destruction of the Temple in 586 B.C. It is an important group as it includes more than 2,800 people according to the two lists of return (Ezra 2:6 and Nehemiah 7:11).
H3097I.origine: The name Joab literally means "The Lord is father" (Jehovah is father). In the Old Testament, this name is first made famous as that of the formidable general in chief of King David's army, the son of Zeruiah. However, the provided usages refer to a family bearing this name, likely descended from a namesake ancestor or linked to this patronymic for a genealogical reason that is lost.
H3097I.emploi: The only two biblical occurrences of this Joab are found in the lists of families that returned from Babylon after the exile (Ezra 2:6 and Nehemiah 7:11). These two passages, nearly identical, record "the sons of Pachath-Moab, the sons of Joshua and Joab" numbering 2,812 or 2,818 according to the version. This family group belonged to the tribe of Judah and was part of the larger movement to restore Jerusalem during the times of Zerubbabel and Ezra.

sens: Military leader in the service of King David
Name meaning "The Lord is father"
H3097J.detail:
1. Joab is the son of Zeruiah, David's sister, and he becomes the general in chief of King David's royal army. He plays a crucial military role in establishing the kingdom of Israel.
2. His Hebrew name literally means "The Lord is father" (a combination of "Yo" for the Lord and "Ab" for father), reflecting his family's faith in God as a protective father.
H3097J.origine: The name Joab is composed of two Hebrew elements: the abbreviated divine name "Yo" (the Lord) and "ab" which means "father." It is a theophoric name, that is, a name that incorporates the name of God, a common practice in ancient Israel to express the family's relationship to God. The root "ab" (father) evokes divine protection and authority.
H3097J.emploi: Joab is one of the most important military figures in the kingdom under David. Being the son of David's sister, he commands the king's armies and plays a decisive role in the wars to establish the kingdom. The passage in Ezra 8:9 mentions a family bearing the name Joab that returns from exile in Babylon: descendants of this same Joab or a family that bears his name join the restored community of Judah. This mention attests to the lasting importance of the name and lineage in Israel's memory.

sens: Son of Asaph, royal scribe of King Hezekiah in the 8th century B.C.
H3098G.detail: Joach is an officer of the royal court of Judah under King Hezekiah. His title of scribe (one who keeps documents and archives) makes him a trusted man, responsible for managing the administrative affairs of the kingdom. He appears alongside Eliakim and Shebna during the embassy to Rabshakeh, the Assyrian general (2 Kings 18:18). Joach participates in these delicate negotiations, asking that the enemy speak in Aramaic rather than Hebrew so that the people on the wall do not understand the threats (2 Kings 18:26). After the failure of the talks, he returns to King Hezekiah, tearing his clothes, a gesture of mourning or dismay, to report the threatening words of the Assyrian envoy (2 Kings 18:37).
H3098G.origine: The name Joach means "The Lord is brother" (from Hebrew Yah, "the Lord," and ach, "brother"). This patronymic expresses the idea that God is a protective brother for the one who bears it. Joach is the son of Asaph, a name that evokes the lineage of musicians and scribes serving in the Temple worship.
H3098G.emploi: Joach is mentioned exclusively in the parallel accounts of the Assyrian crisis under Hezekiah (2 Kings 18 and Isaiah 36). He fulfills the role of royal scribe, a title that indicates his importance in the administration of the kingdom. All his mentions show him associated with two other officials, Eliakim and Shebna, forming an official delegation. The six mentions always describe him in contexts of national importance: diplomatic negotiations with an enemy power and reports to the king. His role underscores the administrative order of the court of Judah in the face of the Assyrian threat.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, son of Zimmah and father of Iddo
Musician or temple servant during the divided monarchy
H3098H.detail:
1. Joach is a Levite mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Zimmah. He appears in the list of ancestors of the temple musicians of Israel, in the lineage of the children of Levi assigned to the service of worship (1 Chronicles 6:21).
2. During the divided monarchy, Joach is among those Levites whose function was to serve in the temple and participate in the worship of Israel, inserted into the priestly genealogies that mark the importance of their lineage.
H3098H.origine: The name Joach means "Jehovah is brother" in Hebrew, composed of Jah (God) and an element meaning "brother." It is a theophoric name, common in Levitical families, which expresses the proximity of the clan to God and its covenant with the people.
H3098H.emploi: Joach appears only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 6:21, where he is listed in the genealogy of the Gershonite Levites. Several characters bear this name in Scripture (a son of Asaph, a Korahite, a chronicler of King Josiah), but the mention provided here specifically refers to the son of Zimmah in the Levitical lineage of the temple.

sens: Son of Obed-Edom, temple porter during the reign of King David
H3098I.detail: Joach is a Levite of the tribe of Levi, son of Obed-Edom. He serves as a porter in the temple during the reign of King David (around 1000 B.C.). He is the third son listed among the children of Obed-Edom in 1 Chronicles 26:4, after Shemaiah and Jozabad. As a porter, he was responsible for guarding the temple entrance and controlling access for people and offerings.
H3098I.origine: The name Joach is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Yo" (abbreviation of the divine name "Yahweh") and "ach" ("brother"). It thus means "Yahweh is brother" or "the Lord is my brother." This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common among Levitical families, expressing the covenant relationship with the God of Israel.
H3098I.emploi: Joach appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:4, in the list of the sons of Obed-Edom established by the chronicler. This genealogical list enumerates the children of Obed-Edom, an important porter of the temple under David. Joach is presented as the third son, which likely also indicates his order of succession in the porter functions. His insertion in this genealogical succession shows that he was an officially recognized Levite in the temple records.
H3098I.portee: Joach illustrates how God provided for the guarding of His temple by entrusting this responsibility to entire families of Levites. His appearance in the biblical genealogies reminds us that even the simplest religious services—guarding a door—are recognized and recorded by God. The theophoric name that Joach bears also expresses the deep conviction of Levitical families: the Lord is with those who serve Him faithfully, even in modest tasks.

sens: Son of Joachaz and secretary of King Josiah
H3098J.detail: Joach is a minor character mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Joachaz and served as the archivist (or secretary) to King Josiah of Judah. In 2 Chronicles 34:8, the king sends him with other officials to oversee the repairs of the temple of the Lord after the period of religious purification he led.
H3098J.origine: The name Joach means "the Lord is brother." It was borne by several figures in the history of Israel at different times: a son of Asaph (chronicler of King Hezekiah), a Gershonite Levite, a porter during the time of David, and this one who lived under Josiah. It is a typical theophoric name of the Old Testament, meaning it contains the divine name.
H3098J.emploi: Joach appears only once in the Scriptures, in 2 Chronicles 34:8. He is presented as the archivist (or royal secretary) of King Josiah of Judah. His administrative role places him among the high officials of the royal palace. The king charges him, along with other officials, to lead the restoration work of the temple, which shows that he enjoyed royal trust and had authority over these important religious projects.

sens: Son of Zimma, Levite of the Gershonite line
H3098K.detail: Joach is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, during a religious reform under King Hezekiah. He belongs to the tribe of Levi, specifically to the branch of the Gershonites (descendants of Gershon, son of Levi). His father is Zimma. He rises up with other Levites to participate in the purification of the temple and the restoration of divine worship under the reign of King Hezekiah, around 715 B.C. (2 Chronicles 29:12).
H3098K.origine: The name Joach means "Jehovah is brother" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: the divine name YHWH (Jehovah) and the root expressing brotherhood. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common among the Israelites and reflected the covenant relationship between God and His people.
H3098K.emploi: Joach is mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 29:12. He appears in the list of Levites who rose up during the religious reform of King Hezekiah, probably in the 8th century B.C. His appearance underscores the importance of the role of Levites in the restoration of temple worship. Joach represents a generation of temple servants involved in renewing the religious life of Israel.

sens: Levite of the Gershonite tribe, son of Zimma
H3098L.detail: 1. Joach is a Levite belonging to the family of the Gershonites (one of the three major families of Levi). He is the son of Zimma. In 2 Chronicles 29:12, he is named among the Levites whom King Hezekiah calls to purify the temple, right after Machath and Joel. His sudden appearance in this important role shows that he was a man of responsibility among the Levites of his time.
H3098L.origine: The name Joach means "Yahweh is brother." It is composed of "Yo" (Yahweh) and "ach" (brother), which evokes the idea of divine brotherly protection. In the Bible, several Joach bear this same name: a chronicler of King Hezekiah, another of King Josiah, and others, indicating that this name was common among Levites and worship officials. All these Joach share the conviction that God is the protective brother of His people.
H3098L.emploi: Joach appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 29:12, during the account of the purification of the temple under King Hezekiah (around 715 B.C.). He is cited among the Levites chosen by the king to carry out this holy task: to clean the vessels of the sanctuary, remove impurities, and restore legitimate worship. His name alongside that of other prominent Levites suggests that he was a respected figure in the Levitical hierarchy. This is a concrete example of the responsibility that Levites bore in the religious life of Israel.
H3098L.portee: Joach reminds us that God calls and raises faithful servants for His worship, even when His temple has been profaned or neglected. His involvement in the restoration of the temple illustrates how believers can participate in spiritual renewal by responding to the call of those who lead them. It is also a testimony to the continuity of divine service through the generations.

sens: Father of Joach, scribe during the time of King Josiah
H3099G.detail: Joachaz is a man living at the time of the divided monarchy, father of Joach. He is mentioned only once in the Bible: in 2 Chronicles 34:8, where his son Joach is designated as the archivist (the scribe in charge of the archives) whom King Josiah sent to repair the Temple.
H3099G.origine: The name Joachaz means "the Lord has seized" or "the Lord has taken": it is composed of the contracted form of the divine name (Jo-) and the verb "to seize, to take." It is a typical profession of faith of the Hebrew people, expressing that God has cared for this child from birth.
H3099G.emploi: Joachaz appears only once in the Scriptures, in 2 Chronicles 34:8. He is simply the father of the scribe Joach, mentioned as his patronymic during the repair of the Temple under Josiah in the 7th century B.C. He represents a generation of temple servants about whom we know little.

sens: King of Israel in the 9th century B.C., son of Jehu
Father of Joash
H3099H.detail:
1. Joachaz was a king of the Northern Kingdom (Israel) during the time of the divided monarchy. He reigns after his father Jehu and before his son Joash. The Bible notably mentions him in 2 Kings 14:1, where he is referred to as "Joachaz, king of Israel," the father of King Joash.
2. His name means "The Lord has seized," expressing God's grace. Joachaz is also sometimes called Jehoahaz — two spellings for the same king.
H3099H.origine: The name Joachaz literally means "The Lord has seized" (from Yah, a short form of the divine name, and achaz, to seize or take). It is an abbreviated form of Jehoahaz. The Bible uses several spellings for this same character, reflecting variations in the transliteration of ancient Hebrew.
H3099H.emploi: Joachaz is a king of the Northern Kingdom mentioned in the history of the kings of Israel during the period of the divided monarchy (9th-8th centuries B.C.). Son of Jehu and father of Joash, he is part of the dynastic line of Jehu. The reference in 2 Kings 14:1 cites him to establish the chronology of his son Joash's reign in the context of the parallel reign of King Amaziah of Judah.

sens: King of Judah in the 7th century B.C.
Son of King Josiah
Brother of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah
H3099I.detail:
1. Joachaz was a king of Judah who reigned only three months, shortly after the death of his father Josiah. He was twenty-three years old when he became king (2 Chronicles 36:2). His very short reign was interrupted by the intervention of Pharaoh Necho of Egypt, who deposed him and took him captive to Egypt (2 Chronicles 36:4).

2. Joachaz was the son of King Josiah and Hamutal. He had several brothers, including Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, who both reigned after him over Judah. His half-brother Jehoiakim was actually placed on the throne in his place by Pharaoh Necho (2 Chronicles 36:4).
H3099I.origine: The name Joachaz comes from Hebrew and means "The Lord has seized" or "The Lord has taken firmly." It is composed of the divine name Yah (Jehovah) and the verb "to seize." It is a theophoric name, meaning it bears the name of God, which was common among the kings of Judah. Another form of the same name, longer, is Jehoahaz.
H3099I.emploi: Joachaz appears only twice in the Bible, both in 2 Chronicles 36, verses 2 and 4. These passages constitute the complete historical account of his reign: his ascension at twenty-three years old, his short reign of three months, and his deposition and deportation by Pharaoh Necho of Egypt. His reign marks one of the last stages of Judah's independence before increasing foreign domination and ultimately the Babylonian exile. It is an example of the fragility of the kingdom of Judah during this troubled time at the end of the divided monarchy.
H3099I.portee: The story of Joachaz reminds the reader that even the kings of Israel and Judah, despite their apparent power, remained under the sovereign control of God. His short reign illustrates how God disciplined His unfaithful people through foreign powers. It is a lesson in humility for the believer: human power is fragile and fleeting.
